selection_reason: With no prior experiments, the primary uncertainty is whether RNA data alone carries sufficient signal for the task and what baseline performance looks like. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration: it uses a standard linear encoder (PCA), a single profile, and no image or fusion components, so any observed performance can be cleanly attributed to the raw RNA signal with minimal processing. Establishing this baseline is essential before evaluating more complex choices (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, or fusion strategies), because it provides the reference against which all subsequent design decisions—encoder choice, profile aggregation, modality combination, and fusion method—can be measured. It is the highest-information first experiment under a limited budget because it anchors the entire comparison space with minimal confounding variables.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit over the RNA-only baseline. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal, clean extension of config_001: it keeps the same RNA encoder and profile setting while introducing the image modality with the most standard encoder (ResNet-50) and the simplest fusion (concat). If accuracy improves meaningfully, it confirms the multimodal direction is worth further exploration (better encoders, multiprofile, weighted fusion). If it does not improve, it tells us the image modality adds little on top of this RNA representation, allowing us to redirect budget toward RNA-only improvements (better encoders, multiprofile aggregation). This single experiment thus resolves the highest-leverage design question under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA, single) scored 0.4849 acc and config_016 (multimodal, PCA+ResNet50, single, concat) scored 0.5266 acc, a ~4-point gain. However, with only two experiments we cannot attribute this gain: it could come from the image modality alone, from genuine cross-modal synergy, or a mix. Uncertainty: We lack the image-only baseline (ResNet50, single profile) to decompose the multimodal result. Question tested: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly measures how much of the 0.5266 is attributable to image features versus RNA features. Why best next step: This single experiment is the highest-information-value test under the limited budget—it tells us whether the fusion is truly additive (image alone << 0.5266) or whether RNA contributes little (image alone ≈ 0.5266). The answer reshapes every subsequent decision: if image dominates, we prioritize image-encoder and aggregation choices; if synergy is real, we invest in fusion strategies and RNA-encoder quality. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the core design question of this study.

Evidence: The current best is config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) at 52.7% acc, modestly above RNA-only (48.5%) and far above image-only (20.8%). All three completed experiments use singleprofile, leaving the multiprofile dimension entirely unexplored. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) improve the multimodal model over the single-profile baseline, while keeping the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and concat fusion? Why this experiment: config_018 is the minimal logical extension of the current best into the untested multiprofile space—it changes only the profile setting and adds the necessary avgpool aggregation. This balances exploitation (staying in the proven multimodal/pca/resnet50/concat regime) with exploration of a potentially high-impact architectural choice. A positive result directly upgrades our best configuration; a negative result efficiently rules out multiprofile in the multimodal setting and redirects budget toward other dimensions (fusion strategy, image encoder, RNA encoder).

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best performance so far (acc=0.619, F1=0.610), showing a large gain over the singleprofile multimodal baseline (config_016, acc=0.527). This jump suggests that how multiple profiles are aggregated is a critical design axis. Uncertainty: we have only tested avgpool for aggregation; it is unclear whether a learned transformer aggregation could capture richer inter-profile relationships and further improve performance, or whether simple averaging is already near-optimal. This experiment (config_020) isolates the aggregation choice (transformer vs. avgpool) while holding all other settings constant (pca_n2000, resnet50, multiprofile, concat fusion), directly testing whether the aggregation mechanism is a meaningful lever. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step: it either confirms avgpool sufficiency (reducing search space) or identifies transformer aggregation as a new promising direction to exploit in subsequent experiments.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, showing that multimodal + multiprofile + avgpool is a strong combination. However, all multimodal experiments so far have used 'concat' fusion; the 'weighted' fusion strategy remains untested. Question: Does learned/weighted fusion of the two modality embeddings improve over simple concatenation in the best-performing setup? This is a single-variable change (fusion: concat→weighted) from config_018, making any performance difference cleanly attributable to the fusion mechanism. Why best next: Under a limited budget, resolving whether concat is already near-optimal or whether weighted fusion unlocks further gains is a high-information experiment. If weighted fusion helps, it opens a new optimization axis for all future multimodal configs; if it does not, we can confidently fix fusion=concat and redirect budget toward the more uncertain image-encoder (ViT-L vs ResNet50) or RNA-encoder (scvi/scgpt vs PCA) axes. It is the lowest-cost, highest-clarity test available.

The current best (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) establishes that multimodal fusion with multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, and weighted fusion is the strongest configuration so far. However, the image encoder dimension is completely unexplored — all multimodal results use resnet50, and we have zero data on imagenet_vit_l. Since the image modality contributes a meaningful ~4% gain in the multimodal setting (config_016 vs config_001), a stronger image encoder could provide a larger complementary signal. Config_025 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings at the current best, giving a clean A/B comparison that isolates the image-encoder effect. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact untested dimension, making it the most informative use of the next experiment under a limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.639 acc / 0.620 F1. The evidence clearly establishes that multimodal + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted is the strongest design family, and that image encoder choice (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) makes negligible difference (0.639 vs 0.635). The major untested design dimension is the RNA encoder: all multimodal experiments so far use pca_n2000 (a linear projection), while scvi_n200 and scgpt offer learned, nonlinear representations that may capture biological structure more effectively. Config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) isolates the RNA encoder variable within the best-performing configuration, directly testing whether a learned single-cell representation can push performance beyond the PCA baseline. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact remaining decision: if scvi improves on PCA, it opens a new optimization direction; if not, it confirms PCA sufficiency and redirects effort toward other levers. Under a limited budget, resolving this key architectural question is more informative than testing lower-impact variations (e.g., transformer+weighted, which is unlikely to beat avgpool given prior evidence).

The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.678). With pca_n2000, the image encoder choice made negligible difference (resnet50: 0.639 vs imagenet_vit_l: 0.635), but that was with a simpler RNA representation. Now that scvi_n200 provides a richer, learned RNA embedding, the interaction with the image encoder may shift—imagenet_vit_l's stronger visual features could complement the more expressive RNA profile. config_037 changes only the image encoder (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) while holding all other settings at their empirically validated best (multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted). This single-variable test is the most informative next step: it directly extends the strongest direction, keeps the result interpretable, and if it yields a gain, it confirms a path to further improvement; if not, it confirms resnet50 is sufficient and redirects budget toward RNA-encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt).

Evidence: The strongest performance driver identified so far is the RNA encoder choice—switching from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 in an otherwise identical setup (resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) yielded a ~4% accuracy gain (0.639→0.678). The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted + multiprofile) achieves 0.706 acc. The one major untested dimension is whether scgpt, a more expressive pre-trained scRNA-seq encoder, can surpass scvi_n200. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder in the best-performing multimodal pipeline? Why this experiment: config_049 changes exactly one variable (RNA encoder: scvi_n200→scgpt) from the current best (config_037), keeping the validated optimal image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) fixed. This is the highest-information single experiment: if scgpt ≥ scvi_n200 it identifies a new best configuration; if scgpt < scvi_n200 it confirms scvi_n200 as the optimal RNA encoder and closes the last major design dimension, allowing focus on finer-tuning. Under a limited budget, resolving the RNA encoder question in the strongest pipeline is more valuable than testing secondary dimensions (e.g., transformer aggregation, which already showed inferior performance).

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), which is a weak baseline. (4) Under a tight budget, this single experiment reduces the most critical uncertainty and maximally informs the structure of the remaining search space.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieved 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) was very weak at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant signal. With only two data points, the key uncertainty is whether the profile structure (single vs. multi) adds meaningful information beyond what a single profile captures. Question tested: config_002 isolates the multiprofile + avgpool aggregation effect while holding the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison to config_001. Why best next: It is the most controlled experiment available—changing only profile_setting and adding aggregation—so any performance delta can be attributed to multiprofile structure. The result will determine whether to invest subsequent experiments in multiprofile variants (including multimodal) or to focus on encoder improvements, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with multi-profile and PCA_n2000 (config_002, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, a large jump over single-profile RNA (config_001, 0.485) and far above image-only (config_010, 0.208). This confirms RNA is the dominant modality and that multi-profile aggregation adds substantial signal. However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool). Question: config_003 isolates the effect of aggregation method by swapping avgpool → transformer while holding every other factor (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA_n2000) constant relative to config_002. This is a clean, controlled comparison that tells us whether learned attention-based aggregation can further improve on simple averaging, or whether avgpool is already near the ceiling for this encoder. Why best next step: it is the most direct exploitation of the strongest result (config_002) while probing an untested design dimension. If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, subsequent experiments can pair the better aggregator with alternative encoders (scvi, scGPT); if the gain is marginal, we learn that aggregation is not the bottleneck and should pivot to encoder choice. Under a limited budget, this single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the aggregation axis before committing to more complex multimodal or encoder-variation experiments.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.591 acc, showing multiprofile+avgpool is the strongest RNA configuration. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), suggesting the image modality may contribute little signal. Uncertainty: We have only tested PCA n2000 as the RNA encoder; it is unclear whether a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) captures complementary biological signal that PCA misses. This experiment (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean controlled comparison to config_002, changing only the RNA encoder. It will clarify whether encoder choice is a meaningful design axis before we invest limited budget in multimodal fusion experiments. If scvi substantially outperforms PCA, we know to prioritize it in multimodal configs; if it does not, PCA is sufficient and we can focus remaining budget on testing whether multimodal fusion adds value at all.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality (best RNA-only: 0.650 vs best image-only: 0.208), and within RNA-only, multiprofile+avgpool+scvi_n200 (config_005, 0.650) is the current best. The RNA encoder choice is a critical, underexplored design axis: we've only tested pca_n2000 and scvi_n200. scgpt is a fundamentally different (generative, pretrained) encoder that could capture richer biological structure. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 when all other variables are held at their known-best settings (multiprofile, avgpool)? Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests the most impactful remaining RNA-only design decision with a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. The result will determine which RNA encoder to anchor all future multimodal experiments on, making it high-value for the limited budget. Testing aggregation (config_006) is lower priority since avgpool already showed a large margin over transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), and multimodal configs are premature before establishing the best RNA backbone.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.48–0.65) vastly outperform image-only (0.21), and the best RNA config is multiprofile + scvi_n200 + avgpool (config_005, acc=0.650). The critical open question is whether the weak image signal (resnet50, acc=0.208) can provide complementary information when fused with the strong RNA signal, or whether it will dilute performance. This experiment (config_031) pairs the best-performing RNA setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) with resnet50 image features using weighted fusion, which lets the model learn the relative modality importance. If it beats config_005, multimodal exploration is justified; if it does not, we can deprioritize the 36 remaining multimodal configs and focus budget on refining the RNA-only space (e.g., config_006 for transformer aggregation with scvi_n200). Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image modality adds value at all is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact question before committing further experiments to the multimodal branch.

Evidence: config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best result so far (acc 0.678, F1 0.646), a modest +2.8 pp gain over the best RNA-only config (config_005, acc 0.650). The image modality alone was very weak (0.208), so the source of the multimodal gain is uncertain. Question: Does the fusion mechanism (weighted vs. concat) materially affect performance in this best-performing multimodal setup? config_030 is identical to config_031 except it uses concat fusion, providing a clean one-variable A/B test. Why this is the best use of the next budget slot: it is the lowest-uncertainty, highest-information experiment available—it directly clarifies whether the learned weighted fusion is a meaningful design choice or whether any fusion strategy yields similar results. This knowledge determines whether subsequent multimodal experiments should prioritize weighted fusion, and it avoids over-investing in a fusion mechanism whose contribution is currently confounded with the overall multimodal gain.

The best configuration so far is config_031 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted) at 0.678 acc. The image-only resnet50 was very weak (0.208 acc), yet in multimodal it contributed ~3% over RNA-only scvi_n200 (0.650). The key uncertainty is whether the image modality's contribution is encoder-limited: resnet50 may be too coarse to capture relevant spatial/morphological features. Config_037 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted) is a minimal, single-variable change from the best config, isolating the effect of a stronger image encoder. If ViT-L substantially improves over resnet50, it identifies a clear exploitation path; if not, it tells us the image signal is inherently limited and we should focus optimization on the RNA side. This is the highest-information experiment under the budget because it resolves a major design-axis uncertainty (image encoder quality) while building directly on the strongest evidence.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) achieves 0.706 acc. We know avgpool > transformer for pca_n2000 (0.591 vs 0.519), but that comparison used a weaker, linearly-reduced encoder. With scvi_n200's richer learned latent representations, transformer-based attention aggregation could better capture inter-profile interactions that simple averaging discards. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool when paired with the strongest RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and image encoder (imagenet_vit_l)? Why this experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of the best-performing configuration (only aggregation changes), directly resolving whether the aggregation choice that was suboptimal for PCA might be optimal for learned embeddings. A positive result would open a new optimization direction; a negative result would confirm avgpool as the correct choice and let us focus remaining budget on other dimensions (e.g., fusion strategy or RNA encoder alternatives). This is the highest-information experiment available under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.5266 acc, a clear ~4.2% gain over the RNA-only baseline config_001 (0.4849 acc), confirming the image modality is valuable. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most natural and controlled extension of the current best result, tests a major architectural axis (single vs. multi profile) that gates many downstream decisions (aggregation method, encoder choices), and its outcome will efficiently prune or validate a large subtree of the remaining 49 configurations under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is our best result at 61.9% acc, showing that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation drives the largest gain (+9.2% over singleprofile). However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) that can model inter-profile interactions would outperform the simple mean-pooling, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this task. This experiment (config_020) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat fusion, multiprofile) constant relative to config_018, making it a clean single-variable test. Under the limited budget, resolving whether transformer aggregation adds value over avgpool is critical: if it helps, it opens a new optimization axis; if it does not, we can rule it out and redirect effort toward fusion strategy or image encoder choice. This is the highest-information-per-experiment next step.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc, and we have zero evidence on fusion strategy since all completed multimodal experiments used concat. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation for combining RNA and image features in the multiprofile+avgpool setting? This is a single-variable change from the best config, isolating the fusion decision. Rationale: Under a tight budget, the most informative next step is a controlled ablation of the one untested dimension on the current best configuration. If weighted fusion helps, we immediately gain a better config; if it doesn't, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect effort to image encoder (ViT-L) or RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt) with confidence that fusion is not the bottleneck. This minimizes risk while maximizing information gain per experiment.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.639 acc / 0.620 F1, and we've established that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest combination for the resnet50 image encoder. However, the image encoder dimension remains largely untested—only resnet50 has been used in multimodal settings. Question: Does upgrading to a substantially stronger pretrained image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) improve performance when paired with the already-validated multiprofile + avgpool + weighted pipeline? Why this is the best next experiment: The image encoder is a major design axis with high potential impact. ViT-L is significantly larger and more expressive than ResNet50, so this test has high information value: if it helps, it opens a strong new direction; if it does not, we confirm ResNet50 suffices and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder choices (scvi, scgpt). This is a logical exploitation of the best-known configuration while probing the single largest untested architectural lever.

The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) has established that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest design so far. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as pca_n2000 across all multimodal runs, leaving a critical design dimension unexplored. config_031 isolates the RNA encoder by swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 while holding all other parameters at their best-known values (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted). This directly tests whether a learned latent RNA representation (scvi) can match or surpass a linear PCA projection in the multimodal setting. If scvi_n200 matches pca_n2000, the RNA encoder is not a bottleneck and we can focus on other dimensions; if it improves, we gain a new promising direction; if it degrades, we rule it out and can pivot to scgpt next. Under a limited budget, this single experiment reduces the most important remaining uncertainty (RNA encoder choice) within the already-validated high-performing region, making it the most information-dense next step.

With pca_n2000, resnet50 and imagenet_vit_l were nearly equivalent (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison was made with a weaker RNA encoder. Under the limited budget, this is the highest-information exploitation step.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted; 0.706 acc) was reached by sequentially improving RNA encoder (pca→scvi, +4%), image encoder (resnet50→vit_l, +3%), aggregation (avgpool over transformer), and fusion (weighted over concat). The one major design dimension not yet tested in this optimal context is the scgpt RNA encoder. Testing config_049 (scgpt, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap from the current best, directly asking: can scgpt match or exceed scvi_n200 given the richest image and fusion setup? This is high-information: if scgpt ≈ scvi, the RNA encoder is saturated and further gains must come from other axes; if scgpt > scvi, we find a new best; if scgpt < scvi, we confirm scvi is optimal and can stop exploring RNA encoders. Under a limited budget, resolving this last major untested variable in the strongest configuration is more informative than re-testing aggregation (transformer already shown weaker) or fusion (weighted already shown stronger) in a new encoder context.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation is the dominant design choice (+0.092 over singleprofile). Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, showing that multiprofile + avgpool + multimodal is a strong combination. Evidence: The current best (config_037, acc 0.706) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. The current best configuration (config_039: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. With no experiments completed, the highest-priority uncertainty is establishing a performance baseline and determining whether RNA alone carries sufficient signal. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal, interpretable configuration: a standard linear dimensionality reduction on a single RNA profile with no learned encoder, no aggregation, and no fusion. Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) has been completed, yielding 48.5% accuracy / 46.4% F1 — a very weak baseline with no information about whether the image modality, better encoders, or multiprofile aggregation contribute. This isolates the effect of modality addition with minimal confounds. If multimodal outperforms the RNA-only baseline, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies subsequent investment in better encoders/fusion. Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, PCA, ResNet50, concat) outperformed config_001 (RNA-only PCA) by ~4.2% accuracy, confirming that adding an image branch with concat fusion is beneficial. Under a limited budget, resolving whether multiprofile helps is more informative than testing minor fusion variants (e.g., weighted vs concat) because it determines whether an entire axis of the search space is worth further exploration.

Evidence: The current best (config_018, acc=0.619) shows that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation in a multimodal setting is a strong direction, with a large gain over singleprofile (+0.092). The current best (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc 0.619) has only been tested with concat fusion. Evidence: The current best is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639). Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all completed multimodal experiments share this encoder. The dominant design decisions (multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) are well-established, but the RNA encoder is the largest untested variable. Question: Does replacing PCA with scvi_n200 (a learned, biologically-informed latent representation) improve performance when all other settings match the current best? This is the highest-information next step because the RNA encoder has the largest remaining uncertainty—if scvi_n200 helps, it opens a productive exploitation path (scgpt, etc.); if it does not, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can redirect budget to other dimensions. It avoids the smaller, already-nearly-resolved image-encoder question (resnet50 vs ViT-L differ by only ~0.4%).

Evidence: The strongest finding so far is that scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA for the RNA encoder (config_031: 0.678 vs config_019: 0.639, a ~4-point gain), while other design choices (avgpool over transformer, weighted over concat, ResNet50 ≈ ViT-L) show smaller, more settled effects. The RNA encoder remains the largest unexplored lever: scgpt has not been tested in any context. Evidence: The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at acc=0.678. With pca_n2000, resnet50 and vit_l performed nearly identically (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison was made with a weaker RNA encoder. If vit_l matches or exceeds resnet50, it validates the current architecture and frees the next experiment to explore other axes (e.g., transformer aggregation with scvi_n200). This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.7062 acc. Aggregation has shown the larger historical effect (avgpool beat transformer by ~4-6 pp with PCA+ResNet50), so testing whether that ordering holds with the best encoders is the higher-value question. With no completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is establishing a reliable performance floor for the RNA modality, which is the primary signal in cellular profiling. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard configuration: PCA with 2000 dimensions is a well-understood linear encoder, and singleprofile removes aggregation as a confound. This experiment tests whether the basic RNA pipeline yields meaningful predictive signal. Without this baseline, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable (we could not tell whether multimodal fusion helps or whether the individual modalities are simply weak).

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task. This is the foundational question for a multimodal cellular profiling study: if image has no discriminative power, all multimodal configurations lose their main rationale. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides a clean, controlled comparison to config_001—both use singleprofile with no aggregation—so any performance difference is attributable to the modality itself rather than to profile setting or aggregation. ResNet50 is chosen as the standard, well-calibrated image encoder baseline before exploring ViT-L. This experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty (modality-level signal) and directly informs whether to invest subsequent budget in multimodal fusion or to focus on improving the RNA side (e.g., better encoders or multiprofile aggregation).

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA n2000 (single profile) achieves 0.485 accuracy, while image-only with ResNet50 is far weaker at 0.208, indicating RNA is the dominant signal source. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, a substantial ~10.5-point gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485). This confirms multiprofile aggregation is a high-impact design choice. However, we have no evidence yet on whether the aggregation method itself matters. Evidence: config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.591) and F1 (0.573), substantially outperforming singleprofile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile + pca_n2000 + avgpool (config_002, acc 0.591) is the clear best so far, while image-only with resnet50 (config_010, acc 0.208) is very weak. Evidence: The current best is config_019 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted; acc 0.639). With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 at ~48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any useful signal at all. Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is the strongest result at 0.650 acc, showing multiprofile + scvi_n200 is a clear winning combination. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget because it resolves the key uncertainty about whether to optimize encoder choice or profile structure first.

Evidence: The best RNA-only setup so far is multiprofile + scvi_n200 + transformer (config_006, acc=0.653), and scvi_n200 consistently outperforms pca_n2000 across both profile settings. However, scgpt is entirely untested, leaving a critical uncertainty about whether a third encoder could substantially improve the RNA signal before we commit budget to multimodal fusion experiments. Question: Does scgpt match or exceed scvi_n200 under the same multiprofile + transformer conditions? This is a clean 1-factor comparison (encoder) against config_006. Why this is the best next step: The RNA encoder is the most fundamental design choice—it determines the quality of the primary signal in every downstream multimodal experiment. Resolving whether scgpt is competitive (or superior) before testing multimodal fusion avoids wasting limited budget on multimodal configs built on a suboptimal encoder. If scgpt ≈ scvi_n200, we confirm the current best and pivot to multimodal; if scgpt is markedly better, we redirect the multimodal search toward scgpt-based configs.

Evidence: The best RNA-only result is scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer (0.653 acc, config_006), and image-only resnet50 single-profile is very weak (0.208 acc, config_010). The critical open question is whether adding the image modality to the strongest RNA pipeline yields any complementary signal, or whether the weak image performance (0.208) means fusion will be neutral-to-harmful. Config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) directly tests this by taking the proven best RNA configuration and adding image with the simplest fusion (concat). This is the most informative next step because: (1) it exploits the strongest known RNA setup, (2) it answers the highest-uncertainty design question—does multimodal help at all in this task—before spending budget on more complex fusion variants or alternative image encoders, and (3) the result will determine whether subsequent experiments should invest in multimodal exploration (ViT, weighted fusion) or refocus on RNA-only refinements.

The current best is config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) at 0.688 acc. The image-only baseline was very weak (0.208), suggesting the image modality contributes limited signal and may benefit from reweighting rather than equal-weight concatenation. This isolates the fusion-strategy question: does the image branch need to be down-weighted relative to the RNA branch, or are the features complementary enough that simple concatenation suffices? Under a limited budget, this single-variable test reduces uncertainty about an important design decision (how to combine modalities) without confounding other factors (encoder, aggregation, profile setting all held constant at their best-known values). The result will directly inform whether to invest further in multimodal configurations and, if weighted fusion wins, which modality to trust more.

The current best configuration (config_033, acc 0.713) uses scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted fusion in a multimodal multiprofile setting. The image encoder dimension is completely unexplored in multimodal fusion—only resnet50 has been tested, and image-only resnet50 performed very poorly (0.208), suggesting the image signal may be underutilized. Under a limited budget, this single experiment resolves a major unexplored design axis while building on the most promising configuration.

With zero completed experiments, the most critical design question is whether multimodal fusion (RNA + image) provides a meaningful advantage over unimodal approaches — the core hypothesis of this study. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) directly tests this question while using the simplest, most standard components at each level (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for image, single profile, concat fusion), minimizing confounding variables. This establishes a performance reference for the multimodal direction: if it performs well, subsequent experiments can explore richer encoders (scvi, scgpt), multi-profile aggregation, and alternative fusion; if it underperforms, follow-up experiments can isolate whether the bottleneck is the fusion strategy, encoder choice, or the data itself. Choosing a simple, well-understood multimodal baseline over a complex one ensures the first data point is interpretable and maximally informative for guiding the next several experiments under a tight budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_016: multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, singleprofile, concat → 52.7% acc), the most fundamental uncertainty is the individual contribution of each modality. Without single-modality baselines, we cannot determine whether the multimodal result is driven primarily by image features, RNA features, or a genuine synergistic effect. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) uses the exact same image encoder and profile setting as the multimodal baseline, making it a clean ablation. If image-only approaches or exceeds 52.7%, RNA is adding little and future effort should focus on image encoder upgrades (e.g., ViT-L). If image-only is substantially lower, RNA is contributing meaningfully and we should prioritize exploring RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) and fusion strategies. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most important design axis before committing budget to more complex multimodal variants.

Evidence: The multimodal model (config_016: pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) achieves 52.7% accuracy, while image-only resnet50 (config_010) achieves only 20.8%. This ~32-point gap tells us RNA contributes substantially, but we cannot yet decompose how much of the multimodal performance comes from RNA alone versus genuine cross-modal fusion. Uncertainty: We lack an RNA-only baseline with the same encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile) used in config_016. Question tested: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) provides a clean ablation that isolates RNA performance. Why best next: If RNA alone ≈ 50%, the image adds little and future effort should focus on RNA encoders/fusion; if RNA alone ≈ 30%, the multimodal gain is genuine and investing in better image encoders or fusion strategies (e.g., weighted fusion, ViT) becomes prioritized. This single experiment resolves the most critical design uncertainty and directly guides all subsequent allocation decisions under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieves 0.527 acc, only ~4.2% above RNA-only (config_001, 0.485), while image-only (config_010) is very weak at 0.208. This suggests the image modality contributes modestly under the current singleprofile setup. Uncertainty: the multiprofile axis is completely untested across all three modalities, and it is a major structural design choice that could substantially change how image (and RNA) information is aggregated before fusion. Question: config_018 keeps the exact same encoders (pca_n2000, resnet50) and fusion (concat) as config_016 but switches to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, isolating the effect of multi-view aggregation. Why best next step: it is a controlled, single-axis extension of the current best configuration, so any performance shift is attributable to the profile/aggregation change. A positive result would validate multiprofile as a productive direction and unlock a large family of follow-up experiments (better encoders, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion); a null or negative result would efficiently rule out multiprofile and refocus the budget on encoder or fusion improvements. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-uncertainty structural axis before investing in more expensive encoder swaps maximizes information per experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best result at 0.6186 acc / 0.6103 F1, a large jump over the singleprofile multimodal baseline (config_016: 0.5266). This strongly indicates that multiprofile + aggregation is the key design axis. Uncertainty: whether the aggregation mechanism itself can be improved beyond simple avgpool. This directly tests whether a more expressive aggregation (capturing inter-profile interactions) yields further gains over the simple mean. If transformer aggregation helps, it opens a high-value sub-space (configs 021, 026, 027, 032, 033, 038, 039, 044, 045, 050, 051); if it does not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect effort to fusion or encoder choices. It is the most logical exploitation step from the current best result without introducing multiple confounding variables.

Evidence: Our best result is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.6186 acc / 0.6103 F1, showing multiprofile+avgpool is a strong combination. However, fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' across all experiments; 'weighted' fusion remains completely unexplored. Question: config_019 is a clean single-variable change from config_018 (only fusion: concat → weighted), directly testing whether learnable per-modality weighting improves over fixed concatenation. This is critical because if weighted fusion helps, it can be stacked with future improvements (better RNA encoder, ViT image encoder); if it does not, we can eliminate that axis and focus budget on other variables. Rationale: Under a limited budget, the most informative next step is to resolve this fundamental architectural uncertainty with the minimal confound (one variable changed from the current best), rather than jumping to a multi-variable change that would be harder to interpret.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.6390 acc. We know multiprofile+avgpool+weighted is the strongest combination, and that image alone is very weak (0.2079) compared to RNA alone (0.4849), suggesting the image modality may be underutilized with resnet50. Uncertainty: We have never tested a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) in the multimodal setting. It is unclear whether the image branch is a bottleneck or whether resnet50 already captures most useful visual signal. Question tested: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve the multimodal model when all other components (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) are held at their best-known settings? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable change from the current best configuration, directly testing whether the weaker image modality can be strengthened. A positive result would justify further investment in image representation; a null result would redirect effort toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi/scgpt). Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about which modality to prioritize under the remaining budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, 0.639 acc) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and RNA is the dominant signal (0.485 alone vs 0.208 image-only). However, the RNA encoder axis is completely unexplored in the multimodal setting—we have only tested a linear PCA projection. Question: config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a single-variable change from config_019, swapping PCA for a learned variational autoencoder representation. This directly tests whether a non-linear, biologically-informed RNA representation can improve over PCA in the best-known configuration. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It tests the highest-leverage unexplored axis—improving the dominant modality's representation has the largest potential upside. (2) It is a controlled comparison (only RNA encoder changes), so any performance shift is cleanly attributable to the encoder. (3) The result will determine whether to invest further in learned RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) or confirm PCA is sufficient, shaping all subsequent experiments. (4) Compared to filling the transformer+weighted cell (config_021), the RNA encoder question has greater uncertainty and greater potential impact given RNA's dominance.

Evidence: The current best (config_031, scvi_n200/resnet50/avgpool/weighted/multiprofile, acc=0.678) shows that RNA encoder choice is a high-impact design decision (scvi_n200 gave +4 pts over pca_n2000). However, scgpt—a fundamentally different pre-trained single-cell encoder (generative vs. variational vs. linear PCA)—has zero experimental evidence. Meanwhile, the image encoder axis (resnet50 vs. imagenet_vit_l) showed negligible difference (~0.4 pts) with pca_n2000, making further image-encoder exploration lower-value. Question: config_043 (scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) directly compares scgpt against scvi_n200 in an otherwise identical, best-performing setup, isolating the RNA encoder effect. Why best next experiment: It resolves the largest remaining uncertainty (which RNA encoder is optimal) with a single experiment, and the answer will guide all subsequent multimodal configurations. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the best encoder and can focus remaining budget on finer-tuning aggregation/fusion interactions.

The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted; acc 0.678). With PCA, the image encoder choice (resnet50 vs ViT-L) was nearly irrelevant (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison used a linear PCA representation. scvi_n200 produces a learned latent embedding that may interact differently with a more expressive image encoder. config_037 is a clean single-variable extension of the current best (only swapping resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l), directly testing whether the image modality is underutilized with resnet50 when paired with the superior RNA encoder. This is the highest-value next experiment because it isolates one important design axis, builds on the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + avgpool + weighted), and the result will either confirm resnet50 sufficiency (focusing future effort on aggregation/fusion) or reveal a meaningful image-encoder gain that opens a new promising direction—all with minimal risk of a wasted run.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit. The most critical uncertainty is establishing a performance baseline before testing more complex configurations. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration: it uses a standard linear encoder (PCA), avoids aggregation and fusion complexity, and isolates the RNA signal. This gives a clean reference point to determine whether (a) image modality adds value, (b) multimodal fusion outperforms either single modality, and (c) more complex encoders (scvi, scgpt) or aggregation strategies (transformer) provide meaningful gains over this simple baseline. Starting here maximizes interpretability of all subsequent comparisons and ensures that any performance improvement in later experiments can be attributed to specific design choices rather than confounded by multiple simultaneous changes.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), giving us a baseline for the RNA modality but no information about whether image features carry useful signal. The highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design question right now is whether the image modality is informative at all, because this determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing or whether we should focus on improving the RNA pipeline. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly answers this: it isolates image signal with a standard, well-understood encoder. Comparing its accuracy to the 48.5% RNA baseline will tell us (a) whether image features are competitive, (b) whether they are complementary (motivating multimodal experiments), or (c) whether they are weak (redirecting budget toward RNA encoder/aggregation improvements). ResNet50 is chosen over ViT-L because it is the encoder used in the multimodal configs, making the single-modality result a direct ablation reference. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential architectural decision (modality choice) before committing budget to more complex multimodal or encoder-variant experiments.

Evidence: Our only strong baseline is config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) at 48.5% acc, while image-only is very weak (20.8%). We have only 2 data points, so uncertainty is high across all design axes. Question tested: config_002 changes exactly one factor from config_001—switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation—while keeping the same PCA encoder. This cleanly isolates whether capturing the distribution of cell states (multiprofile) adds signal beyond a single representative profile. Why it's the best next experiment: (1) It is a minimal, single-factor comparison to our best baseline, making the result easy to interpret. (2) The multiprofile decision is a foundational axis that affects all downstream multimodal configurations (configs 018–051 all require an aggregation strategy). If multiprofile+avgpool helps, it validates investing in more complex aggregations (transformer) and multimodal multiprofile variants. If it doesn't help, we can prune the multiprofile branch and focus budget on RNA encoder improvements. (3) avgpool is the simplest aggregation, so a negative result would implicate the multiprofile representation itself rather than aggregation complexity, reducing uncertainty efficiently under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large improvement over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming multiprofile aggregation is highly beneficial. However, we have not yet tested whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple average pooling. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation of multiple profiles capture inter-profile interactions that avgpool misses, or is the simple average sufficient? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable change from our current best (config_002), isolating the aggregation method. The answer directly informs the aggregation choice for all subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 018-051), making it a high-leverage, low-uncertainty experiment. If transformer wins, we gain a clear direction; if it ties or loses, we confirm avgpool is adequate and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder choice or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) is strong at 0.591, while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 0.208. Avgpool clearly beats transformer for aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multimodal fusion adds value on top of the already-strong RNA signal, or whether the weak image channel is merely noise that degrades performance. This experiment (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests whether combining the best-known RNA configuration with the available image encoder yields any benefit over RNA-only. It uses the best-validated settings for each component (pca_n2000 + avgpool for RNA, resnet50 for image) and the simplest fusion (concat), isolating the fusion question. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information experiment: if multimodal helps, we justify investing remaining runs in better image encoders (ViT-L) and fusion strategies; if it does not, we redirect effort toward improving the RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt). Either outcome sharply narrows the search space.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, modestly above RNA-only multiprofile+avgpool (0.591). Image-only is very weak (0.208), so the image modality's contribution in the multimodal setting is uncertain. Question: Does the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) meaningfully affect multimodal performance? config_019 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while holding all other hyperparameters identical to the best config. This is the cleanest single-variable test of whether the image features are being optimally mixed or merely appended. Why best next step: It directly exploits the strongest evidence (config_018) with a minimal, interpretable perturbation, reducing uncertainty about whether the modest multimodal gain is robust to fusion design or an artifact of concat. If weighted fusion improves or matches concat, we gain confidence in the multimodal direction and can then explore other axes (image encoder, RNA encoder); if it degrades, it signals the image channel may be diluting the RNA signal and we should prioritize RNA-encoder improvements instead.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant signal (RNA-only multiprofile avgpool: 0.591 vs image-only singleprofile: 0.208), and the best config so far (config_019, multimodal/multiprofile/pca_n2000/resnet50/avgpool/weighted at 0.639) relies entirely on PCA as the RNA encoder. The RNA encoder is the single largest unexplored design axis, and since RNA drives most of the performance, improving it has the highest potential payoff. Question tested: Does a learned single-cell latent representation (scVI, 200-dim) outperform a linear PCA (2000-dim) in the multimodal setting? config_031 is a minimal, controlled change from the best config—only the RNA encoder is swapped—so any performance shift is cleanly attributable to the encoder choice. Why best next: It directly extends the strongest evidence we have, tests the highest-leverage unexplored variable, and its outcome (whether learned representations help or PCA suffices) will guide all subsequent multimodal experiments, making it the most information-dense use of the next budget slot.

The current best (config_031: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, acc=0.678) has only been tested with resnet50 as the image encoder. The image encoder dimension is completely unexplored in the multimodal setting—image-only resnet50 scored very low (0.208), but in a fused model the image may provide complementary signal that a stronger encoder like ViT-L could better capture. config_037 is a clean single-variable extension of the best config (only image encoder changes from resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l), so any performance difference is directly attributable to encoder quality. This is the highest-information next step: if ViT-L improves performance, it identifies image encoder strength as a productive axis for further gains; if it does not, it confirms the image modality's contribution is encoder-independent and redirects effort toward RNA encoder or aggregation choices. Under a limited budget, resolving this unexplored binary question is more valuable than testing a second RNA encoder (scgpt) or re-testing aggregation, both of which have weaker expected information gain given the strong existing evidence.

Evidence: The best configuration so far (config_037: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, 0.706 acc) establishes that learned RNA encoders (scvi_n200 > pca_n2000) and a strong image encoder (ViT-L > ResNet50) both contribute meaningfully. However, we have not yet tested scgpt in any multimodal setting, leaving uncertainty about whether the RNA encoder dimension is saturated among learned encoders or whether scgpt's different pretraining objective could yield further gains. Question: Does scgpt, in the otherwise-best multimodal configuration (imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted), match or exceed scvi_n200's performance? Why this is the best next experiment: It directly probes the most impactful remaining design axis (RNA encoder quality) in the strongest known context, so the result will either confirm scvi_n200 as the optimal encoder (focusing future effort on other dimensions) or reveal a new promising direction. This is more informative than re-testing aggregation (avgpool already dominates transformer by ~7 pts in RNA-only) or profile setting (multiprofile clearly superior), both of which have strong existing evidence.

The current best (config_037: scvi_n200 + ViT-L + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted, 0.706 acc) was reached by incrementally improving each component. The one architectural choice not yet tested with this strongest encoder combination is transformer aggregation. In prior experiments, avgpool outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519 for RNA-only; 0.619 vs 0.519 for multimodal with pca_n2000), but those comparisons used the weaker pca encoder. With scvi_n200's richer learned representations and ViT-L's patch-level features, transformer aggregation could potentially capture longer-range interactions that avgpool discards. Config_039 is a clean single-variable change (avgpool→transformer) from the current best, making it a direct A/B test. If it matches or exceeds 0.706, it opens a new optimization axis; if it underperforms (as the trend suggests), it definitively rules out transformer aggregation for this task and allows us to commit remaining budget to fine-tuning the avgpool+weighted path. Under a limited budget, resolving this last major architectural uncertainty is more valuable than testing a second-order variable (e.g., concat vs weighted) that already has two consistent data points favoring weighted.

With no prior experiments, the highest-priority need is to establish a performance baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard configuration in the search space: a single modality, single profile, and the most conventional linear encoder (PCA). It will (1) calibrate what accuracy/F1 levels are achievable in this task, (2) serve as the reference against which all other RNA encoder choices (scvi, scgpt), profile settings (multiprofile + aggregation), and the addition of image modality can be measured, and (3) is computationally inexpensive, reducing the cost of the first data point. Establishing this floor first ensures that every subsequent experiment—whether testing a richer RNA encoder, adding image features, or trying multimodal fusion—can be interpreted as a meaningful delta rather than an absolute number in isolation. This is the most information-efficient use of the first budget slot.

Evidence: Only one experiment is complete (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), which is near-chance and tells us almost nothing about whether image information or other design choices matter. Uncertainty: The most critical open question in a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries independent predictive signal. Without knowing this, we cannot rationally allocate budget across the 51 remaining configs (RNA-only improvements vs. image-only vs. multimodal). What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest ablation counterpart to config_001—same profile setting, same architectural simplicity, but swapping RNA for image. Together they establish the independent contribution of each modality. Why it is the best next experiment: It reduces the single largest source of uncertainty (is image useful?) with one experiment, using a standard resnet50 backbone to keep the comparison fair and the compute cost moderate. The answer directly determines whether subsequent budget should be spent exploring multimodal fusion strategies or instead refining RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. No other single experiment provides this level of strategic information for the cost of one run.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the stronger modality. However, we have only one RNA data point, so we cannot yet tell whether the profile setting (single vs. multi) is a meaningful design lever. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles with a simple average pool improve RNA performance over the single-profile baseline? This isolates one variable (profile_setting + aggregation) while holding the RNA encoder fixed at pca_n2000. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly extends our best result with the minimal change, giving a clean read on whether multiprofile adds value. If avgpool helps, it validates the multiprofile branch and justifies testing transformer aggregation next; if it does not help, we can deprioritize multiprofile configurations and focus budget on encoder choice or multimodal fusion. This single experiment reduces uncertainty about a design axis that affects roughly half of the remaining configuration space.

Evidence: Multiprofile with avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) substantially outperforms singleprofile (config_001, acc=0.485), confirming that multi-profile aggregation is a major source of gain. However, we have not yet tested whether a transformer-based aggregation can further improve over simple average pooling. Question: Does transformer aggregation (config_003) outperform avgpool under identical conditions (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000)? This is a clean single-variable ablation that isolates the aggregation strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: The aggregation choice directly affects 24+ downstream multimodal configurations (configs 018-051). Resolving whether transformer > avgpool now will let us focus the remaining budget on the better aggregation path in multimodal settings, rather than spending experiments testing both aggregation methods in every multimodal combination. It is the highest-information-per-experiment choice given the current evidence.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, while image-only resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208. This establishes RNA as the dominant modality and multiprofile+avgpool as the best RNA pipeline, but leaves the critical question of whether multimodal fusion can improve upon the RNA-only baseline. Question being tested: Does adding image features (resnet50) via simple concat fusion to the best RNA configuration (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) yield any gain over 0.591, or does the weak image signal (0.208 standalone) degrade performance? Why this is the best next experiment: config_018 is the minimal, most direct extension of our top configuration—identical RNA encoder, profile, and aggregation—so any performance delta is cleanly attributable to the image modality and fusion. It resolves the highest-priority uncertainty (does multimodal help at all?) before spending budget on more complex variants (weighted fusion, ViT-L, alternative RNA encoders). If it helps, we exploit further; if it hurts, we can refocus on RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) with confidence that image is not the bottleneck.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, beating RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591) by ~3 points, confirming that adding image with concat fusion provides a modest gain. However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat). Uncertainty: We do not know whether the fusion mechanism matters—weighted fusion could allow the model to better calibrate the contribution of the weak image modality (image-only was only 0.208) versus the strong RNA signal. This experiment (config_019) changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, holding all other settings identical to config_018. This clean A/B comparison will clarify whether fusion strategy is a meaningful design axis, directly informing whether future multimodal experiments should prioritize concat or weighted fusion. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information single step: it exploits the current best configuration while resolving a key uncertainty that affects all subsequent multimodal choices.

Evidence: The current best is config_019 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc. We know weighted fusion > concat (0.639 vs 0.619) and avgpool > transformer for aggregation, but the image encoder (resnet50) is very weak in isolation (0.208 acc in config_010). The ~3-5% multimodal boost over RNA-only (0.591→0.639) is real but modest, and it's unclear whether this reflects a genuine image signal or a ceiling imposed by the weak resnet50 encoder. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l (config_025) while keeping the validated best RNA encoder (pca_n2000), aggregation (avgpool), and fusion (weighted) yield a meaningful additional gain? Why this is the best next experiment: It directly extends the current best by changing only the weakest component, cleanly isolating the image encoder's contribution. If config_025 substantially exceeds 0.639, image modality is a real signal source worth further investment (e.g., better aggregation or fusion). If it barely improves, the image contribution is inherently limited and budget should shift to RNA encoder exploration (scvi/scgpt). This single experiment resolves a critical design-direction question under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all completed experiments have used only this encoder. The RNA encoder is the single largest untested design axis—no scvi_n200 or scgpt results exist yet. Aggregation (avgpool > transformer) and fusion (weighted > concat) are already characterized, and the image encoder choice (resnet50 vs ViT-L) shows negligible difference (0.639 vs 0.635). Question: Does a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) improve over PCA in the best-performing multimodal configuration? Why this is the best next step: config_031 is identical to config_019 except for the RNA encoder, giving a clean one-variable comparison.
