If it matches or beats config_036, it opens config_039; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool as the reliable choice and redirects budget toward other axes. This is the highest-information next step: it exploits the strongest direction while resolving a design choice that previously showed a meaningful performance gap.

With no prior experiments completed, there is no evidence to exploit, so the priority is establishing a reference baseline that maximizes information gain for all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest 'null' configuration in the search space: no image modality, no multiprofile aggregation, and the most straightforward RNA encoder (PCA). Establishing this baseline is critical because every other design decision—adding image data (config_010/016), switching to multiprofile (config_002/003), upgrading the RNA encoder to scVI or scGPT (config_004/007), or introducing multimodal fusion (config_016/017)—can be evaluated as a delta relative to this reference. Without it, we cannot determine whether any added complexity actually improves validation accuracy or F1. It is also the lowest-risk configuration (fewer moving parts, less chance of implementation issues), making it the most reliable first data point under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), evidence is extremely sparse. The most fundamental uncertainty for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries independent predictive signal. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly tests this: if image-only accuracy is substantially higher than 0.485, it confirms the image channel is informative and justifies investing subsequent budget in multimodal fusion configurations; if it is similarly low, it suggests the task is intrinsically difficult or that neither single modality suffices, redirecting effort toward better encoders or multiprofile aggregation. ResNet50 is chosen over ViT-L as the lighter, more standard first probe. This experiment reduces the largest structural uncertainty (modality contribution) before committing budget to the many multimodal combinations, making it the highest-information next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieved 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) achieved only 20.8% acc, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. The key uncertainty now is whether the RNA representation itself can be improved. PCA (2000-dim linear projection) is a very basic encoder; scvi_n200 is a learned nonlinear generative encoder that may capture more task-relevant cell structure in a compact 200-dim latent space. This experiment (config_004) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001 (same singleprofile setting, only the RNA encoder changes), directly testing whether a learned encoder outperforms PCA. It is the best use of the next budget slot because the RNA encoder choice is the most fundamental design decision—it will inform every subsequent multimodal experiment and determines whether we should prioritize encoder quality or structural changes (multiprofile, aggregation) in later experiments. A large gap would shift strategy toward learned encoders; a small gap would confirm PCA sufficiency and redirect exploration toward profile structure or fusion.

Evidence: scVI n200 (config_004, acc 0.520) is our best result and clearly outperforms PCA n2000 (config_001, acc 0.485), establishing a strong RNA encoder. Image-only (config_010, acc 0.208) is very weak, making the RNA pathway the dominant signal. Uncertainty: We have zero data on whether multiprofile aggregation can improve upon single-profile performance, and this is a fundamental design axis that will affect all downstream multimodal experiments. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles with a transformer (the most expressive aggregation) on top of the best RNA encoder (scVI n200) yield a meaningful gain over the single-profile baseline? Why this is the best next experiment: It directly extends our strongest result along the most unexplored and consequential dimension (profile count + aggregation), uses the most powerful aggregation to establish an upper bound, and the answer will inform whether subsequent multimodal experiments should use single or multiprofile. If transformer aggregation fails to improve, avgpool likely won't either, saving future budget.

Evidence: config_006 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) achieved 0.653 acc, a large jump over config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) at 0.520, confirming multiprofile is highly beneficial. However, we cannot yet disentangle whether the gain comes from having multiple profiles per se or specifically from the transformer aggregation. Uncertainty: Is transformer aggregation the critical component, or would a simpler avgpool suffice? This experiment (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation of our best result. If avgpool approaches transformer performance, aggregation is a low-priority design choice and we can focus budget on encoder selection or multimodal fusion. If avgpool drops substantially, transformer is confirmed as essential, locking in that design decision for all future multimodal experiments (configs 020/021, 032/033, 038/039, 044/045, 050/051 all depend on this choice). Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental architectural question before investing in multimodal configurations is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: multiprofile + scvi_n200 + transformer achieved the best result so far (0.653 acc), and multiprofile was the single largest gain (+0.13 over singleprofile). scvi_n200 outperformed pca_n2000 in singleprofile (0.52 vs 0.485), but scgpt remains untested. Uncertainty: we do not know whether a generative pre-trained encoder (scgpt) could surpass scvi_n200 in the multiprofile regime, or whether the 0.65 ceiling is encoder-specific. This experiment tests whether scgpt + multiprofile + transformer can push past the current best, directly exploiting the strongest known configuration while exploring the last untested RNA encoder. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it targets the most impactful remaining design axis (RNA encoder quality) within the already-validated multiprofile/transformer setting, and the outcome—whether scgpt matches, beats, or falls below scvi_n200—sharply narrows the search space for all downstream multimodal experiments.

Evidence: RNA-only with scVI_n200 + multiprofile + transformer achieves the best result (0.653 acc), while image-only ResNet50 is very weak (0.208 acc). The multi-profile gain (~0.13) and encoder choice (scVI >> PCA >> scGPT) are well-established. The critical untested question is whether adding the weak image modality to the strong RNA signal via fusion provides any benefit or merely adds noise. This experiment (config_032) takes the proven best RNA backbone (scVI_n200, multiprofile, transformer) and adds ResNet50 image features via concat fusion, directly testing whether multimodal fusion can improve upon the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. It is the highest-information next step because the answer determines whether the entire multimodal search space (configs 016-051) is worth exploring further, or whether resources should be redirected to refining the RNA-only pipeline. Concat is chosen as the simpler, standard first fusion test before trying weighted variants.

Evidence: config_032 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, concat) is the best result so far at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1, showing that multimodal fusion adds ~3.5 points over the best RNA-only config (0.653). The only untested design dimension in this top-performing setup is the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted). Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation when combining the (relatively weak) image signal with the strong RNA signal? Rationale: This is a clean one-variable A/B test against the current best, making the result fully interpretable. If weighted fusion helps, it gives an immediate performance gain and suggests the model benefits from learned modality balancing; if not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward the image-encoder question (ViT-L vs. ResNet50). Under a limited budget, resolving this binary design choice in the context of the strongest configuration is the highest-information-per-experiment next step.

The current best is config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted; 0.713 acc). The most impactful untested variable in the multimodal pipeline is the image encoder: resnet50 alone yields only 0.208 acc in image-only mode, suggesting its features may be suboptimal. config_039 swaps resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings at their known-best values (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion). This is a clean single-variable experiment that directly tests whether a stronger, pretrained ViT-L encoder improves multimodal fusion. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it (1) extends the strongest evidence (config_033) along the most uncertain axis, (2) avoids re-testing already-clarified variables (fusion type, aggregation, RNA encoder), and (3) will inform whether further investment in image-encoder quality is worthwhile for subsequent experiments.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_039: ViT, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.7250 acc / 0.6847 F1. We have strong evidence that multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT image encoder, and weighted fusion are the right choices. However, the importance of transformer vs. avgpool aggregation in the multimodal setting remains uncertain: in RNA-only, the gap was negligible (0.6530 vs. 0.6501), suggesting aggregation may not be critical. Question: config_037 (ViT, avgpool, weighted) tests whether transformer aggregation is truly necessary in the multimodal context or whether the simpler avgpool suffices. If performance is comparable, it confirms a simpler, more efficient architecture; if it drops significantly, it validates that transformer aggregation is essential for integrating image and RNA features. This is the best next experiment because it is a single-variable perturbation of the current best, directly reduces uncertainty about a key architectural choice, and the RNA-only prior (tiny aggregation gap) makes the outcome genuinely informative rather than redundant.

No experiments have been completed, so the primary uncertainty is whether the basic pipeline is sound and what performance level to expect. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable baseline in the design space: it uses a fast, well-understood encoder (PCA), the simplest profile setting, and a single modality. Running this first establishes a reference performance level against which all subsequent encoder, profile, modality, and fusion choices can be meaningfully compared. If it performs poorly, we immediately know the issue lies in representation or task difficulty before investing budget in complex multimodal or transformer-based configurations. If it performs reasonably, it confirms the pipeline and lets us efficiently test whether multiprofile aggregation, learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), or adding an image modality provide incremental gains. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget by anchoring the entire search to a clear baseline.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries discriminative signal for this task. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to the existing baseline: same profile setting, a standard pretrained encoder, and no aggregation/fusion confounds. The result will (a) establish an image-only performance anchor, (b) reveal whether image features are informative at all, and (c) directly inform whether the large multimodal sub-space (configs 016–051) is worth pursuing or whether budget should be redirected to improving RNA representations. Under a tight budget, resolving this top-level modality question before committing to multimodal or encoder-specific experiments maximizes information gain per trial.

Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while image-only (resnet50, singleprofile) is near-random at 20.8%, strongly indicating RNA is the dominant signal. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether multiprofile aggregation (capturing multiple cell profiles per sample) improves over a single profile. Question tested: config_002 isolates the profile/aggregation axis by keeping the same encoder (pca_n2000) as config_001 but switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This directly compares single-profile vs. multi-profile representation for the RNA modality. Why this is the best next experiment: Since RNA is clearly the primary signal, optimizing its configuration is the highest-leverage use of a limited budget. Testing multiprofile+avgpool is the simplest and most natural extension of the current best result, providing a clean one-variable comparison. If it improves, we gain a stronger RNA baseline before exploring multimodal fusion or more complex aggregations (transformer). If it does not, we rule out multi-profile benefit and can redirect effort toward encoder choice (scvi, scgpt) or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large jump over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is highly beneficial. Image-only (config_010, 0.208) is far weaker, so the RNA pathway is the primary signal. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether transformer aggregation can outperform simple avgpool for multiprofile RNA. This experiment (config_003) isolates that single variable—aggregation method—while holding model_setting, profile_setting, and encoder constant, making it a clean A/B comparison against config_002. If transformer helps, it validates a more expressive aggregation strategy that would benefit all downstream multimodal configurations; if it does not, we can confidently default to avgpool and redirect budget toward encoder or fusion choices. Under a limited budget, resolving this foundational design question before exploring encoders or multimodal fusion is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: RNA-only with multi-profile + avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the clear best setup so far, and it uses PCA-2000 — the only RNA encoder tested. Image-only (config_010, acc=0.208) is far weaker, so the RNA branch dominates. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether a learned encoder (scvi_n200, scgpt) can outperform the simple linear PCA-2000 representation. This is a fundamental design axis that, if it matters, would reshape the entire search. What this tests: config_005 is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002 (same multi-profile, same avgpool aggregation; only PCA-2000 → scvi_n200). It directly measures whether a nonlinear, learned embedding captures cell-type structure that PCA misses. Why best next: With only 4 experiments done, the encoder choice is the largest unexplored dimension on the dominant modality. If scvi_n200 improves substantially, we know to prioritize encoder selection before investing in fusion; if it does not, we can confidently fix PCA-2000 and shift budget toward multimodal fusion experiments. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about a high-leverage design decision.

Evidence: The largest performance gain so far came from the RNA encoder choice (PCA→SCVI improved accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 with multiprofile+avgpool). Multiprofile and avgpool are now well-supported as the optimal settings. SCGPT is the only remaining untested RNA encoder. Question: Does SCGPT outperform SCVI under the same optimal multiprofile+avgpool setup? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only encoder changes) that directly tests whether we can push beyond the current best of 0.650. Why best use of budget: The encoder has been the dominant source of improvement; resolving whether SCGPT is superior or inferior to SCVI either yields a new best configuration or confirms SCVI as the ceiling for this dimension, allowing us to redirect remaining experiments toward other design axes (e.g., multimodal fusion or image encoder quality) with greater confidence.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (config_005) is the current best at 0.650 acc, and image-only (resnet50) is very weak at 0.208. The critical open question is whether combining the strong RNA signal with the weak image signal via fusion can exceed the RNA-only ceiling. This experiment (config_030: scvi_n200, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the most direct multimodal extension of the current best RNA-only configuration, using the simplest fusion (concat) and the already-characterized image encoder (resnet50). It tests the highest-level design question—does any image information add value on top of the best RNA setup?—while keeping all other hyperparameters matched to config_005 so any delta is attributable to the addition of the image modality and fusion. If it improves, it justifies further exploration of fusion type and image encoder; if it does not, it efficiently rules out a large block of multimodal configs and confirms RNA-only as the optimal architecture, saving budget for other refinements.

Evidence: The best RNA-only config (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 acc, while the only multimodal test (config_030: same RNA setup + resnet50 + concat fusion) achieves 0.632, slightly underperforming the unimodal baseline. This raises the question of whether concat fusion is the bottleneck or whether the image modality itself is unhelpful. Question tested: config_031 changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) while keeping all other settings identical to config_030, providing a controlled test of whether the fusion strategy explains the multimodal underperformance. Why best next experiment: It is the most informative single-variable experiment available. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds 0.650, we identify fusion strategy as a critical design lever and have a promising multimodal direction to exploit. If it also underperforms, we can rule out fusion as the issue and redirect budget toward testing a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) or confirming that RNA-only is the superior architecture. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about the most important remaining design decision (whether and how to combine modalities) under a tight budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc. The image-only ResNet50 baseline was very weak (0.208 acc), yet it still contributed ~2.8 points over RNA-only (0.650→0.678), suggesting the image modality's value may be bottlenecked by encoder quality. Uncertainty: Whether upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to a much larger pretrained VIT-L can unlock additional multimodal signal, or whether the image contribution is fundamentally limited regardless of encoder. This experiment (config_037) tests exactly that: it takes the proven best configuration and swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l while keeping the validated scvi_n200 RNA encoder, multiprofile, avgpool, and weighted fusion. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly probes the single largest unexplored axis (image encoder capacity) on the current best configuration, with high information value: a gain confirms the image modality is underutilized and justifies further image-side tuning, while a flat result tells us to focus remaining budget on RNA-side or fusion refinements.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) achieves 0.7062 accuracy. The only untested dimension within this best-performing combination is the aggregation method. Prior evidence (pca_n2000: avgpool 0.591 vs transformer 0.519) suggests avgpool may be preferred, but that was with a linear encoder; scvi_n200 produces richer, non-linear embeddings where a transformer could better capture inter-profile interactions. Config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is a clean single-variable ablation of the current best, directly testing whether transformer aggregation can push performance above 0.7062 or confirm avgpool as optimal. This is the highest-value next step: it either yields a new best or definitively closes the aggregation question for the top-performing pipeline, allowing the remaining budget to focus on other axes (e.g., scgpt multimodal or singleprofile variants).

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no baseline performance for any modality or design choice. The entire configuration space spans RNA-only, image-only, and multimodal settings with multiple encoders, profile strategies, and aggregation/fusion options, making it critical to first establish a reference point. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard baseline—using a well-understood linear encoder (PCA) on a single RNA profile with no image input. It establishes how much predictive signal RNA alone provides under a minimal pipeline. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting from the simplest configuration maximizes the information gained per experiment. Every subsequent configuration (adding image, switching to multiprofile, using scvi/scgpt, changing aggregation/fusion) can be interpreted as a controlled modification relative to this baseline. This anchors the sequential search, allowing later experiments to attribute performance gains or losses to specific design decisions rather than to an unknown compound effect. It is also the fastest to run (no image encoder, no aggregation), conserving compute for later, more complex experiments.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), so nearly all design dimensions remain unexplored. The most consequential architectural question is whether the image modality adds value at all. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is a minimal, clean extension of config_001: it keeps the exact same RNA pipeline and profile setting and adds only the image branch with the simplest standard fusion (concat). This lets us directly attribute any accuracy/F1 change to the inclusion of image features. If it improves over 48.5%, we gain strong evidence to invest further in multimodal configurations (encoder choice, fusion strategy, multiprofile). If it does not, we can rule out the image modality early and concentrate the remaining budget on RNA-only design choices (encoder, multiprofile, aggregation). Resnet50 is chosen over ViT-L as the more standard, lower-risk starting point. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-impact design decision under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.5266 acc / 0.5104 F1, a clear ~4% gain over the RNA-only baseline (config_001, 0.4849). This confirms that image features add value, but we have no information on whether the simple concat fusion is optimal or whether a learned weighted fusion could further improve the combination. Question tested: config_017 is an isolated change from config_016—only the fusion strategy shifts from concat to weighted—so it cleanly measures whether the fusion mechanism matters at this stage. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is the most controlled comparison available, changing exactly one variable, so the result is interpretable without confounding. (2) The fusion choice is a foundational design decision that propagates to every subsequent multimodal configuration (multiprofile, different encoders); knowing whether weighted > concat now prevents wasting budget on suboptimal fusion variants later. (3) If weighted fusion yields a meaningful gain, it signals that the combination mechanism is a lever worth exploring further; if it does not, we can confidently fix concat and redirect budget toward higher-uncertainty questions like multiprofile aggregation or alternative RNA encoders.

Evidence: The three completed experiments show that adding a ResNet50 image encoder to PCA-2000 RNA features (config_016, acc 0.527) substantially outperforms RNA alone (config_001, acc 0.485), and concat fusion slightly edges out weighted fusion (0.527 vs 0.523). However, all experiments used singleprofile, leaving the multiprofile + aggregation axis completely untested. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) into the multimodal pipeline improve over the single-profile baseline, and if so, by how much? config_018 is the minimal, controlled extension of the best-performing config_016—changing only profile_setting to multiprofile and adding avgpool aggregation—so any performance shift can be attributed to the multiprofile/aggregation design choice. Why best next: Under a limited budget, resolving whether multiprofile is beneficial is the highest-leverage uncertainty; it gates whether the many transformer-aggregation and multiprofile variants (configs 020–051) are worth pursuing, and it directly extends the strongest evidence we already have rather than exploring a new encoder in isolation.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, a ~9-point jump over the best singleprofile multimodal result (config_016, 0.527). This strongly suggests multiprofile aggregation is a critical design axis. However, we have only tested the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether a transformer-based aggregation can capture inter-profile relationships that simple mean-pooling misses, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this task. This experiment (config_020) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat fusion, multiprofile) constant, making it a clean controlled comparison against config_018. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, it identifies aggregation architecture as a high-value axis to further explore; if it performs similarly, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and redirects budget toward other axes (image encoder, RNA encoder). This is the best use of the next experiment because it directly extends the strongest finding with a minimal, interpretable change that reduces uncertainty about a key architectural decision.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile + avgpool + concat is the strongest architecture. However, all experiments to date use only pca_n2000 (a linear dimensionality reduction) as the RNA encoder, leaving a major design axis unexplored. Question: Does replacing PCA with a learned nonlinear RNA representation (scvi_n200) improve performance in the best multimodal pipeline? config_030 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n200 to scvi_n200 while keeping the proven multiprofile/avgpool/concat/resnet50 architecture, making it a clean single-variable test. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA modality is the primary biological signal; PCA may discard nonlinear structure that scvi's VAE latent captures. If scvi_n200 improves accuracy, it identifies RNA representation as a key lever for further gains (and motivates testing scgpt). If it does not, we learn PCA is sufficient and should pivot to the image encoder (ViT-L) or fusion strategy. Under a limited budget, this single-variable extension of the current best config maximizes information about the most impactful untested design choice.

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) with acc=0.632. All completed experiments have used resnet50 as the image encoder; the image encoder architecture is a completely unexplored, high-impact design dimension given that adding the image modality was the single largest gain observed (0.485→0.619). Question tested: Does upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to a stronger pretrained ViT-L (imagenet_vit_l) improve performance when all other settings are held at their best-known values (multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, concat)? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of the current best, isolating the image encoder effect while keeping the already-validated choices (multiprofile > singleprofile, scvi_n200 ≥ pca_n2000, avgpool > transformer, concat ≈ weighted). A positive result would identify a new promising direction; a null result would confirm ResNet50 is sufficient and redirect budget toward other unexplored dimensions (e.g., scgpt encoder or fusion strategy). Under a limited budget, resolving this major architectural question is more informative than testing smaller variations (e.g., weighted vs. concat fusion, which showed negligible difference).

Evidence: config_036 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.715 acc / 0.687 F1. The largest gains came from ViT-L over ResNet50 (+8.3%) and multi-profile over single-profile. Fusion strategy evidence is weak: concat marginally beat weighted with ResNet50 (0.527 vs 0.523, ~0.4% gap, within noise). Question: Does the fusion strategy (concat vs weighted) interact differently with the much stronger ViT-L image features? This experiment changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while holding all other dimensions at their empirically best values (scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, multiprofile). Why best use of budget: It is a minimal, clean one-variable test that directly reduces uncertainty about whether fusion is an important design axis under the strongest image encoder. If weighted outperforms concat here, it opens a new optimization direction; if not, it confirms concat is sufficient and we can focus remaining budget on untested dimensions (e.g., scgpt RNA encoder or transformer aggregation with ViT-L).

The current best configuration is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 acc. The evidence clearly shows that multimodal + multiprofile + scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat is the dominant design, but the RNA encoder dimension remains under-explored: scgpt has never been tested in any completed experiment. Config_048 (scgpt + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is a single-variable change from the current best, isolating the RNA encoder choice (scgpt vs scVI) while holding all other factors at their known-optimal settings. This is the highest-information next step: if scgpt matches or exceeds scVI, we discover a new best configuration; if it underperforms, we can confidently eliminate the entire scgpt branch (configs 040–051) and focus remaining budget on refining the scVI+ViT-L pipeline (e.g., testing transformer aggregation in config_038). Given the limited budget, resolving whether scgpt is competitive is more informative than testing a second aggregation variant where existing evidence (config_018 vs 020) already favors avgpool.

The best-performing configuration so far is config_036 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.7150 acc. The only aggregation method tested in this top regime is avgpool. Prior evidence (config_018 vs 020) showed avgpool > transformer by ~4 pts, but that was in a much weaker regime (pca_n2000 + resnet50). With the substantially stronger scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l encoders, the feature representations are richer and a transformer aggregation might better capture cross-profile interactions, potentially closing or reversing the gap. Config_038 (transformer, concat) is the minimal, logical extension of the best config that tests whether the aggregation choice is a binding constraint in this regime. If it matches or beats avgpool, it opens a new design axis; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool is optimal and frees budget to explore other dimensions. This is the highest-information single experiment because it directly probes the one untested variable in the current best configuration.

With no prior evidence, the highest-priority uncertainty is establishing a clean single-modality baseline. config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, least confounded configuration: it uses a standard linear encoder (PCA), avoids aggregation complexity (single profile), and isolates the RNA signal. This gives a reference accuracy/F1 against which I can later (a) compare the image modality (config_010) to determine which modality carries more discriminative signal, and (b) assess whether multimodal fusion actually adds value over the best single modality. Starting with a minimal baseline maximizes interpretability of every subsequent experiment and prevents attributing multimodal gains to encoder or aggregation choices that are simultaneously being varied.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether adding image information at all is beneficial in this multimodal cellular profiling task. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal, clean extension of the baseline: it keeps the same profile setting (singleprofile) and RNA encoder (pca_n2000), adds a standard ResNet50 image encoder, and uses the simplest fusion (concat). This directly tests the core hypothesis of the study—does the image modality contribute complementary signal beyond RNA?—while changing the fewest possible variables. If multimodal significantly outperforms the 48.5% baseline, we gain strong evidence to invest remaining budget in optimizing image encoders, fusion strategies, and multiprofile aggregation. If it does not, we learn early that the image branch is not helping and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder upgrades (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. Under a tight budget with near-zero evidence, resolving this top-level design question is far more informative than tuning secondary choices (aggregation, fusion type, or encoder variant) within a modality whose value we have not yet established.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieved 0.485 acc, and config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) improved to 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, confirming that adding image features with concat fusion is beneficial. However, we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile aggregation provides additional value over singleprofile. This is a major architectural axis that, if positive, could unlock a whole family of higher-performing configs. Config_018 directly extends the current best (config_016) by switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while holding all other factors constant (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat), making it a clean ablation of the profile/aggregation decision. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because it resolves a binary architectural question that gates many downstream decisions.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, and the single→multi-profile jump (+9.2%) was the largest improvement observed, indicating that how multiple profiles are aggregated is a critical design lever. Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc, showing that multi-profile + avgpool aggregation and multimodal fusion are both critical. Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder with resnet50, avgpool, and weighted fusion. This is more informative than filling in the transformer+weighted cell (config_021), where the expected gain is small given that avgpool already dominates transformer by ~0.04 with concat fusion.

Evidence: The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) at 0.678 acc. Evidence: The current best (config_037, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706) establishes that multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion, and imagenet_vit_l are all beneficial. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 and redirects budget toward other levers (e.g., transformer aggregation at the top level or singleprofile trade-offs). The current best configuration is config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 acc. With scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l producing richer, higher-dimensional representations, a transformer aggregation could potentially capture inter-profile interactions that simple averaging misses. Testing config_039 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) directly extends the best configuration along the most uncertain remaining axis. With no completed experiments, there is no evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest and most standard configuration in the design space: it uses PCA (the most common and well-understood dimensionality reduction), a single profile (no aggregation complexity), and no image modality. This gives a clear reference performance against which every other design axis—multiprofile vs. singleprofile, alternative RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), adding image data, and fusion strategy—can be meaningfully compared in subsequent experiments. Starting from the simplest RNA-only baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment because any future performance delta can be attributed to one specific design change rather than confounded by multiple simultaneous deviations from an unknown starting point.

We have only one data point (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), so the most critical uncertainty is whether adding image information (the core premise of a multimodal study) provides any benefit over the RNA-only baseline. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) differs from config_001 by exactly one design decision—adding image features via the simplest fusion (concat) and a standard encoder (resnet50). This makes it a clean, interpretable A/B comparison: if accuracy improves meaningfully over 48.5%, we confirm multimodal fusion is worthwhile and can then explore encoder/aggregation/fusion variants; if it does not, we redirect budget toward RNA-only improvements (better encoders, multiprofile). Testing multimodal first is more informative than testing image_only alone, because even weak image features can be complementary to RNA, and the direct comparison to our existing baseline isolates the fusion benefit. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieved 0.485 acc, while config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) improved to 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, confirming that adding the image modality with concat fusion is beneficial. With only 2 experiments completed, resolving this major axis is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best result so far (acc=0.619, F1=0.610), showing that multiprofile + multimodal is the strongest direction. Transformer aggregation could capture non-linear, context-dependent interactions between profiles that avgpool cannot, potentially yielding further gains. Isolating this one variable (rather than changing both aggregation and fusion as in config_021) maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation is the dominant architectural choice. Evidence: The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) clearly establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest combination tested. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc. Evidence: The current best (config_019, avgpool+weighted, acc=0.639) sits within a 2×2 grid of aggregation×fusion that is nearly complete: avgpool+concat=0.619, transformer+concat=0.579, avgpool+weighted=0.639, but transformer+weighted is untested. Under a tight budget, locking down this core architectural decision (so we don't waste future experiments on a suboptimal aggregator) is more informative than exploring scvi_n200, which is less likely to surpass pca_n2000 given scgpt's large deficit.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted. We know scgpt as an RNA encoder performs poorly (config_043, acc=0.525, a ~11-point drop), but scvi_n200 remains untested in the multimodal multiprofile regime. Evidence: config_031 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted + multiprofile) is the current best at 0.6776 acc, establishing that scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA encoder and avgpool+weighted is the best aggregation/fusion pairing. The only untested dimension within this 'best-known' configuration is the image encoder: with pca_n2000, ViT-L was marginally worse than ResNet50 (0.6352 vs 0.6390), but the interaction with a stronger RNA encoder is unknown. With no prior experiments completed, there is zero evidence about which design choices matter. With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 at ~48.5% accuracy), the dominant uncertainty is which modality carries the most discriminative signal. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly compares the image modality against the RNA baseline while holding profile_setting constant, isolating the modality effect. Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image-only, singleprofile, resnet50) is much weaker at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc=0.591, F1=0.573), a substantial +10.6% improvement over singleprofile (config_001, acc=0.485). This experiment (config_003) isolates the aggregation variable by changing only avgpool→transformer while holding everything else at the known-best setting (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000). Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with pca_n2000 and avgpool (config_002) is the clear best at 0.591 acc, while image-only resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208 acc. It is the most informative next step because: (1) it tests the single most important open question—whether multimodal fusion adds value over the best unimodal result; (2) concat is the simplest fusion, so if it fails to beat 0.591, we gain strong evidence that the image signal is too weak/noisy to be useful regardless of fusion strategy; (3) it uses the already-characterized resnet50 encoder, isolating the fusion question from encoder choice. Under a limited budget, this single experiment most efficiently reduces uncertainty about the core design decision of whether to pursue multimodal fusion at all.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, only marginally above RNA-only avgpool (0.591). Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses PCA n2000 as the RNA encoder within a multimodal multi-profile avgpool weighted-fusion setup. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The RNA encoder choice has shown the largest single-factor improvement so far (pca_n2000 → scvi_n200 yielded +3.9% acc in the multimodal setting: 0.639 → 0.678). The current best config (config_031: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, resnet50) achieves 0.678 acc. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether scgpt, a more expressive pre-trained RNA encoder, can further improve on scvi_n200 in this multimodal context. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of the most productive design axis identified so far (RNA encoder quality), keeps all other knobs at their validated optima, and directly determines whether the RNA encoder dimension still has headroom to exploit before investing budget in less-certain axes like the image encoder (which showed very weak standalone signal at 0.208 acc).

Evidence: config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the current best at 0.678 acc, clearly outperforming pca_n2000 (0.639) and scgpt (0.525) under identical settings. Evidence: The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 acc. All multimodal experiments so far have used avgpool aggregation; transformer aggregation has only been tested in RNA-only settings where it underperformed avgpool by ~7 points (0.519 vs 0.591). However, in the multimodal context with a strong ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation might capture cross-profile interactions that avgpool averages away, potentially complementing the image signal differently. Why this experiment: It is the single most informative next step because (1) it is a minimal, controlled change from the current best (only aggregation differs), isolating the effect of one design variable; (2) if it improves, it identifies a new promising direction; if it does not, it definitively rules out transformer aggregation for the top-performing family, saving future budget from exploring dead ends; (3) under a limited budget, confirming or refuting the best aggregation strategy at the highest-performing operating point maximizes information per experiment.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about which design choices (modality, encoder, profile strategy, aggregation, fusion) matter or interact. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard baseline in the design space. With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), the dominant uncertainty is whether adding image information in a multimodal setup meaningfully improves over the RNA-only baseline.
