If it improves, we identify a better aggregation strategy to build on; if it does not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or fusion-method variations. Under a tight budget, this maximizes information per experiment by isolating one hypothesis on the most promising configuration.

The current best is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 acc, and all multimodal experiments so far have used concat fusion. The only untested fusion strategy is weighted, which directly tests whether the modality combination mechanism matters beyond simple concatenation. This is a clean single-variable change from the current best, so any performance shift can be cleanly attributed to fusion strategy. Given the limited budget, exploiting the strongest known direction (multiprofile + vit_l + avgpool) while resolving the fusion question is more informative than introducing an untested RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt) whose standalone performance is unknown. If weighted fusion improves on concat, we gain a better configuration immediately; if not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect effort to RNA encoder choice.

The current best (config_025, acc=0.635) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all completed multimodal experiments share this encoder. We have zero evidence on whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) could improve the RNA representation in the multimodal context. The aggregation (avgpool > transformer) and fusion (weighted > concat) questions are relatively well-resolved with small deltas (~3-6%), but the RNA encoder is a major unexplored design axis with potentially larger impact. Config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap from the current best, directly testing whether a variational autoencoder-based RNA representation outperforms linear PCA. This is the highest-information experiment: it either reveals a new best configuration or confirms PCA is sufficient, and the answer will guide all subsequent encoder choices across the remaining search space.

The strongest evidence so far is that switching the RNA encoder from PCA (config_025, 0.6352) to scVI (config_037, 0.7062) yielded a ~7-point accuracy gain, confirming that a learned RNA representation is the most impactful design axis. However, we have only tested one learned encoder (scVI). Config_049 (scGPT, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) isolates the question of whether the specific learned encoder matters or whether any learned representation suffices, while holding all other settings at their proven-best values. If scGPT matches scVI, we learn the key insight is 'use a learned encoder' and can redirect budget to other axes (e.g., aggregation). If scGPT underperforms, we confirm scVI's architecture is specifically important. This reduces uncertainty on the highest-leverage untested design dimension, making it the most informative use of the next experiment.

The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200, vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted; acc 0.706). With PCA, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer aggregation (config_024: 0.629 vs config_026: 0.599). However, scvi_n200 produces a structured, learned latent representation rather than a linear projection, so a transformer aggregator may be able to exploit inter-profile dependencies that simple averaging discards. Config_039 changes exactly one variable (avgpool→transformer) from the current best while keeping the proven scvi_n200 + vit_l + multiprofile + weighted backbone. If transformer matches or exceeds avgpool here, it reveals that the aggregation choice is encoder-dependent and opens a new design axis; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool is robustly superior regardless of RNA encoder, reducing future search uncertainty. This is the highest-information single-step exploitation from the current best under a limited budget.

With zero completed experiments, the dominant uncertainty is the absolute performance level of this task and the contribution of each design axis. Config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable RNA-only baseline: PCA is a well-understood linear encoder and singleprofile removes all aggregation/fusion confounds. Establishing this floor is the single most informative first step because (1) it anchors every subsequent comparison—without it, a multimodal or multiprofile result cannot be attributed to a specific design choice; (2) it isolates the RNA signal quality and the task difficulty, which are the two variables that gate all downstream decisions; and (3) it is computationally cheap, preserving budget for the follow-up experiments (image-only baseline, multiprofile aggregation, and multimodal fusion) that will follow logically once the RNA floor is known. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the most fundamental question: 'how well can RNA alone solve this task with a minimal pipeline?'

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) has been completed, yielding ~48.5% accuracy. This gives us almost no information about which design dimensions matter. The most fundamental question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit over RNA-only. Question: Does multimodal fusion (adding resnet50 image features via concat) improve validation accuracy over the RNA-only baseline? config_016 keeps the RNA side identical to config_001 (pca_n2000, singleprofile) and adds the simplest, most standard image setup (resnet50, concat fusion), cleanly isolating the effect of the image modality. Why this is the best next step: With only one data point, the highest-uncertainty decision is whether multimodal is worth pursuing at all. A positive result justifies investing remaining budget in fusion strategies, image encoder choices, and multiprofile aggregation within the multimodal space. A negative result redirects effort toward RNA-encoder and profile-setting improvements. No other single experiment reduces uncertainty about this pivotal design choice as efficiently.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.5266 accuracy, a clear +4.2% gain over the RNA-only baseline (config_001, 0.4849), confirming that adding image features via concat fusion is beneficial. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether multiprofile (with an aggregation step) adds further value on top of the multimodal gain, or whether singleprofile is already sufficient. Question: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) isolates the multiprofile dimension while keeping the proven multimodal+resnet50+concat backbone. Why best next: It is the most informative single experiment because a positive result opens the entire multiprofile+aggregation subspace (transformer aggregation, other encoders) for further exploitation, while a negative result confirms singleprofile sufficiency and redirects budget toward RNA/image encoder or fusion-strategy variations. It directly extends the strongest configuration with one new variable, maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best result (acc=0.619, F1=0.610), showing a large gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_016, acc=0.527). This jump was driven by the multiprofile+avgpool combination, but we have not yet tested whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over simple average pooling. Question: config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat fusion) identical to the current best. This is a clean single-variable test of whether the aggregation strategy is at its ceiling or whether capturing inter-profile interactions via a transformer yields additional gains. Why this is the best next experiment: the aggregation method is the most fundamental architectural decision in the multiprofile pipeline, and resolving it early (before exploring RNA encoder variants, image encoder variants, or fusion strategies) maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget. If transformer outperforms avgpool, it opens a new promising axis; if not, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and can redirect effort to other design dimensions.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far at 0.619 acc, and avgpool clearly outperforms transformer aggregation (0.619 vs 0.579). However, all multimodal results to date used concat fusion; the effect of weighted fusion is entirely untested. Question: config_019 is a single-variable change from config_018 (concat → weighted fusion), cleanly isolating whether learned modality weighting can improve upon simple concatenation in the best-performing setup. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the lowest-risk, highest-information-value exploitation of the current best configuration. If weighted fusion helps, we immediately have a better config and a new productive axis; if it does not, we rule out fusion as a lever and can confidently pivot to testing a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or learned RNA encoder (SCVI/scGPT) in subsequent experiments, avoiding wasted budget on a dimension that does not matter.

The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest architecture. However, the image encoder axis is completely unexplored in the multimodal setting—we have only tested ResNet50. Config_025 swaps the image encoder to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L while holding all other settings at their proven-best values (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, pca_n2000). This is a clean single-variable test: if ViT-L improves performance, it reveals the image modality is underutilized and opens a new optimization direction; if it does not, it confirms ResNet50 is sufficient and redirects effort toward the RNA encoder axis (scVI, scGPT). Under a limited budget, this experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about one of the two major unexplored design axes (image encoder vs. RNA encoder) while preserving all settings that have shown strong evidence of benefit.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all six completed experiments share this encoder. The key unexplored dimension is whether a learned RNA representation (scvi_n200) can improve upon PCA in the multimodal setting. Config_031 tests scvi_n200 while holding all other settings at their empirically best values (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion). This is the highest-information experiment because: (1) it directly addresses the largest remaining uncertainty—whether the RNA bottleneck is the encoder or something else; (2) if scvi_n200 improves, it opens a strong exploitation path; if it does not, we can rule out learned RNA encoders as a lever and focus remaining budget on other axes; (3) compared to testing transformer+weighted (config_021), which is unlikely to beat avgpool+weighted given the 4-point gap already observed with concat, the RNA encoder question has far greater potential to shift the performance landscape.

1) Evidence: The current best (config_031: SCVI+ResNet50+avgpool+weighted, acc 0.678) was achieved by upgrading the RNA encoder from PCA to SCVI (+4%). The image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT) showed negligible difference under PCA (0.639 vs 0.635), but this interaction has not been tested under SCVI's richer latent representations. 2) This experiment (config_037: SCVI+ViT+avgpool+weighted) completes the 2×2 grid of RNA encoder × image encoder within the confirmed-best framework (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted), directly testing whether ViT's hierarchical features complement SCVI's learned space more effectively than ResNet50's. 3) Under a limited budget, this is the highest-value exploitation step: it is low-risk (all other components are validated winners), it could yield a new best configuration, and it definitively resolves whether the image-encoder dimension still matters once SCVI is in place—freeing future experiments to focus on the remaining unexplored RNA encoder (SCGPT) or aggregation variants.

Evidence: The current best (config_037, scvi_n200 + vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706) establishes that multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion, and vit_l are strong choices, and scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 by ~4%. However, scgpt—a fundamentally different generative RNA encoder—has never been tested in any multimodal configuration, leaving a major source of uncertainty about whether an alternative learned representation could match or exceed scvi_n200. This experiment (config_049: scgpt + vit_l + avgpool + weighted + multiprofile) isolates the RNA encoder as the single variable against the best-known settings for all other dimensions. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it reduces uncertainty on the highest-impact unexplored axis: if scgpt performs comparably, it opens a new search branch; if it underperforms significantly, it confirms scvi_n200 as the optimal encoder and lets us concentrate remaining experiments on finer-grained choices (e.g., transformer vs avgpool with scvi_n200, or concat vs weighted).

Evidence: The current best (config_037: scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.706 acc. Prior experiments show avgpool outperformed transformer by ~0.06 (config_019 vs config_020, both pca_n2000/resnet50), the largest single-variable effect observed. However, this aggregation comparison was only tested with the weaker pca_n2000 encoder. Uncertainty: It is untested whether transformer aggregation might interact favorably with the richer scvi_n200 representations and the higher-dimensional vit_l features, potentially closing or reversing the gap. This experiment (config_039) is a clean single-variable swap (avgpool→transformer) from the current best, directly testing whether the aggregation preference is encoder-agnostic. If transformer is again inferior, we can confidently lock in avgpool for all remaining experiments; if it performs competitively or better, it reveals an important interaction effect that changes the design space. Under a limited budget, confirming or ruling out the aggregation choice for the top-performing encoder pair is the highest-information next step before further exploitation.

With no prior experiments, the highest-priority uncertainty is the performance floor of the simplest baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most basic configuration in the search space: a linear PCA projection of a single RNA profile with no image branch, no learned encoder, and no aggregation. Running it first establishes a clear reference accuracy/F1 against which every subsequent design decision—multiprofile vs. singleprofile, learned encoders (scvi, scgpt) vs. PCA, image modality addition, and fusion strategy—can be measured. It is also computationally the cheapest option (no image encoding, no transformer), preserving budget for the more expensive multimodal experiments that follow. Without this anchor, any improvement observed in later, more complex configurations would be uninterpretable: we could not distinguish gains from added modality, added profile complexity, or simply a better encoder. Starting here maximizes information per experiment by reducing the largest source of uncertainty (the baseline) before exploring the higher-complexity regions of the space.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries complementary or superior signal relative to RNA. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to the existing baseline: same profile_setting (singleprofile), same simplicity (no aggregation/fusion), only the modality changes. If image_only substantially outperforms 48.5%, it justifies investing remaining budget in multimodal configurations and tells us the image encoder is the stronger backbone. If it performs similarly or worse, it indicates RNA is the primary signal and we should prioritize RNA encoder upgrades or multiprofile aggregation. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (modality) before committing budget to more complex multimodal or aggregation variants, making it the highest-information-use next step under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA n2000 (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while image-only with ResNet50 (config_010) is very weak at 20.8%, making RNA the dominant signal. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether multiprofile aggregation improves upon the single-profile RNA baseline. This experiment (config_002) isolates the profile-setting variable by keeping the same PCA n2000 encoder and adding multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, directly testing whether multiple cell profiles per sample carry complementary information. It is the best next step because it is the cleanest single-variable extension of our best-performing configuration, uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) as a principled baseline before trying more complex alternatives, and its outcome will determine whether to invest further in multiprofile+transformer, better RNA encoders, or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large +10.6pp gain over singleprofile (config_001, 0.485 acc), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is the most impactful design choice so far. Image-only is very weak (0.208), so the RNA side is where the signal lives. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over the simple avgpool, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this data. This experiment (config_003) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002—only the aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer—so any performance difference is directly attributable to the aggregation strategy. Why it is the best next step: (1) it resolves a fundamental structural question that will inform every subsequent multiprofile and multimodal experiment (e.g., configs 020/021/026/027 all use transformer aggregation); (2) if transformer helps, it justifies investing in transformer-based multimodal configs; if it does not, we can prune that axis and focus budget on encoder choice or fusion strategy; (3) it stays within the well-characterized RNA-only space where signal is strong, making the result interpretable rather than confounded by the weak image modality.

Evidence: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, and the only RNA encoder tested so far is PCA. We have zero data on whether a learned encoder (scvi, scgpt) can improve upon PCA. Image-only is very weak (0.208), so the RNA branch dominates performance. Uncertainty: The RNA encoder choice is a fundamental design decision that propagates to all multimodal configurations, yet it is completely untested. What this tests: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean A/B comparison against config_002—identical profile setting and aggregation, only the encoder changes. This isolates the effect of a learned variational encoder vs. linear PCA. Why best next: If scvi significantly outperforms PCA, it reshapes the entire search (prioritize scvi in multimodal); if it is comparable, PCA is sufficient and we can pivot to fusion strategy. Either outcome reduces the largest remaining uncertainty and directly informs the next 3-4 experiments, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved the best performance so far (acc=0.650, F1=0.628), clearly outperforming pca_n2000 under identical settings (config_002: acc=0.591). This confirms that learned RNA encoders help, but we have not yet tested scgpt, the third available RNA encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder under the same multiprofile+avgpool conditions? Why this is the best next step: config_008 provides a clean, controlled comparison against config_005 (only the RNA encoder changes). Resolving which learned encoder is superior is a critical design decision that directly determines the baseline for all subsequent multimodal experiments. Testing multimodal fusion now with an unconfirmed RNA encoder risks confounding the fusion question with an encoder choice. This experiment reduces uncertainty on the most impactful single variable before committing budget to the larger multimodal search space.

Evidence: The best unimodal result is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc, with clear evidence that scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 > scgpt, multiprofile > singleprofile, and avgpool > transformer. Image alone (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 0.208. The critical open question is whether multimodal fusion can surpass the best RNA-only result, and whether a stronger image encoder (ViT-L vs ResNet50) changes the picture. This experiment (config_036) pairs the best-supported RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) with the strongest available image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) and a standard concat fusion. It directly tests whether adding a powerful visual signal to the dominant RNA signal yields a meaningful gain over 0.650. If it does, subsequent experiments can explore fusion strategy and image encoder trade-offs; if it does not, the budget is better spent refining RNA-only designs. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the single most consequential design decision (unimodal vs. multimodal) using the strongest available components on each side.

Evidence: config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.715 acc, a substantial jump over the best RNA-only (0.650), confirming that the image modality adds meaningful signal. However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat) in the multimodal setting. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation when combining a strong RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with a strong image encoder (imagenet_vit_l)? Given that the two modalities have very different standalone performance (RNA ~0.65 vs image ~0.21), a weighted fusion that down-weights the weaker modality could improve the joint representation. Why this is the best next experiment: config_037 is a minimal, single-variable change from the current best (only fusion: concat→weighted), giving a clean A/B comparison that directly reduces uncertainty about whether the fusion mechanism is a bottleneck. The result will inform whether to invest further in fusion tuning or to pivot toward other dimensions (e.g., aggregation strategy or image encoder choice) in subsequent experiments.

The current best configuration (config_036: multimodal, scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat; acc=0.715) establishes that multimodal fusion with scvi_n200 and ViT-L is the strongest direction. However, we only have one aggregation test in the multimodal setting (avgpool). In the RNA-only setting, aggregation choice was a major factor (avgpool 0.591 vs transformer 0.519 for PCA), but this has not been validated in the multimodal regime where the interaction between image features and RNA features may alter the optimal aggregation strategy. Config_038 (multimodal, scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat) is a minimal, controlled change from config_036 that directly tests whether transformer aggregation can outperform avgpool when both modalities are present. If transformer underperforms, it confirms avgpool as the robust choice and lets us focus remaining budget on other dimensions (e.g., RNA encoder or image encoder). If transformer outperforms, it reveals a new promising direction. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves a key architectural uncertainty in the currently best-performing family with a single clean comparison.

Evidence: The strongest direction is clearly multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l (config_036: 0.715, config_037: 0.706, config_038: 0.721). Within this family, we have a 2×2 grid of aggregation (avgpool/transformer) × fusion (concat/weighted) with three of four cells filled. The missing cell is transformer + weighted (config_039). Current evidence suggests concat > weighted (0.715 vs 0.706) and transformer ≥ avgpool (0.721 vs 0.715), but each comparison rests on a single data point. Question tested: Does the weighted-fusion penalty persist under transformer aggregation, or does transformer aggregation mitigate the information loss from weighted fusion? This clarifies whether the interaction between aggregation and fusion is significant or whether the main effects (prefer concat, prefer transformer) are sufficient. Why best next experiment: Completing this small factorial design is the highest-information, lowest-risk use of the next budget slot. It sits squarely in the proven best-performing region, will yield a configuration likely near 0.71+, and will give a definitive recommendation on the aggregation×fusion choice for the final architecture without the uncertainty of jumping to an untested dimension (e.g., resnet50 image encoder, which performed poorly standalone at 0.208).

No experiments have been completed, so the primary uncertainty is what the baseline performance looks like and which modality/architecture choices matter. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard configuration in the space: it uses a well-understood linear encoder (PCA), the simplest profile setting, and isolates the RNA signal without confounding from image features, complex aggregation, or fusion. Establishing this baseline is essential before interpreting any multimodal or image-only result, because it tells us (a) how much signal RNA alone carries, (b) the performance floor, and (c) how much headroom exists for the image modality or more complex architectures to exploit. Under a limited budget, this single experiment reduces the most uncertainty per trial by anchoring the entire comparison space.

The sole completed experiment (config_001, rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000) yields a low accuracy of 0.485, leaving substantial uncertainty about where the performance bottleneck lies. The most fundamental open question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries any independent predictive signal. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) cleanly tests this by isolating the image channel with a standard, well-understood encoder while removing RNA entirely. If image_only performs well, it confirms the image modality is informative and justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion strategies. If it performs poorly, it indicates the image channel needs a stronger encoder (e.g., ViT) or that signal is primarily in the RNA modality, redirecting effort toward better RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt). This experiment maximizes information per trial because the answer bifurcates the entire search strategy: it determines whether to prioritize multimodal configurations or RNA-encoder improvements in the remaining budget.

Evidence: RNA (PCA n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while image (ResNet50, singleprofile) achieves only 0.208—near chance level. This large gap raises a critical strategic question: is the image modality fundamentally uninformative for this task, or does it simply need a stronger encoder? This experiment (image_only, singleprofile, ViT-L) directly tests that question by changing only the encoder relative to config_010, keeping profile setting constant for a clean comparison. If ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, it validates the image modality and justifies investing in multimodal fusion experiments; if it remains poor, we can confidently deprioritize all ~36 multimodal configurations and focus remaining budget on RNA encoder/aggregation optimization. With only 2 experiments completed, resolving whether image is viable at all is the highest-information decision that shapes the entire subsequent search strategy.

Evidence: RNA-only with pca_n2000 (config_001) achieves 0.485 acc, far exceeding both image-only baselines (~0.21-0.23), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (pca_n2000, a linear projection). Uncertainty: whether a learned non-linear encoder (scvi_n200) captures richer single-cell structure that translates to better classification. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, isolating the RNA encoder choice while holding profile setting constant. It is the best use of the next budget slot because (1) it directly tests whether encoder sophistication matters before investing in more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations, (2) a positive result would justify exploring scvi_n200 in multimodal settings, while a null result would confirm pca_n2000 is sufficient and redirect effort toward profile aggregation or fusion strategies, and (3) it reduces uncertainty on a foundational design axis that underlies many downstream configuration choices.

Evidence: RNA-only models (pca_n2000: 0.485, scvi_n200: 0.520) substantially outperform image-only models (resnet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227), establishing RNA as the dominant signal. However, image performance is only slightly above chance, leaving genuine uncertainty about whether image features provide complementary information in a fused setting or merely add noise. Question tested: Does combining the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with the best image encoder (ViT-L) via simple concatenation in a singleprofile setting yield any gain over the RNA-only baseline of 0.520? This is the cleanest multimodal test—singleprofile minimizes confounding variables, and concat is the simplest fusion. Why best next experiment: Resolving whether multimodal fusion is viable at all is the highest-leverage structural decision. A positive result validates ~36 multimodal configurations for further exploration; a null or negative result efficiently prunes that entire branch, redirecting budget toward RNA-only multiprofile/aggregation and encoder choices where the signal clearly resides.

Evidence: RNA encoders (scvi_n200 at 0.520, pca_n2000 at 0.485) dominate over image-only models (~0.21-0.23), and the best result so far (config_034, multimodal scvi_n200+ViT concat) is only marginally above RNA-only scvi_n200. The multiprofile dimension is completely untested across all 5 completed experiments, representing the largest source of uncertainty in the design space. Question: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly compares against config_004 (same RNA encoder, singleprofile) to isolate whether aggregating multiple profiles improves the dominant RNA signal, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool) as a conservative first probe. Why this is the best next experiment: Since RNA carries most of the predictive signal, establishing whether multiprofile helps at the RNA level before committing to more complex multimodal-multiprofile configurations (which confound profile-setting, aggregation, and fusion effects) is the most information-efficient use of the next budget slot. A positive result would justify investing in multimodal multiprofile variants (e.g., config_036/038); a null result would redirect effort toward fusion strategies or alternative encoders.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, a dramatic ~13-point gain over its singleprofile counterpart (config_004, 0.520). This makes multiprofile + scvi_n200 the clearly dominant direction. However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool) for this setting. The aggregation method is the critical mechanism that determines how multiple profiles are combined, and transformer-based aggregation could capture inter-profile relationships that simple averaging discards. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for multiprofile scvi_n200, and if so, by how much? Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most direct exploitation of our strongest result while resolving a high-uncertainty design choice (aggregation) that could meaningfully shift performance. A large gap would justify further transformer-based multimodal experiments; a small gap would confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect budget toward other levers (e.g., adding image in multiprofile mode). Under a limited budget, clarifying this binary choice before branching into multimodal multiprofile variants is the most information-efficient use of the next run.

Evidence: Multiprofile RNA (scvi_n200) is the strongest configuration found so far (acc ~0.65), while image-only models are very weak (acc ~0.21-0.23). The only multimodal test (config_034, singleprofile) showed only a marginal gain over RNA-only (0.532 vs 0.520), suggesting image adds little in singleprofile mode. Critical uncertainty: does the multiprofile setting—which unlocked a ~13% gain for RNA alone—also unlock complementary signal from the image modality? This experiment (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) directly tests whether the best RNA encoder combined with the best image encoder in a multiprofile multimodal setting can exceed the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. It uses transformer aggregation (marginally better than avgpool in config_006) and concat fusion (the only fusion tested in config_034). If it beats 0.653, image is a useful complement in the richer profile space; if it does not, we can confidently deprioritize all remaining multimodal and image-only configurations, saving budget for RNA-encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt).

The current best configuration (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) achieves 0.721 accuracy. The most significant unexplored design dimension is the RNA encoder choice: we have evidence that scvi_n200 > pca_n2000, but scgpt has never been tested. Config_050 isolates this single variable by swapping scvi_n200 → scgpt while keeping all other settings identical to the best config. This directly answers whether a generative-model-based encoder (scGPT) can outperform the VAE-based encoder (scVI) in the highest-performing multimodal regime. Under a limited budget, resolving this major architectural question is more informative than testing minor variations (e.g., concat vs. weighted fusion) on an already-validated encoder, because a positive result would open an entirely new optimization direction, while a negative result would confirm scvi_n200 as the correct choice and focus remaining budget on fusion/aggregation refinements.

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is the clear best at 0.7207 acc / 0.6815 F1, and all its individual components (scvi_n200 over pca_n2000, multiprofile over singleprofile, transformer over avgpool, imagenet_vit_l over resnet50, multimodal over unimodal) are supported by prior experiments. However, the fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' in this top-performing regime. Question: config_039 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, directly testing whether learned modality weighting can further improve over a fixed concatenation in the best-known setting. Rationale: This is the highest-value exploitation step—every other hyperparameter is already at its empirically best value, so isolating the fusion choice gives a clean read on whether this design axis still has headroom. If weighted fusion helps, it identifies a new improvement direction; if it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects budget toward other untested axes (e.g., alternative image encoders or profile counts). Under a limited budget, this single-variable change from the current best is the most informative next experiment.

No experiments have been completed, so all design dimensions carry maximum uncertainty. The most informative first step is to establish the simplest possible performance baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components). This tells us (1) whether the task is tractable with minimal modeling, (2) what performance floor to compare against when adding complexity (better encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, fusion), and (3) whether the RNA signal alone is sufficient or whether multimodal integration is necessary. Every subsequent experiment can be interpreted as a delta over this reference, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a tight budget. It is also computationally inexpensive, reducing the risk of a costly failure on the first run.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001, rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000) has been completed, yielding a low baseline of ~48.5% accuracy. This tells us little about whether the image modality carries any useful signal for this task. Uncertainty: The most consequential architectural question is whether image features contribute meaningfully at all—if they do not, ~28 multimodal/image-only configurations can be eliminated from consideration. What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest possible probe of image-modality signal, using a standard, well-established backbone (ResNet-50) and matching the singleprofile setting of the RNA baseline for a fair unimodal comparison. Why it is the best next experiment: Under a tight budget, resolving the binary question 'does image modality help?' has the highest information value because it branches the entire remaining search space. If image accuracy is comparable to or below the RNA baseline, I can focus subsequent experiments on RNA encoder and profile improvements. If it is substantially higher, I can prioritize multimodal fusion strategies. No other single experiment would reduce uncertainty about this many downstream decisions.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA-2000 and single profile (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy, far outperforming image-only ResNet50 (config_010, 20.8%), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile aggregation improves the RNA signal, and this is a foundational design axis that affects all downstream multimodal experiments. What this tests: config_002 is a minimal, controlled extension of config_001—same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), same modality—adding only multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This gives a clean A/B comparison of single vs. multi profile for the dominant modality. Why it is the best next experiment: (1) RNA is the performance driver, so improving it has the highest expected impact; (2) the result directly informs whether the entire multiprofile branch (configs 003, 005–009, 018–051) is worth pursuing, reducing uncertainty across ~40 remaining configurations; (3) the minimal change from config_001 makes the comparison interpretable without confounding variables; (4) under a tight budget, resolving this binary question (does multiprofile help?) is more informative than jumping to a new encoder or fusion strategy whose interpretation would be muddied by the unknown profile effect.

Evidence: Multi-profile RNA with PCA_n2000 + avgpool (config_002, acc 0.591) substantially outperforms single-profile (config_001, acc 0.485), confirming that profile aggregation is a high-impact design choice. Image-only (config_010, acc 0.208) is very weak, so the RNA pathway is the primary signal source and must be optimized before multimodal fusion is informative. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for combining multiple profiles—this is the next most consequential architectural decision after establishing that multi-profile helps. This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding everything else at the best-known RNA settings (PCA_n2000, multi-profile), making it a clean, minimal test of one variable. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly extends the strongest configuration, reduces uncertainty on a design axis that will propagate into all multimodal experiments, and avoids the confound of simultaneously changing encoder, profile setting, and fusion strategy.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool; acc 0.591), showing that multiprofile + avgpool is a strong RNA setup. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA) across all experiments, leaving the encoder choice as a major unexplored design axis. Question: Does a learned single-cell encoder (scvi_n200) outperform linear PCA in the best-performing multiprofile+avgpool configuration? This directly tests whether the encoder captures non-linear biological structure that PCA misses. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is a foundational design decision that will propagate into all multimodal experiments. Resolving whether scvi or PCA is superior here (with a clean single-variable change from config_002) reduces uncertainty efficiently before committing budget to the larger multimodal grid. If scvi matches or beats PCA, it reshapes the multimodal search; if it underperforms, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can pivot to multimodal fusion with confidence.

Evidence so far shows RNA (scvi_n200, multi, avgpool) is the strongest modality at 0.650 acc, while image-only (ResNet50) is very weak at 0.208. The critical open question is whether the image modality contributes complementary signal when fused with the best RNA configuration, or whether it is purely noise that degrades performance. Config_030 (multimodal, multi, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests this by pairing the strongest RNA setup with the weakest image encoder under the simplest fusion (concat). If accuracy exceeds 0.650, multimodal fusion is worth further exploration (ViT, weighted fusion); if it falls below, the image branch is not useful and remaining budget should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation refinements. This single experiment resolves the highest-uncertainty design decision—whether to invest in multimodal or unimodal strategies—making it the most budget-efficient next step.

Evidence: RNA encoder choice is the strongest lever so far—pca_n2000 (config_002, 0.591) vs scvi_n200 (config_005, 0.650) with identical multiprofile/avgpool setup shows a ~6-point gain. scgpt is completely untested. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable A/B against config_005, isolating whether scgpt matches, exceeds, or underperforms scvi_n200. Why best next: the RNA encoder is the most fundamental design axis and propagates into every multimodal configuration; resolving this uncertainty before further multimodal/fusion experiments avoids wasting budget on suboptimal encoder choices. If scgpt is clearly superior, all subsequent multimodal tests should use it; if similar or worse, we can confidently commit to scvi_n200 and pivot to fusion-method or image-encoder questions.

Evidence: The current best is config_005 (RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650. The only multimodal test (config_030: scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) scored 0.632, slightly *worse* than RNA-only, suggesting the weak resnet50 image encoder (image-only acc=0.208) adds noise. Key uncertainty: is the image modality fundamentally uninformative, or was resnet50 simply too weak to contribute useful signal? This experiment (config_036) pairs the best-validated RNA setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) with the strongest available image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) using the same concat fusion. It directly tests whether a stronger visual encoder can make multimodal fusion competitive with or exceed the RNA-only baseline. If it succeeds, it opens a promising multimodal direction; if it fails, we can confidently abandon multimodal and focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinements. This is the highest-information experiment available because it resolves the single most consequential design question (is multimodal worth pursuing?) with one test, rather than incrementally tuning a direction that already appears suboptimal.

Evidence: config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.715) and F1 (0.687), substantially outperforming both RNA-only (0.650) and the resnet50-based multimodal (0.632). This establishes that the combination of scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + avgpool is the strongest design. Uncertainty: The only untested dimension within this top-performing configuration is the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted). Question tested: Does weighted fusion improve over simple concatenation when combining the scvi_n200 RNA embedding with the imagenet_vit_l image embedding? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a minimal, single-variable change from the current best configuration, so any performance delta is cleanly attributable to the fusion method. If weighted fusion helps, we immediately identify an even better configuration; if not, we confirm concat is optimal and can redirect exploration. Under a limited budget, exploiting the strongest direction with the smallest remaining uncertainty is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

The best result so far is config_036 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 acc. In RNA-only experiments, avgpool consistently outperformed transformer aggregation (pca: 0.591 vs 0.519; scvi: 0.650 vs untested), but that evidence comes from weaker encoder combinations. The key remaining uncertainty for the top-performing multimodal setup is whether transformer aggregation could exploit cross-profile interactions more effectively when paired with the strong ViT image features. config_038 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer (keeping concat fusion, which slightly beat weighted), directly testing this interaction. If transformer improves performance, it opens a new optimization axis; if it confirms avgpool superiority, we can confidently lock in the aggregation choice and focus remaining budget on other design dimensions. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the last untested design variable in the strongest configuration family.

With no completed experiments, there is zero evidence about any design axis (modality, encoder, profile strategy, aggregation, fusion). The most informative first step is to establish a minimal, well-understood baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) uses the simplest standard RNA representation (PCA, 2000 components), avoids confounding from multi-profile aggregation or fusion choices, and is computationally lightweight. It anchors the RNA performance floor against which every subsequent experiment—image-only, multimodal, alternative encoders, multiprofile—can be compared. Establishing this floor first lets the next experiments directly test whether adding images, switching encoders, or using multimodal fusion provides a meaningful gain, making each follow-up experiment maximally interpretable under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy, establishing RNA as the dominant modality, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) is very weak at 0.208, suggesting image contributes little signal on its own. This makes the RNA representation quality the most critical design decision for any future multimodal experiment. Question tested: Does a learned nonlinear RNA encoder (scvi_n200) outperform the simple linear PCA (pca_n2000) baseline? This is a clean single-variable change from config_001, isolating the encoder choice. If scvi_n200 substantially improves on 0.485, it justifies investing in learned encoders for multimodal fusion; if it does not, PCA is sufficient and we should focus budget on profile/aggregation/fusion choices instead. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design axis before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.485–0.520) substantially outperform image-only (0.208), and scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 for RNA encoding. The critical unresolved question is whether multimodal fusion adds value at all, given how weak the image modality is in isolation. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is a clean ablation against config_001 (same RNA encoder, same profile setting) with the only change being the addition of resnet50 image features via concat fusion. This directly tests whether the image modality contributes complementary signal or introduces noise. Resolving this early is the highest-value use of the next experiment: if multimodal does not improve over RNA-only, an entire branch (~36 configs) can be deprioritized, freeing budget for RNA-only multiprofile and scgpt experiments. If it does help, we gain a validated direction to exploit with better encoders and fusion strategies.

Evidence: scvi_n200 clearly outperforms pca_n2000 in the RNA-only setting (0.520 vs 0.485, ~3.5% gap), and the current best result is multimodal with pca_n2000+resnet50+concat (0.527), which barely exceeds scvi RNA-only. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether the RNA encoder advantage carries into the multimodal setting, and whether the modest image contribution from resnet50 is sufficient to justify the added complexity. This experiment (config_028: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_016, isolating the RNA encoder effect in the multimodal context. If it substantially beats 0.527, it confirms scvi_n200 is the right backbone for further multimodal exploration; if it plateaus near 0.520, it signals that resnet50 adds little and we should pivot to a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or multiprofile strategies. Under a tight budget, this is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the strongest observed signal (better RNA encoder) into the most promising model family (multimodal) while keeping all other variables fixed for a clean attribution.

Evidence: All 5 completed experiments used singleprofile. The best config (config_028: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + concat) achieves 0.536 acc / 0.516 F1, confirming scvi_n200 as the superior RNA encoder and that multimodal fusion with resnet50 adds value. However, the multiprofile axis (with aggregation over multiple cellular profiles) is entirely unexplored, representing a major source of uncertainty about whether richer cellular representations can push performance further. Question: config_030 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + concat, multiprofile) is the minimal, direct extension of config_028—same encoders, same fusion—changing only the profile representation from single to multiple with average-pool aggregation. This cleanly isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation. Why this is the best next experiment: It tests the single largest unexplored design axis while holding all other variables at their best-known settings. If multiprofile+avgpool improves on 0.536, it opens a productive direction (then test transformer aggregation, ViT-L, weighted fusion). If it does not, we gain strong evidence that singleprofile suffices, saving budget from exploring 20+ multiprofile variants. Under a limited budget, resolving this binary question is more informative than, e.g., testing weighted fusion (a smaller expected delta) or a new image encoder (a secondary axis given image-only performance was very weak at 0.208).

Evidence: The largest performance jump in the study came from switching singleprofile→multiprofile (config_028: 0.536 → config_030: 0.632, +10 pts), with avgpool aggregation. scvi_n200 consistently outperforms pca_n2000, and concat fusion is the only fusion tested in the multiprofile regime. Uncertainty: We have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) for multiprofile. It is unclear whether a transformer-based aggregation could capture richer inter-profile interactions and push performance further, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal. What this tests: config_032 is a clean one-variable change from the current best (config_030), replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation while keeping scvi_n200, resnet50, and concat fusion fixed. This isolates the effect of the aggregation mechanism. Why this is the best next experiment: The aggregation method is the dimension most directly responsible for the largest observed gain, so resolving whether transformer aggregation helps (or hurts) relative to avgpool is the highest-information single experiment. It either opens a promising new direction (if transformer >> avgpool) or confirms avgpool sufficiency, allowing budget to be redirected to other axes (e.g., fusion method or image encoder).

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the best so far at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1, confirming that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + scvi_n200 + concat fusion is a strong recipe. However, the image encoder remains at resnet50, which performed very poorly as image-only (0.208 acc), suggesting the image modality may be underutilized. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a substantially larger, ImageNet-pretrained ViT) meaningfully improve multimodal performance while keeping all other winning settings fixed? Why this is the best next experiment: It is the single highest-impact untested axis in the context of our top configuration. The image encoder is a major design lever with only one option (resnet50) explored in the multiprofile multimodal regime, and the weak image-only baseline hints that a stronger encoder could unlock additional signal. Testing config_038 isolates the image-encoder effect cleanly, reducing uncertainty about whether to invest further in image quality or pivot to other axes (fusion type, scgpt RNA encoder).

Evidence: The best configuration so far (config_038, acc=0.721) uses multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, and concat fusion. All top-performing experiments use concat fusion; weighted fusion has never been tested in the multiprofile+transformer+ViT-L regime. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform concat when all other components are at their best-known settings? This isolates fusion strategy as the single variable changed from the current best. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a minimal, targeted extension of the strongest configuration, directly testing an important and unexplored design axis (fusion method) without introducing multiple confounding changes. The result will either yield a new best configuration or confirm that concat is optimal, reducing uncertainty about a key architectural choice with a single experiment.

Evidence: The current best (config_039, 0.7250) uses scVI as the RNA encoder with ViT-L, transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion in a multiprofile multimodal setup. We have strong evidence that learned RNA representations (scVI) outperform linear ones (PCA) by ~1-4 points across settings, but scGPT—a generative model-based encoder—has never been tested in any multimodal configuration. This is the largest remaining source of uncertainty about the RNA encoder choice. Question: Does scGPT match or exceed scVI in the optimal multimodal pipeline? Why this experiment: config_051 (scgpt, ViT-L, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) is a single-variable swap from the current best (config_039), isolating the RNA encoder effect. A positive result would identify a new promising direction; a negative result would confirm scVI as the best RNA encoder and redirect budget toward other levers (e.g., fusion refinements or additional image encoders). Under a limited budget, resolving this high-impact uncertainty with a clean A/B comparison is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

No experiments have been completed, so the first priority is to establish a clean, minimal baseline that calibrates the search space. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration: it uses a linear, well-understood encoder (PCA), requires no image processing or fusion, and has no aggregation complexity. This experiment will (1) confirm the pipeline runs end-to-end, (2) quantify how much signal is available from RNA data alone, and (3) set a performance floor against which all image-only and multimodal configurations can be compared. Choosing the simplest RNA baseline first is the most budget-efficient use of the first experiment because it is fast to execute (no image encoder or fusion overhead), minimizes the risk of confounding from multiple design choices, and directly informs whether the image modality or multimodal fusion is necessary to achieve strong performance. Subsequent experiments can then systematically add image modality, upgrade encoders, or test multiprofile aggregation with a clear reference point.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA → 48.5% acc), which provides a weak baseline and leaves the most critical question for a multimodal study unanswered: does image data carry a stronger or complementary signal? Testing config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) establishes the image modality's standalone performance under the same profile setting as config_001, giving us a clean unimodal comparison. This is essential before evaluating any multimodal fusion configuration, because without knowing each modality's ceiling we cannot attribute gains (or losses) to fusion versus to a stronger single modality. If image alone substantially outperforms RNA, it reshapes the entire search toward image-centric or fusion-weighted configurations; if it is comparable, it motivates testing whether multimodal combination adds value. Under a tight budget, this single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design axis (modality contribution) and directly informs the next 2–3 experiments.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is only 20.8%, confirming RNA is the dominant modality. The current best RNA encoder is a simple linear PCA (2000 dims). Uncertainty: We have no evidence yet about whether a powerful learned RNA encoder (scgpt, a pretrained single-cell transformer) can extract substantially more signal than PCA. This experiment (config_007: rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, isolating the RNA encoder choice. If scgpt significantly outperforms PCA, it validates investing in learned encoders and justifies exploring them in multimodal settings. If it does not, it indicates the RNA signal is already well-captured by linear structure, redirecting effort toward profile settings or fusion. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-impact, high-uncertainty question before testing multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion avoids confounding multiple design changes in a single experiment.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality (pca_n2000 singleprofile acc=0.485 vs image-only resnet50 acc=0.208), and among tested RNA encoders pca_n2000 outperforms scgpt. However, we have zero data on whether multiprofile aggregation improves over singleprofile—a fundamental design axis that governs a large fraction of the remaining search space. This experiment (config_002) directly tests that question by taking our best-performing configuration (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) and changing only the profile setting to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). It isolates the multiprofile effect while holding the encoder constant, giving a clean comparison to config_001. Choosing avgpool over transformer avoids introducing a second confounding variable; if avgpool already shows a gain, we can then test transformer in a follow-up. Under a tight budget, resolving whether multiprofile is worth pursuing at all is the highest-information next step, as it determines whether the many multiprofile and multimodal-multiprofile configurations are worth further exploration.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile + avgpool with PCA (config_002, acc=0.591) substantially outperforms singleprofile PCA (config_001, acc=0.485), indicating that multi-profile aggregation is a critical design axis. The natural next question is whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve on avgpool within the same multiprofile+PCA setup. config_003 is a clean single-variable change (avgpool → transformer) from the best result, so any performance difference can be attributed to the aggregation method. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it either confirms avgpool sufficiency (freeing us to explore other dimensions like multimodal fusion or alternative encoders) or reveals a further gain that justifies committing to transformer-based aggregation in subsequent multimodal experiments. Testing multimodal fusion now would be premature given the very weak image-only signal (config_010, acc=0.208), and testing alternative RNA encoders in multiprofile is lower priority since PCA already dominates scgpt in singleprofile.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, while image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208 acc). The critical open question is whether combining the strong RNA signal with the weak image signal via multimodal fusion yields any benefit over the RNA-only baseline. This experiment (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly extends the best-performing RNA configuration by adding the image modality with the simplest fusion strategy. It tests whether the image carries any complementary information not captured by RNA alone. This is the highest-information next step because: (1) it answers the fundamental multimodal question before investing further in image-encoder or fusion-variant experiments, (2) it builds on the strongest validated RNA setup (pca_n2000 + multiprofile + avgpool), and (3) the result will decisively guide whether to pursue weighted fusion, better image encoders (ViT-L), or refocus entirely on RNA-encoder improvements. Under a limited budget, resolving the 'does multimodal help at all?' question before branching into 30+ multimodal variants is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multi, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far (acc=0.619, F1=0.610), showing that adding a weak image modality (ResNet50 alone: 0.208) via concat fusion to the strong RNA multi-avgpool baseline (0.591) yields a modest but consistent gain. The fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) is a fundamental design choice that governs how the two modalities interact, and it is currently untested. Question: Does learned weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation for combining the (dominant) RNA features with the (weak) image features? This is a clean single-variable A/B against config_018, changing only the fusion mechanism. Why best next: It directly exploits the strongest configuration while resolving a high-leverage uncertainty—if weighted fusion helps, it reshapes the optimal recipe for every subsequent multimodal experiment (ViT-L, scGPT, transformer aggregation); if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward stronger image encoders or alternative RNA encoders. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, multimodal/multiprofile/PCA/ResNet50/avgpool/weighted, acc=0.639) was built on the finding that avgpool outperformed transformer in the RNA-only multi-profile setting (0.591 vs 0.519). However, that comparison was made without an image modality present. Question: Does transformer aggregation, which can model higher-order interactions, provide a benefit in the multimodal setting where it must integrate both aggregated multi-profile RNA features and image features? This is a single-variable change from the current best (only aggregation differs), making the result directly attributable to the aggregation choice. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, confirming or refuting the transferability of the avgpool>transformer finding to the multimodal context reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision that will affect all future multimodal experiments. If avgpool is confirmed, we can lock it in and pivot to testing image encoder quality (ViT-L) or RNA encoder alternatives; if transformer unexpectedly helps, it reveals an important cross-modal interaction effect and reshapes the search space.

Evidence: The current best is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639). We know multiprofile+avgpool+weighted is the validated best combination, and PCA outperforms SCGPT for RNA. However, image-only ResNet50 was very weak (acc=0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image modality's modest contribution in the multimodal setting (0.639 vs 0.591 RNA-only) is limited by encoder quality. Question: Does a stronger, more expressive image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) provide substantially better complementary features that push multimodal performance higher? This experiment (config_025) is a clean single-variable swap from the current best—only the image encoder changes—so any performance shift is attributable to encoder quality. Why best next: It directly exploits the validated best pipeline while resolving the key uncertainty about the image modality's ceiling. A positive result opens a strong exploitation path; a null result tells us the image signal is inherently limited, redirecting budget toward RNA-side improvements (e.g., scvi_n200). Either outcome is highly informative under a limited budget.

The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and scgpt was clearly inferior to PCA in single-profile RNA-only (0.411 vs 0.485). However, scvi_n200 has never been tested in any experiment, making the RNA encoder choice the largest remaining source of uncertainty in the best-performing configuration. config_031 tests scvi_n200 within the exact best-performing framework (multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), isolating the encoder variable. If scvi_n200 matches or exceeds PCA, it opens a new optimization direction; if it underperforms, we can confidently rule it out and focus remaining budget on other levers (e.g., image encoder or profile count). This is the highest-information-gain experiment because it resolves a completely unexplored design axis while keeping all other settings at their empirically validated optima.

No experiments have been completed, so all design choices carry maximum uncertainty. The first experiment must establish a performance floor to interpret all subsequent results. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration: PCA is the most basic, well-understood RNA encoder with no learned parameters, singleprofile avoids the added complexity of aggregation, and no image modality is involved. This gives us (1) a clean baseline accuracy/F1 against which every other configuration can be compared, (2) a reference for whether multimodal fusion or more complex encoders actually add value, and (3) a fast, low-risk computation that won't waste budget on a complex setup before we know the system works end-to-end. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with the simplest baseline maximizes the interpretive value of every future experiment.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is which modality carries the most signal. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_001, isolating the modality choice while holding profile setting constant. Knowing whether image features alone match, exceed, or fall short of the RNA baseline is the highest-level design decision: it determines whether subsequent budget should focus on RNA encoder refinement, image encoder refinement, or multimodal fusion. Without this anchor, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable (we could not tell whether a gain came from the image, the RNA, or their interaction). ResNet50 is chosen over ViT-L as the first image probe because it is a standard, well-calibrated backbone that gives a clear read on whether spatial image features are informative at all before committing to a larger or more domain-mismatched model.

Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 0.208, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether aggregating multiple profiles per cell (multiprofile) provides meaningful additional signal over a single profile, and this is a foundational design choice that gates many downstream experiments (all multiprofile and multimodal configurations). What this tests: config_002 changes exactly one variable from config_001—switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool)—while keeping the same PCA encoder. This gives a clean single-variable comparison. Why it is the best next experiment: With only 2 data points, reducing uncertainty about the profile-setting axis is critical. If multiprofile+avgpool improves over 0.485, it validates the multiprofile pathway and justifies investing in multiprofile variants with stronger encoders and multimodal fusion. If it does not improve, we avoid wasting budget on the entire multiprofile sub-grid. The minimal change (one variable) makes the result interpretable, and avgpool as the simplest aggregation isolates the profile-count effect from aggregation-complexity effects.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc is the clear best so far, showing multiprofile aggregation adds ~10.6% over singleprofile (config_001). Image alone (config_010, 0.208) is very weak, so the RNA pipeline is the primary driver. Uncertainty: We don't yet know whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) outperforms simple avgpool for combining multiple profiles. This experiment (config_003) is a clean single-variable test of aggregation method, changing only avgpool→transformer while holding everything else identical to config_002. It is the best next use of budget because: (1) it directly extends the strongest configuration, (2) it isolates one design decision so the result is interpretable, (3) the outcome informs every subsequent experiment—both RNA-only and multimodal—by telling us which aggregation to pair with other components, and (4) it avoids prematurely investing in multimodal fusion while the image modality's contribution remains unproven.

Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile + pca_n2000 + avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest result so far, while image-only with resnet50 (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak. The critical unresolved question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding the image modality via fusion provides any complementary signal beyond the already-strong RNA features. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the direct multimodal extension of the best RNA-only config, isolating the effect of image addition with the simplest (concat) fusion. This is the highest-information next experiment: if it beats 0.591, it justifies further exploration of fusion strategies and image encoders; if it does not, it tells us to concentrate remaining budget on RNA encoder and aggregation refinements rather than the full 36-config multimodal grid. It is the best use of one experiment because it resolves the single most important design decision (multimodal vs. unimodal) before committing budget to finer-grained variations.

The current best (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc=0.619) shows that adding image features to RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591) yields a modest +0.028 gain. The only fusion method tested so far is concat. Config_019 is an identical setup except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, making it a clean single-variable A/B test against the current best. This directly tests whether the fusion strategy is a meaningful lever or whether concat is already near-optimal. If weighted outperforms concat, it signals that the image contribution can be amplified and justifies further exploration of weighted-fusion variants (e.g., with ViT-L or scvi). If they are comparable, it rules out fusion as a high-priority axis and redirects budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder choices. Under a limited budget, this low-risk, high-information experiment is the most efficient next step because it resolves a binary question that gates multiple downstream decisions.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder in a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted-fusion setup. RNA is clearly the dominant signal (RNA-only multiprofile+avgpool=0.591 vs image-only=0.208), and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (~5%), suggesting the RNA representation quality is the primary bottleneck. We have zero data on how learned RNA encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt) compare to PCA. Question tested: Does replacing pca_n2000 with scvi_n200 in the best-performing multimodal configuration improve validation accuracy, i.e., does a learned generative latent representation outperform a linear PCA projection for downstream classification? Why best next experiment: config_031 is a clean single-variable swap (RNA encoder only) against the current champion config_019, making the result directly interpretable. It targets the highest-impact unexplored design axis (RNA encoder) while holding all other settings at their empirically validated best values (multiprofile, avgpool, resnet50, weighted fusion), maximizing information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The largest single-factor improvement observed so far is the RNA encoder swap from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 in the multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/weighted setup (config_019→config_031: +3.9% acc, +2.7% F1). We have zero data on the scgpt encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder in the currently best configuration? Why this experiment: config_043 is an isolated, controlled comparison against config_031—only the RNA encoder changes. This resolves the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design choice (RNA encoder) in the context where it matters most. If scgpt wins, we have a new best and a direction to exploit; if it loses, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can redirect remaining budget toward the image encoder (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) or aggregation strategy. Under a limited budget, this single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most influential factor.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_031: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.678) has been built through systematic elimination: multiprofile > singleprofile, avgpool > transformer, weighted > concat, and scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 > scgpt. The one major untested dimension in this best configuration is the image encoder—only resnet50 has been used. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a larger, more expressive ViT-L model) further improve multimodal performance? Why this is the best next experiment: config_037 is the minimal, direct extension of the current best, changing only the image encoder while holding all other settings at their empirically validated optima. This isolates the image encoder's contribution under the strongest known RNA/fusion/aggregation stack, giving the cleanest signal on whether a stronger visual backbone is worth the added cost. It is both an exploitation of the proven configuration and an exploration of the highest-impact remaining variable, making it the most informative use of the next budget slot.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.706 accuracy. The only prior evidence on aggregation (config_002 vs config_003) showed avgpool > transformer by ~7 points, but that was with the weaker pca_n2000 encoder. With the stronger scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l combination, it is unclear whether transformer aggregation could close or reverse that gap. Config_039 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a single-variable change from the current best, directly testing whether aggregation strategy matters under the strongest encoder pair. If transformer underperforms, we can confidently lock in avgpool and redirect budget to other axes; if it matches or exceeds avgpool, it opens a new optimization direction. Under a limited budget, resolving this uncertainty with the best-known encoders is more informative than testing a lower-priority axis (e.g., scgpt, which already showed a ~15-point deficit).

No experiments have been completed yet, so the most critical need is to establish a performance baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: it uses the most standard and computationally cheap encoder (PCA), the simplest profile setting (single), and no image modality. This experiment will (1) provide a reference accuracy/F1 against which all subsequent unimodal and multimodal configurations can be compared, (2) reveal how well RNA data alone performs, which is essential for determining whether image or multimodal fusion adds value, and (3) reduce uncertainty about the overall difficulty of the classification task. Under a limited budget, starting with the simplest baseline is the highest-information first step because every subsequent experiment's value is interpreted relative to this reference point.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001, rna_only/pca_n2000/singleprofile) has been completed, yielding a low accuracy of 0.485 and F1 of 0.464, indicating the task is challenging and the current RNA representation captures limited signal. Uncertainty: The most fundamental unknown is whether the image modality carries useful discriminative signal for this task. Without knowing this, it is impossible to prioritize among the many multimodal configurations or to decide whether to invest in better RNA encoders. What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001, isolating the effect of modality while holding profile_setting constant. Why it is the best use of the next budget: If image accuracy substantially exceeds 0.485, it justifies prioritizing multimodal configurations and stronger image encoders (ViT-L).
