If it is comparable or lower, it confirms RNA is the stronger (or equally weak) modality and shifts focus to better RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. Either outcome dramatically narrows the search space for all subsequent experiments, making this the highest-information experiment available.

Evidence: RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image-only (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have only one RNA data point and don't know whether multiprofile aggregation (vs singleprofile) meaningfully improves the RNA signal. This experiment (config_002) tests multiprofile + avgpool with the same pca_n2000 encoder, providing the cleanest isolated comparison to config_001 by changing only the profile setting and adding a simple aggregation. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it directly extends our strongest configuration, (2) it resolves whether the profile/aggregation axis matters for the dominant modality before we invest in more complex encoders or multimodal fusion, and (3) the result will inform whether multiprofile is worth pursuing in any multimodal setup, reducing uncertainty across a large portion of the remaining search space.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a strong +10.6% gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485), confirming multiprofile aggregation is the most impactful design choice so far. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether transformer aggregation would further improve multiprofile performance or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this encoder. This experiment (config_003) provides a clean, single-variable comparison against config_002 (only aggregation changes: transformer vs avgpool), isolating the effect of aggregation architecture. Why it is the best next step: (1) it directly extends our best-performing configuration with a logical, minimal change; (2) the result will tell us whether to invest subsequent budget in transformer-based pipelines (which would also benefit multimodal fusion experiments) or whether avgpool is sufficient and we should pivot to testing RNA encoder quality (scvi, scgpt); (3) it is the highest-information experiment per unit budget because a clear win/loss here partitions the remaining search space into two very different strategies.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.591 acc, showing that multi-profile + avgpool is a strong aggregation strategy. Image-only is very weak (0.208), suggesting the RNA modality carries most of the signal. The key untested variable within the best-known RNA pipeline is the encoder: PCA n2000 is a simple linear projection, while scvi_n200 is a learned nonlinear variational representation. Question: Does a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) improve over PCA n2000 when paired with the best-known multi-profile + avgpool aggregation? Why this is the best next experiment: It isolates a single high-impact design choice (RNA encoder) while holding the proven-best settings fixed, giving a clean comparison. If scvi_n200 helps, it opens the door to scgpt and multimodal variants with learned encoders; if it does not, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects budget toward the multimodal or image-encoder questions. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA dominates (0.485–0.650) while image-only is weak (0.208). Within RNA, we know scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 (0.650 vs 0.591) and avgpool > transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), both under multiprofile. The key remaining uncertainty among RNA encoders is where scgpt falls relative to scvi_n200. Question tested: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) holds profile and aggregation fixed at their best-known settings, isolating the encoder variable for a clean three-way comparison (pca_n2000 vs scvi_n200 vs scgpt). Why this is the best next experiment: RNA is the dominant signal source, so the encoder choice is the highest-leverage design decision. Resolving whether scgpt beats, matches, or trails scvi_n200 under identical conditions will either (a) confirm scvi_n200 as the optimal RNA backbone, letting us confidently move to multimodal fusion tests, or (b) reveal a superior encoder that reshapes the entire search. This is a low-variance, high-information experiment that reduces uncertainty on the most impactful axis before committing budget to the larger multimodal configuration space.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200, multiprofile, and avgpool (config_005) is the clear best at 0.650 acc, while image-only (config_010) is very weak at 0.208. This creates a critical uncertainty: does adding image features to the strong RNA signal provide complementary information, or does the weak image branch dilute performance? This is the single most consequential design decision for the remaining search. Config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the natural extension of the best RNA configuration into the multimodal setting, using the simpler concat fusion to minimize confounding variables. If it matches or beats 0.650, multimodal is a promising direction worth further exploration; if it underperforms, we can confidently rule out the large multimodal sub-space and concentrate budget on RNA-only refinements (e.g., scvi_n200 + transformer in config_006, or other RNA improvements). Resolving this question maximally reduces uncertainty about which branch of the search tree to pursue, making it the highest-information-value experiment under a limited budget.

The best result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. We know avgpool outperformed transformer for pca_n2000 (0.591 vs 0.519), but scvi_n200 produces learned nonlinear embeddings where attention-based aggregation might better capture inter-profile relationships. Config_006 is a clean single-variable extension of our best result (changing only aggregation from avgpool to transformer). If transformer helps, it reveals an encoder-aggregation interaction and raises the ceiling for all future multimodal experiments. If it doesn't, we confirm avgpool is optimal for scvi_n200 and can redirect effort toward fusion strategy or stronger image encoders. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step: it directly probes the most promising configuration space around our current best with a well-motivated hypothesis.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool is the strongest RNA-only setup (0.650-0.653). The only multimodal test (config_030, resnet50, concat) scored 0.632, slightly *below* the RNA-only baseline (0.650), and image-only with resnet50 was very poor (0.208). This raises a critical uncertainty: is the image modality fundamentally unhelpful, or was resnet50 simply too weak an encoder to contribute useful signal? Question: config_036 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) isolates the image-encoder variable by swapping resnet50 → ViT-L while holding all other settings identical to config_030. If ViT-L multimodal exceeds the RNA-only baseline, it confirms the image modality is useful and justifies further multimodal exploration (fusion strategy, transformer aggregation). If it still underperforms RNA-only, it strongly indicates images are not contributing and remaining budget should focus on RNA-only refinements. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because the answer directly determines the direction of all subsequent experiments.

The current best configuration (config_036, acc=0.7150) uses concat fusion to combine scvi_n200 RNA features with imagenet_vit_l image features. The fusion mechanism (concat vs weighted) has not been tested in any completed experiment, making it a major source of uncertainty. config_037 is a clean single-variable change from config_036 (only fusion: concat→weighted), allowing us to directly assess whether weighted fusion captures complementary modality information more effectively than simple concatenation. This is the highest-value next experiment because: (1) it exploits the strongest evidence (best RNA encoder, best image encoder, multiprofile, avgpool) while probing the one untested design axis at the top of the performance landscape; (2) if weighted fusion helps, it opens a clear path to further gains; if it does not, we can confidently lock in concat and redirect budget toward aggregation (transformer) or other refinements. Under a limited budget, isolating one variable at the current optimum is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about how any modality, encoder, or fusion strategy performs. The most fundamental uncertainty is the baseline performance of the simplest RNA-only pipeline. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) establishes the most basic reference point—a single-profile RNA model with a standard linear encoder (PCA). It isolates the RNA signal quality and the single-profile assumption without confounding from image data, complex encoders, or aggregation. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: It is the simplest, fastest-running configuration in the space, minimizing risk of a failed or noisy first result. It provides the anchor against which all image-only, multimodal, multiprofile, and alternative-encoder experiments can be compared. Establishing this baseline first ensures that subsequent experiments (e.g., adding image, switching to multiprofile, or trying scGPT/SCVI) can be interpreted as marginal gains over a well-defined reference, making the limited budget maximally informative.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 at ~48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries meaningful signal for this task. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest test of this question: it matches config_001 on profile setting (singleprofile) and uses a standard, well-calibrated image encoder, so the primary variable is modality itself. If image-only substantially outperforms RNA-only, the search should pivot toward image encoders and multimodal fusion; if it performs similarly or worse, RNA remains the primary signal and we should explore RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. Resolving this structural question first maximizes information gain per experiment and prevents wasting budget on secondary design choices (aggregation, fusion strategy, encoder variants) before knowing which modality is most informative.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy, far outperforming image-only ResNet50 (config_010, 20.8%), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we only have one RNA data point and no information on whether multiprofile aggregation adds value. Question: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly extends config_001 by changing only the profile setting from single to multi and adding avgpool aggregation, isolating the effect of multi-profile aggregation while keeping the encoder fixed. Why this is best: With only 2 experiments completed, the highest-value uncertainty to reduce is whether the structural choice of multiprofile vs. singleprofile matters for our strongest modality. This is a minimal, confound-free extension of our best result. If multiprofile helps, it validates investing in the broader multiprofile space (including multimodal); if not, it saves budget by narrowing the search. Testing a new encoder (scVI/scGPT) or jumping to multimodal fusion would introduce multiple simultaneous changes and make attribution harder at this early stage.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieves 0.591 acc, substantially better than singleprofile (0.485), confirming multiprofile + aggregation is the strongest direction so far. However, we have no evidence about whether the aggregation method itself matters—avgpool is the simplest option. Question: config_003 is identical to config_002 except it replaces avgpool with a transformer aggregator, giving a clean single-variable test of whether learned attention-based profile combination captures interactions that simple averaging misses. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends our strongest result with a minimal, interpretable change; the outcome (transformer >> avgpool, ≈, or <<) will determine the aggregation architecture for all subsequent multimodal experiments, making it high-information per budget unit. It also avoids the risk of confounding encoder choice (scvi/scgpt) with aggregation choice in a single step.

Evidence: RNA-only with multi-profile + avgpool + PCA (config_002, acc=0.591) is the clear best configuration so far, while image-only with ResNet50 single-profile (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak. The core question for this multimodal study is whether combining the two modalities yields a benefit over the RNA-only baseline. config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests this by pairing the best-known RNA setup with the only image encoder already characterized, using the simplest fusion strategy. If accuracy exceeds 0.591, image contributes complementary signal and justifies exploring better image encoders and fusion strategies; if it falls below, image is currently harmful and the budget should shift toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) or stronger image backbones. This is the highest-information experiment because its outcome determines the entire direction of subsequent experiments in a multimodal study.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is our best result at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, showing that multimodal fusion with avgpool aggregation provides a ~2.8% boost over the best RNA-only config (config_002, 0.591). However, we have only tested concat fusion; the effect of weighted fusion is completely untested. Question: config_019 is an exact single-variable ablation of config_018, changing only fusion from concat to weighted. This directly tests whether a learned weighting of modalities outperforms simple concatenation, which is a critical design decision for any multimodal system. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is the cleanest possible A/B comparison against our current best, isolating one variable; (2) fusion strategy is a high-leverage design choice that, if improved, benefits all future multimodal configurations; (3) it is low-risk and immediately actionable — a positive result gives a free upgrade to our best config, while a negative result confirms concat is sufficient and redirects budget toward other axes (RNA encoder, image encoder); (4) under a limited budget, resolving this binary question before exploring higher-dimensional changes (new encoders) avoids confounding multiple untested factors simultaneously.

Evidence: The current best (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) shows that multimodal fusion with weighted combination and avgpool aggregation is the strongest configuration. However, the image modality is very weak in isolation (config_010: resnet50 singleprofile, acc=0.208), raising the question of whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) could contribute more informative features to the fusion. This experiment (config_025) is a clean single-variable extension of config_019, changing only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while keeping all validated settings (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion, pca_n2000). It directly tests whether the image branch is a bottleneck and whether upgrading it yields meaningful multimodal gains. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information experiment: it either confirms that the current resnet50 features are sufficient (allowing us to focus on RNA encoder improvements) or reveals that a stronger visual backbone unlocks substantially better multimodal performance, guiding all subsequent experiments.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder with multimodal fusion (resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile). All completed experiments have used pca_n2000; the RNA encoder dimension is completely unexplored. The image modality contributes only modestly over RNA-only (0.639 vs 0.591), suggesting the RNA representation quality is the primary performance driver. Question tested: Does a learned single-cell latent representation (scvi_n200) outperform a linear PCA projection in the best multimodal setup? This is a clean single-variable change from config_019. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis with potentially high impact. Resolving whether a nonlinear learned encoder helps (or hurts) in the multimodal context will either open a new improvement direction or confirm PCA sufficiency, thereby reducing the effective search space for all subsequent experiments. It is more informative than re-testing aggregation (avgpool already has strong RNA-only evidence) or image encoder (resnet50 vs ViT-L showed negligible difference).

The strongest evidence so far identifies scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted (config_031, 0.678 acc) as the best configuration, with scvi_n200 providing a large jump over pca_n2000 (+3.9%). The remaining uncertainty is whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l vs resnet50) could further complement the scvi_n200 representation—the prior evidence is weak (only 0.4% difference with pca_n2000, config_019 vs config_025). config_037 isolates this single variable (image encoder) while holding all other proven-optimal settings fixed (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion). This is the best use of the next budget slot because it exploits the strongest known direction while resolving a genuinely uncertain design choice; a positive result would immediately identify a new best configuration, and a null/negative result would confirm resnet50 suffices, freeing subsequent experiments to explore other axes (e.g., scgpt encoder or transformer aggregation).

The RNA encoder has proven to be the most impactful design choice: switching from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 yielded +0.071 accuracy in the multimodal/vit_l setting (0.635→0.706). However, scgpt is completely untested across all experiments, leaving significant uncertainty about whether it could outperform scvi_n200. Config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) changes only the RNA encoder from the current best config (037), making it a clean single-variable test. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi, it opens a new promising direction; if it falls short, it confirms scvi as the superior encoder and lets us focus remaining budget on aggregation or fusion refinements. This is the highest-information experiment available because it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty (encoder choice) in the context of the best-performing configuration.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have zero information about any design dimension. The most fundamental question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the basic multimodal pipeline (RNA + image) is viable and what performance level to expect. All other decisions (encoder choice, profile setting, aggregation, fusion strategy) are secondary to this core question. 2) What this tests: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the simplest end-to-end multimodal configuration. It tests whether combining a basic RNA representation (PCA) with a standard image backbone (ResNet50) via the simplest fusion (concat) yields a working, competitive model. It establishes a reference performance for the multimodal paradigm. 3) Why it is the best use of the first budget: Starting at the center of the configuration space with the most straightforward choices avoids confounding multiple complex design decisions. If performance is strong, it validates the multimodal direction and gives a clear baseline to exploit (better encoders, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). If performance is weak, the diagnosis is cleaner—since each component is a simple, well-understood default, we can isolate whether the bottleneck is the RNA encoder, the image encoder, the fusion strategy, or the lack of multiprofile aggregation. This single experiment thus reduces the most uncertainty per unit of budget and sets the stage for targeted follow-up experiments.

With only one completed experiment (config_016: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat → acc 0.527), we have almost no evidence about which design choices matter. The most critical uncertainty is the standalone contribution of each modality, since the low multimodal accuracy could stem from a weak individual modality, poor fusion, or both. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable ablation of the RNA component from config_016, isolating the image modality's performance with the same encoder and profile setting. If image alone performs comparably to the multimodal result, the RNA modality or fusion is the bottleneck; if it performs substantially better, RNA with PCA may be adding noise; if it performs worse, the multimodal combination is providing some benefit. Establishing this baseline is essential before investing further experiments in more complex multimodal variants (different encoders, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), as it determines whether the image modality is even a viable signal source and guides which multimodal dimensions to prioritize next.

We have two data points: multimodal (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat) at 0.5266 acc and image-only (resnet50) at 0.2079 acc. The large gap suggests RNA dominates, but we lack the RNA-only baseline to confirm this and quantify each modality's contribution. Config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) uses the identical RNA encoder as config_016, making it a clean decomposition: if RNA alone approaches ~0.50, the image adds little and future effort should focus on RNA encoders or fusion; if RNA alone is much lower (~0.30), the multimodal fusion is genuinely leveraging complementary signal and we should explore better fusion strategies or image encoders. With only 2 completed experiments, resolving this fundamental question about modality contribution is the highest-value uncertainty reduction before investing in more specific design choices like weighted vs. concat fusion or multiprofile aggregation.

Evidence: The multimodal concat model (config_016, acc=0.527) only marginally outperforms RNA-only (config_001, acc=0.485), while image-only (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak. This raises a critical uncertainty: is the modest multimodal gain due to a weak image encoder (ResNet50) failing to extract useful signal, or is the image modality fundamentally limited? Question tested: config_022 swaps only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L while keeping everything else identical to config_016 (pca_n2000, concat, singleprofile). This clean A/B comparison isolates the image encoder's contribution. Why best next experiment: Resolving whether a stronger image encoder unlocks meaningful multimodal gains is the highest-priority design question. A large improvement would validate further investment in multimodal + ViT-L configurations; a flat result would redirect the budget toward RNA-side improvements (multiprofile, alternative encoders). No other single experiment reduces this key uncertainty as efficiently.

Evidence: Our best config so far is config_022 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat; acc=0.5353). RNA is the dominant signal (0.485 vs 0.208 for image-only), and the ViT-L image encoder provides a small but consistent boost over ResNet50. However, the multiprofile dimension (with its associated aggregation mechanism) is completely untested, representing the largest source of remaining uncertainty. Question: Does extending the best singleprofile multimodal setup to multiprofile with average-pool aggregation (config_024) improve over the singleprofile baseline (config_022)? This isolates the effect of multiprofile+avgpool while keeping the RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: It tests the single most important unexplored architectural axis in the context of our strongest configuration. A positive result opens a rich sub-space (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, other encoders) worth exploiting; a negative result efficiently prunes that entire branch. Using avgpool first (simpler, more interpretable) before transformer follows a logical exploration order, and the direct comparison to config_022 makes the result highly informative under a tight budget.

The strongest evidence so far is the large jump from config_022 (singleprofile, no aggregation, acc=0.535) to config_024 (multiprofile, avgpool, acc=0.629), showing that multi-profile aggregation is the dominant driver of performance. The critical open question is whether the aggregation method itself matters: does a learned transformer aggregation outperform simple average pooling? config_026 isolates exactly this variable (avgpool → transformer) while holding all other parameters at their best-known values (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, multiprofile). If transformer significantly exceeds avgpool, it opens a promising direction for further refinement; if it is comparable or worse, it confirms that simple aggregation suffices and redirects budget toward other dimensions (e.g., fusion strategy or RNA encoder). This is the highest-information experiment because it tests a fundamental architectural choice at the current performance frontier, directly extending the strongest signal in the history.

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 acc / 0.599 F1, showing that multiprofile + avgpool + vit_l is a strong combination. However, the fusion mechanism has only been tested as 'concat' across all experiments; 'weighted' fusion remains completely unexplored. Question: Does weighted fusion improve over simple concatenation in the best-performing multiprofile + avgpool + vit_l setup? This isolates a single variable (fusion type) from the current best, making the result directly interpretable. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a minimal, high-information extension of the strongest configuration found so far. If weighted fusion helps, it opens a new improvement axis for all future multimodal experiments; if it does not, we efficiently rule out that design choice and can pivot to testing alternative RNA encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt) in the same strong multiprofile/avgpool/vit_l framework. Under a limited budget, resolving the fusion question with a single-variable change from the current best is more informative than jumping to a less-explored axis (e.g., RNA encoder) while an untested factor in the current best setup remains.

The current best (config_025: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, acc=0.635) has established that multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted is a strong architecture, but the RNA encoder remains at the simple PCA baseline (pca_n2000). No experiment has yet tested a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) in this best-known regime. This is the largest unexplored design dimension: whether a generative, learned encoder can capture richer transcriptomic structure than 2000-dim PCA and push accuracy beyond 0.635. Config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) isolates this single variable against the current champion, making the result directly interpretable. Under a limited budget, resolving whether the RNA encoder is a bottleneck (or whether PCA is already near-saturating) is more informative than testing the small weighted-vs-concat interaction (Δ≈0.006) or the already-penalized transformer aggregation.

Evidence: The two largest gains in the search came from (1) switching to multiprofile (0.535→0.629) and (2) switching RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (0.635→0.706). The current best (config_037: scvi_n200, vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) sits at 0.706 acc. The RNA encoder is the dimension with the largest observed effect size, and we have not yet tested scgpt, a learned generative encoder that could capture richer single-cell structure than scvi_n200. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder in the otherwise-optimized multimodal multiprofile setting? config_049 (scgpt, vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap against config_037, isolating the encoder effect. Why best use of budget: If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, we identify a new best direction; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 is the right encoder and can redirect exploration toward aggregation/fusion refinements. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty on the highest-impact design axis, making this the most informative next step under a limited budget.

The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.706). The only aggregation method not yet tested with this RNA+image encoder pair is transformer. With pca_n2000, avgpool outperformed transformer by ~0.03 (config_024 vs 026), but scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different latent representation (VAE-based) that may interact differently with attention-based aggregation. This experiment directly tests whether the aggregation finding generalizes to the superior RNA encoder: if transformer matches or beats avgpool here, we identify a new best configuration; if not, we confirm avgpool as the correct choice and can redirect budget to other design dimensions (e.g., fusion strategy or image encoder). It is the single highest-information experiment in the neighborhood of the current best, requiring only one parameter change from config_037.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit; the priority is to establish a performance baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: it uses a linear, parameter-free RNA encoder (PCA), a single profile (no aggregation), and no image modality. This gives a clean 'floor' reference for validation accuracy and F1 against which every other design decision (multiprofile aggregation, learned RNA encoders, image modality, multimodal fusion) can be measured. Establishing this baseline first is the most information-dense use of the first experiment because it anchors all subsequent comparisons and reveals how much headroom each design axis has to improve upon.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries meaningful signal for this task. If image features are uninformative, the entire multimodal branch (~34 configs) can be deprioritized, saving substantial budget. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest test of this question: it keeps the profile setting identical to config_001 (singleprofile) and uses a standard, well-calibrated image encoder, so any accuracy difference is attributable primarily to the modality switch rather than confounded by aggregation or fusion choices. This single experiment partitions the search space into two very different strategies (RNA-centric vs. image-informative) and is therefore the highest-information next step under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is only 20.8%, confirming RNA is the dominant signal. We have only one RNA data point, so uncertainty is high about which design choices matter most. Question tested: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile (with simple avgpool aggregation) improve RNA performance, holding the encoder constant at pca_n2000? This is a minimal, clean extension of config_001 that isolates the profile-setting effect. Why best next experiment: If multiprofile+avgpool helps, it validates a direction that unlocks many downstream configurations (transformer aggregation, better encoders, multimodal fusion) and justifies further investment there. If it does not help, we learn that singleprofile is sufficient and can redirect budget toward encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) or multimodal fusion. Either outcome significantly reduces uncertainty about a core architectural axis before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a ~10.6 pp gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile + avgpool is the strongest design so far. Image-only is very weak (0.208), so the RNA modality is the primary driver. Uncertainty: We have not tested whether a transformer aggregation can further improve over avgpool for multiprofile RNA. This is a critical architectural decision that, if resolved, applies to all future multiprofile and multimodal configurations. Question tested: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer (holding rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 fixed), giving a clean single-variable A/B comparison against config_002. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly isolates the aggregation question with minimal confounding, and the answer (transformer helps or not) will determine whether we need to spend budget testing transformer variants across encoders and modalities, or whether avgpool is sufficient. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile + avgpool + PCA (config_002, acc=0.591) is the clear best, while image-only with ResNet50 (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak. Avgpool outperforms transformer (0.591 vs 0.519). The key unresolved question is whether combining the strong RNA signal with image features via multimodal fusion can surpass the RNA-only baseline. Config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) pairs the proven-best RNA pipeline (multiprofile + avgpool + PCA) with the only image encoder we have evidence for (ResNet50) and uses the simplest fusion (concat). This is the most informative next step: if it beats 0.591, the entire multimodal design space (ViT-L, weighted fusion, learned RNA encoders) becomes worth exploring; if it does not, we can confidently redirect remaining budget toward improving the RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt) rather than investing in image-side improvements. It is the minimal, clean test of the fusion hypothesis using all currently validated components.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, showing that multimodal fusion with avgpool aggregation adds ~0.028 over the best RNA-only config (config_002, 0.591). The fusion method (concat vs weighted) is the only untested dimension within this exact architecture. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation when combining PCA-encoded RNA with ResNet50 image features under avgpool aggregation? This is a clean single-variable A/B test against config_018. Why best next: Under a limited budget, confirming or ruling out the fusion mechanism before investing in more expensive architectural changes (ViT-L, scvi, scgpt) is the most information-efficient step. A positive result gives an immediate improvement to the best config; a null result cleanly eliminates a design axis and redirects effort toward higher-impact choices like image encoder quality or RNA encoder nonlinearity.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at acc=0.639. We have strong evidence that multiprofile+avgpool+weighted fusion is the right architecture, but we have only tested one image encoder (resnet50), which performed very poorly in isolation (0.208). This leaves significant uncertainty about whether the image modality is simply underutilized by a weak encoder or inherently limited for this task. Question: config_025 swaps resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l while holding all other parameters at their known-best values (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted). This is a clean single-variable test of the image-encoder axis. Why best next: It is the most informative single experiment because (a) it directly extends our best configuration, (b) it resolves whether the image branch can contribute meaningfully with a stronger encoder, and (c) the answer guides all subsequent multimodal experiments—if ViT-L helps, we invest further in image features; if not, we pivot to RNA-encoder improvements (scvi/scgpt) as the remaining high-value axis.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration so far is config_019 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted; acc 0.639, F1 0.620). All multimodal experiments to date use PCA n2000, a simple linear dimensionality reduction, as the RNA encoder. The image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) shows negligible difference (0.639 vs 0.635), suggesting the RNA representation is the more impactful untested axis. Question: config_031 replaces PCA n2000 with scvi_n200 (a learned deep generative encoder) while holding all other settings at their best-known values (multi-profile, avgpool, weighted, ResNet50). This isolates the effect of a biologically-informed learned RNA representation within the multimodal fusion pipeline. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable extension of the current best configuration, making the result directly interpretable. If scvi_n200 improves performance, it validates investing in learned RNA encoders and opens the scvi multimodal family. If it does not, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects budget toward other axes (e.g., transformer aggregation in multimodal, config_021). Either outcome substantially reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision under the limited budget.

The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.678). The largest single improvement in this study was switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi_n200 (~4% gain). The image encoder question remains genuinely unresolved: with pca_n2000, resnet50 (0.639) and imagenet_vit_l (0.635) were nearly tied, leaving it unclear which backbone synergizes better with the richer scvi_n200 representations. Config_037 makes a clean single-variable change (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) from the current best, directly testing whether a stronger pretrained image encoder complements scvi_n200's learned latent space. This is the highest-value next experiment because it either identifies a further improvement or confirms resnet50 sufficiency, reducing uncertainty on the image-modality design axis before exploring other dimensions (e.g., transformer aggregation or scgpt).

The strongest evidence shows that the RNA encoder is a major performance driver: scvi_n200 improved over pca_n2000 by ~4-7% in the multimodal setting (0.639→0.678 with resnet50; 0.635→0.706 with imagenet_vit_l). However, scgpt has not been tested at all, leaving significant uncertainty about whether a third RNA encoder could outperform scvi_n200. Config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) holds all other dimensions at their empirically best values (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, imagenet_vit_l) and isolates the scgpt-vs-scvi_n200 comparison. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, it opens a new optimization direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the optimal encoder and lets us redirect budget to other axes (e.g., transformer aggregation or singleprofile trade-offs). Under a limited budget, resolving the RNA encoder question is the highest-value uncertainty to eliminate before fine-tuning secondary choices.

No experiments have been completed, so the priority is to establish a performance baseline against which all subsequent configurations can be meaningfully compared. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration: it uses the most basic encoder (PCA), requires no aggregation or fusion, and tests only the raw RNA signal. This serves as the 'null model' for the study. Its result will clarify: (1) the performance floor of the task, (2) whether RNA alone carries sufficient signal, and (3) the magnitude of headroom available for more complex encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion. Establishing this anchor first is the most efficient use of the first experiment under a limited budget, because every later comparison (better RNA encoder, adding image, adding aggregation, adding fusion) becomes interpretable only relative to a known single-modality, single-profile baseline.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), the most critical uncertainty is the relative contribution of each modality. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-factor ablation that isolates the image modality's standalone signal while keeping the profile setting (singleprofile) and architectural simplicity (no aggregation/fusion) matched to config_001. This establishes the image baseline needed to interpret all future multimodal experiments: if image_only substantially outperforms rna_only, the image modality is the stronger signal source and multimodal fusion should be prioritized; if it underperforms, RNA-focused improvements (better encoders, multiprofile) become more valuable. Testing multimodal directly (e.g., config_016) would confound the image contribution with fusion strategy, reducing interpretability. Under a tight budget, this one experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (modality) before committing to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA (PCA n2000, single profile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (ResNet50, single profile) achieves only 20.8%, indicating RNA is the dominant signal and image alone is very weak. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested whether multiprofile aggregation improves upon the single-profile baseline, and this axis (profile setting + aggregation method) is a critical design decision that will apply to all future multimodal experiments. Question tested: config_002 isolates the effect of multiprofile + avgpool aggregation while holding the RNA encoder (PCA n2000) constant relative to config_001, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why best next: It is the most natural exploitation of our best result, reduces uncertainty about a design axis relevant to all remaining experiments (multiprofile vs. single, and which aggregation method), and if it improves performance it establishes a stronger RNA baseline before investing budget in multimodal fusion or alternative encoders.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.591) and F1 (0.573), substantially outperforming singleprofile RNA (0.485) and image-only resnet50 (0.208). This establishes that multiprofile RNA with a simple aggregation is the current strongest signal. Uncertainty: We have not tested whether the aggregation method matters—i.e., whether a transformer can capture richer inter-profile relationships beyond simple averaging. Question tested: config_003 is identical to config_002 except it replaces avgpool with a transformer aggregator, isolating the effect of aggregation architecture. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a minimal, controlled extension of the best result, making the comparison clean and interpretable. (2) The aggregation choice is a design axis that propagates into every multimodal configuration (configs 018–051), so resolving it now reduces uncertainty across the largest portion of the remaining search space. (3) If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it signals that profile-to-profile interactions carry predictive signal worth modeling; if they are comparable, we confirm that simple pooling suffices and can focus budget on RNA encoder choice and multimodal fusion. Under a limited budget, this single experiment maximizes information per trial by resolving a high-leverage design decision before committing to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile + avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the clear best so far, while image-only ResNet50 is very weak (config_010, acc=0.208). Aggregation method matters (avgpool > transformer by ~7 pts) and multiprofile > singleprofile by ~10 pts. Key uncertainty: whether adding the image modality to the best RNA configuration provides any complementary signal, or whether the weak image features merely add noise. This experiment (config_018) directly extends the best unimodal config by adding ResNet50 image features via simple concat fusion, keeping all other settings at their best-known values (multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool). It is the most informative next step because it answers the central question of the multimodal study—does fusion help at all—using the simplest fusion mechanism as a baseline. If concat fusion improves over 0.591, we gain a strong direction to explore weighted fusion and stronger image encoders; if it does not, we learn to focus budget on RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scGPT) rather than multimodal combinations.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, only ~3% above RNA-alone multiprofile avgpool (config_002, 0.591), and image-alone is very weak (0.208). This suggests the image modality contributes limited complementary signal and the concat fusion may be diluting the stronger RNA representation. Question: config_019 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted, holding all other settings identical to config_018. This is a clean single-variable A/B test that isolates whether a learnable weighting can better balance the two modalities (e.g., downweighting the weak image channel). Why best next: Fusion strategy is the only design axis we have zero evidence on in the multimodal setting. The result directly determines whether future multimodal experiments should use concat or weighted fusion, and whether the image modality is genuinely adding information or acting as noise. Under a tight budget, this low-variance, high-information comparison is more valuable than jumping to a new encoder or image backbone where multiple variables would change simultaneously.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses PCA as the RNA encoder in a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted-fusion setup. RNA-only experiments show that multi-profile + avgpool is strongly preferred over single-profile or transformer (0.591 vs 0.485/0.519), and weighted fusion edges out concat (0.639 vs 0.619). However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as PCA—a simple linear projection. Image-only performance is very low (0.208), indicating RNA carries the dominant signal, so the quality of the RNA representation is likely the highest-leverage remaining design choice. Question tested: Does a learned nonlinear RNA encoder (scvi_n200) improve over PCA in the best multimodal configuration? This is a single-variable swap from config_019, making the result clean and directly interpretable. Why this is the best next experiment: If scvi_n200 improves performance, it confirms that RNA representation quality is a bottleneck and justifies further investment in learned encoders (scgpt, etc.). If it does not, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and the search can focus on other axes (e.g., image encoder). Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about the most important remaining design decision, making this the most information-efficient use of the next budget slot.

Evidence: The current best (config_031, acc 0.678) uses scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted in a multimodal multiprofile setup. All other dimensions (RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, fusion) have been validated and show clear winners. The image encoder quality is the only major untested axis in the proven-best configuration. Image-only resnet50 was weak (0.208), yet in multimodal context it contributed ~4% over RNA-only, suggesting the image signal is underutilized. Question tested: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a substantially stronger, pretrained vision transformer) increase the image modality's contribution and push overall accuracy beyond 0.678? Why best next: It is a single-variable, direct extension of the current best configuration, preserving all proven design choices while probing the largest remaining source of potential improvement. If ViT-L helps, it opens a new performance ceiling; if it does not, we learn the image modality's contribution is bounded by task relevance rather than encoder capacity, redirecting effort to RNA-side improvements (e.g., scgpt). This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_037 (scVI_n200 + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706). We have strong evidence that the RNA encoder matters (PCA→scVI gave ~4% gain, config_019→config_031) and that the image encoder matters (ResNet50→ViT-L gave ~3% gain, config_031→config_037). However, scGPT has not been tested in any completed experiment, leaving a major design dimension unexplored. Question: Does scGPT outperform, match, or underperform scVI_n200 as the RNA encoder in the best multimodal setting? config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap against config_037, isolating the RNA encoder choice. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly extends the current best configuration, tests the one major unexplored encoder, and provides a decisive comparison that will either open a new promising direction (if scGPT wins) or confirm scVI_n200 as optimal (if it loses), allowing the remaining budget to focus on other levers like aggregation or profile settings.

The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706). The only untested design dimension within this top-performing region is the aggregation method. While avgpool outperformed transformer in the RNA-only setting (0.591 vs 0.519), the multimodal context with a rich ViT-L image encoder may alter this relationship—transformer aggregation could better model cross-profile interactions when fused with strong image features. config_039 changes only aggregation (avgpool→transformer) while keeping all other settings at their empirically best values, making it a clean single-variable test. If it improves on 0.706, we gain a new best; if not, we confirm avgpool is optimal in this regime and can redirect budget to other unexplored dimensions. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step under the limited budget.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero information about the performance landscape. The most critical uncertainty is whether the task is tractable at all and what a reasonable baseline looks like. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard configuration—using PCA (a robust, low-risk encoder) on a single RNA profile. It establishes a performance floor and confirms the pipeline works end-to-end. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Every subsequent result (image-only, multimodal, alternative encoders, multiprofile, different fusion strategies) must be interpreted relative to a baseline. Starting with the most standard, least complex setup minimizes confounding factors (no fusion, no aggregation, no learned encoder risk) and gives a clean reference point. If RNA-only PCA performs well, we can then test whether adding image or multimodal fusion improves on it; if it performs poorly, we know to prioritize encoder or modality changes. This single experiment reduces the most uncertainty per unit budget by anchoring the entire search.

We have only one data point (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), so the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any predictive signal at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) establishes the cleanest possible image baseline: it matches the singleprofile setting of our RNA baseline and uses the standard, well-understood ResNet50 encoder. This lets us directly compare modality-level signal (RNA vs. image) while holding profile complexity constant. If image-only performs near 48%, the image modality adds little and we should focus budget on RNA encoder/aggregation choices. If it substantially exceeds 48%, it strongly justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion. Without this baseline, any multimodal result would be ambiguous (gains could come from image, from multiprofile aggregation, or from fusion). This single experiment resolves the highest-impact design question under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001) achieves 0.485 acc, while image-only with ResNet50 (config_010) is weak at 0.208 acc. We have only two data points and no evidence yet on whether multimodal fusion adds value. Question: Does combining the strong RNA signal with the (currently weak) image signal via simple concatenation improve over the RNA-only baseline? This directly tests the central hypothesis of the multimodal study with the simplest fusion strategy (concat) and the exact components already characterized. Why this is best: It is the minimal, most interpretable multimodal experiment—if it beats 0.485, fusion is validated and we can explore better encoders/aggregation; if it does not, we learn whether the bottleneck is the weak image encoder (motivating ViT-L) or fusion itself. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the core design decision (unimodal vs. multimodal) under the limited budget.

Evidence: Our best result (config_016, 52.7% acc) is multimodal with singleprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, and concat fusion. The image modality alone is very weak (20.8%), so the ~4.2% multimodal gain is modest. Critically, we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile helps, which is a foundational design choice for cellular profiling. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles per cell (via avgpool) improve over singleprofile, holding all other variables constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_018 is the minimal logical extension of our current best (config_016) — it changes only profile_setting (single→multi) and adds the necessary aggregation (avgpool), keeping RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion identical. This isolates the multiprofile effect cleanly. If multiprofile helps, it reshapes the entire remaining search (all subsequent multimodal configs should use multiprofile); if it doesn't, we can focus budget on encoder/fusion variations. Under limited budget, resolving this binary design question has the highest information value per experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 61.9% accuracy, a substantial ~9-point jump over config_016 (singleprofile, 52.7%), establishing multiprofile + multimodal as the clearly dominant design direction. Uncertainty: whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation or whether a more expressive transformer aggregation can further exploit the multi-profile structure. This experiment (config_020) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings identical to config_018, giving a clean single-variable comparison. It is the best next step because it directly exploits the strongest evidence in the search, tests a high-impact architectural choice (aggregation method) that will inform all subsequent multiprofile experiments, and has a reasonable chance of pushing performance above 62% if the transformer captures inter-profile relationships that simple averaging misses.

The current best result is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc, and the only fusion strategy tested so far is concat. Config_019 is a single-variable ablation that swaps concat for weighted fusion while holding every other parameter identical to config_018. This directly tests whether learned modality weighting (vs. simple concatenation) improves the fusion of the two modalities, which is a fundamental design decision that will inform all future multimodal experiments. Given that aggregation choice already showed a ~4pp impact (avgpool vs. transformer), fusion strategy is a comparably important untested axis. Selecting config_019 is the most efficient exploitation of the strongest evidence: it either improves on the current best or confirms concat is sufficient, reducing uncertainty about the fusion design choice with minimal confounding.

The current best (config_019: PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile; acc=0.639) establishes that multimodal + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted is a strong recipe. However, the image encoder remains the largest source of uncertainty: ResNet50 alone achieved only 0.208 accuracy, yet it contributed ~0.15 on top of RNA-only, suggesting the image signal is underutilized by a weak encoder. Config_025 swaps ResNet50 → ImageNet ViT-L while holding every other hyperparameter identical to config_019, giving a clean A/B test of image encoder quality. If ViT-L yields a meaningful gain, it confirms the image modality has untapped potential and justifies further investment in stronger image representations (and combinations with learned RNA encoders). If it yields little gain, it indicates the image contribution is inherently limited and redirects budget toward RNA encoder upgrades (scvi/scGPT). This single experiment resolves the highest-uncertainty design axis while remaining a direct exploitation of the best-known configuration, making it the most budget-efficient next step.

The current best (config_019: pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile; acc=0.639) has established that multiprofile > singleprofile, avgpool > transformer, and weighted > concat. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as PCA (linear) across all multimodal runs. The image encoder comparison (resnet50 vs ViT-L) showed near-equivalence (~0.635 vs 0.639), so further image encoder exploration has low expected information gain. The RNA encoder is the largest unexplored design axis: a learned non-linear representation (scvi_n200) could capture cell-state structure that PCA misses, potentially yielding a larger gain than the marginal differences seen in image/aggregation/fusion choices. Config_031 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding all other parameters at their best-known values (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), making it the most controlled and informative next experiment. A clear improvement would confirm RNA representation quality as a key lever; a null result would indicate PCA is sufficient and redirect budget toward other axes.

Evidence: The largest single-variable gain so far came from upgrading the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (+4 pts, config_019→config_031), while the image encoder choice (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) showed negligible difference (0.639 vs 0.635). Question: Does a more sophisticated RNA encoder (scgpt) continue to improve performance beyond scvi_n200, or does the RNA-encoder axis plateau? config_043 changes only the RNA encoder from the current best (config_031: scvi_n200→scgpt), keeping all other settings (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) fixed. Why best next: It directly tests whether the RNA-encoder trend continues, which is the highest-leverage remaining design question. A positive result opens a new exploitation path (scgpt + vit_l, etc.); a null result confirms scvi_n200 is near-optimal and redirects effort to other dimensions. Under a limited budget, resolving the RNA-encoder ceiling is more informative than re-testing the already-near-resolved image-encoder choice.

The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.6776 acc. The evidence shows that the RNA encoder choice is the dominant factor (scvi_n200: 0.678 vs pca_n2000: 0.639 vs scgpt: 0.525), while the image encoder choice had minimal impact with pca_n2000 (resnet50: 0.639 vs ViT-L: 0.635). However, the interaction between scvi_n200's richer learned representation and a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) is untested. Config_037 is a clean single-variable change from the current best (only swapping resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l), directly testing whether the more powerful ViT-L features complement the scvi_n200 RNA embedding better than resnet50 does. If it improves, it identifies a new best and opens further exploration; if not, it confirms resnet50 is sufficient and redirects budget toward other levers. This is the highest-information single experiment available.

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is establishing a performance baseline against which all design choices (multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, learned encoders) can be meaningfully evaluated. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard configuration in the space: it uses a well-understood linear dimensionality reduction (PCA), a single profile (avoiding aggregation confounds), and no image modality. This gives a clean floor performance. Any future gain from adding images, switching to learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation, or fusion strategies can then be attributed to those specific design decisions. Starting here maximizes the interpretability of every subsequent experiment under a limited budget, since it anchors the entire search to a well-defined reference point.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc / 46.4% F1), which establishes a weak RNA-only baseline. We have no information about whether image features carry discriminative signal for this task. Question being tested: Does the image modality alone provide meaningful classification performance, and how does it compare to the RNA-only baseline? This directly informs the core multimodal hypothesis—without knowing the image-only ceiling, we cannot later attribute any multimodal gain to genuine cross-modal complementarity versus one modality simply being stronger. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the minimal, controlled complement to config_001 (same singleprofile setting, standard resnet50 backbone), giving us both single-modality baselines in just two experiments. This maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design axis (which modality carries signal) before we invest budget in more complex multimodal, multiprofile, or encoder-variant configurations. If image-only is also weak, we know the task is inherently hard and may need better encoders; if it is strong, we know multimodal fusion has a strong partner to complement RNA.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: RNA-only with PCA (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while image-only with ResNet50 (config_010) achieves only 20.8%, near random. This large gap raises a critical strategic question: is the image modality inherently uninformative for this task, or is ResNet50 simply the wrong architecture for cellular images? 2) What this tests: config_013 uses ImageNet-pretrained ViT-Large (a substantially stronger and more general-purpose vision encoder) with the same singleprofile setting, isolating the effect of image encoder quality. A large improvement over 20.8% would confirm the image modality is viable and that ResNet50 was the bottleneck; a similarly poor result would indicate images are not useful, effectively eliminating ~20 multimodal and image-only configurations from consideration. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Under a tight budget, resolving whether the image modality is worth pursuing at all has the highest information value—it determines whether the search should focus on RNA improvements (multiprofile, better encoders) or whether multimodal fusion is a realistic path. Without this answer, investing in multimodal configurations (config_016–051) risks wasting experiments on a modality that may contribute no signal. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (modality viability) before committing budget to more complex combinations.

Evidence: RNA-only (PCA n2000, single profile) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while both image-only models are very weak (ResNet50: 20.8%, ViT-L: 22.7%), suggesting image features carry little standalone signal. The central research question is whether multimodal fusion can combine the strong RNA signal with any complementary image information to exceed the RNA-only baseline. Uncertainty: We have zero data on whether fusion helps or hurts; image features may be too noisy to contribute, or they may capture complementary morphological information. This experiment (config_022: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) directly tests the core multimodal hypothesis using the strongest RNA encoder (PCA n2000) paired with the best-performing image encoder (ViT-L, slightly ahead of ResNet50) and the simplest fusion (concat), keeping the profile setting at single to remain directly comparable to the config_001 baseline. If multimodal does not beat ~48.5%, we can rule out the entire multimodal branch and redirect budget to RNA encoder/aggregation improvements; if it does, it opens a rich search over fusion strategies, aggregation, and encoders. This single experiment resolves the highest-impact uncertainty in the search space.

Evidence: config_022 (multimodal, PCA n2000 + ViT-L, concat, single profile) is the best result so far at 0.535 accuracy, outperforming RNA alone (0.485) and image alone (~0.22). However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat). Uncertainty: whether weighted fusion could further improve upon concat by allowing the model to learn modality-specific importance weights, especially given that the image modality alone is very weak (~0.22) and may be adding noise through a simple concatenation. This experiment (config_023) is a clean A/B test against config_022, changing only the fusion method from concat to weighted while holding all other factors constant (same encoders, same profile setting). It is the best use of the next budget slot because it reduces uncertainty about a critical design choice with zero confounding, and the result directly informs whether all subsequent multimodal experiments should use weighted or concat fusion.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_022 (multimodal, single-profile, PCA+ViT-L, concat) at 0.535 accuracy, showing multimodal fusion provides a ~5% gain over RNA alone (0.485) and that ViT-L is the stronger image encoder. However, all completed experiments use single-profile; the multi-profile dimension (with aggregation) is completely untested and represents the largest source of uncertainty about potential performance gains. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) on top of the best-performing multimodal pipeline improve accuracy beyond 0.535? Why this config: config_024 is the most direct, minimal extension of config_022—same RNA encoder (PCA), same image encoder (ViT-L), same fusion (concat)—changing only profile setting to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the effect of multi-profile aggregation, reducing uncertainty about whether richer profile representation matters, before committing budget to more complex variants (transformer aggregation, different encoders). If it helps, it opens a promising direction; if not, it efficiently rules out that axis and redirects effort toward RNA encoder choice (SCVI/scGPT).

Evidence: config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved the best performance so far (acc 0.629, F1 0.599), a large jump over the singleprofile multimodal baseline (0.535). This shows multiprofile aggregation is a critical design axis. However, we only have one multiprofile data point and do not yet know whether avgpool is near-optimal or whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further exploit the multi-view structure. config_026 tests transformer aggregation while holding all other parameters at their best-known values (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion). This is the best next experiment because it directly exploits the strongest evidence (the multiprofile+multimodal direction) while resolving key uncertainty about the aggregation mechanism—information that will guide all subsequent multiprofile experiments across encoders and fusion strategies. It is more informative than testing weighted fusion (config_025) because the singleprofile data already suggests concat≈weighted, whereas the aggregation choice is an unexplored axis with potentially larger impact.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 acc. The largest gains came from multiprofile (+9.4 pts over singleprofile) and avgpool aggregation (+3 pts over transformer). However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as pca_n2000 across all experiments, and RNA is the dominant signal (0.485 RNA-only vs ~0.21-0.23 image-only). Question: Does a learned, biologically-informed RNA representation (scvi_n200) improve over PCA in the best-performing multimodal multiprofile architecture? Why this is the best next experiment: It sits in the most promising region of the search space (multiprofile + avgpool + concat + ViT-L), directly tests the single most impactful unexplored variable (RNA encoder quality), and has the highest potential to yield a direct improvement on our current best. If scvi_n200 helps, we gain a concrete upgrade; if it does not, we confirm PCA sufficiency and can redirect effort toward image-side or fusion refinements. This is a high-information, high-leverage test under the limited budget.

Evidence: The largest performance jump in the study came from switching the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to SCVI n200 in the multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/concat setting (+8.6 pp: 0.629 → 0.715), establishing that the learned RNA encoder is the dominant design lever. Uncertainty: We have only tested one learned encoder (SCVI n200); it is unknown whether SCGPT—a different learned encoder with a different inductive bias—would match or exceed SCVI, or whether the gain is specific to SCVI's architecture. What this tests: config_048 changes only the RNA encoder from SCVI n200 to SCGPT while holding all other settings at their empirically best values (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why it is the best next experiment: The encoder choice showed the largest effect size observed, so resolving whether SCGPT ≥ SCVI or SCVI > SCGPT is the highest-value uncertainty to reduce. A positive result opens a new promising direction; a negative result confirms SCVI as the encoder of choice and redirects effort to aggregation/fusion refinements. This is more informative than testing a small aggregation or fusion swap on the already-strong SCVI config, where expected gains are likely ≤3 pp based on the PCA-era evidence.

The strongest result so far is config_036 (SCVI n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 acc, showing that the RNA encoder choice is the dominant factor (SCVI >> PCA >> scGPT). However, we only have one data point on aggregation for SCVI (avgpool). For PCA, avgpool outperformed transformer by ~3% (0.629 vs 0.599), but it is unclear whether this ordering holds for the richer SCVI latent representations, which may interact differently with attention-based aggregation. config_038 (SCVI n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat) directly tests this: if transformer is worse or equal, we can confidently lock in avgpool and spend remaining budget on other axes (fusion, image encoder); if transformer is meaningfully better, it reveals that SCVI's structured latent space benefits from attention-based profile integration, opening a new optimization direction. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves a key design uncertainty around the current best configuration without changing multiple variables simultaneously.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit; the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: it uses the most standard RNA encoder (PCA), the simplest profile setting, and no image or fusion complexity. This experiment (1) establishes the performance floor for the RNA modality with a well-understood pipeline, (2) provides the reference point against which all subsequent multimodal and image-only experiments will be interpreted, and (3) isolates the contribution of the RNA signal before layering in additional design choices. Without this baseline, a multimodal result (e.g., config_016) would be ambiguous—we could not tell whether good performance comes from RNA, image, or their interaction. Under a limited budget, spending the first experiment on the most minimal, confound-free baseline maximizes the interpretive value of every subsequent experiment.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, acc≈0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether adding image information provides meaningful gain over RNA alone — the central question in a multimodal cellular profiling study. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) keeps the RNA side identical to config_001 and introduces the simplest image encoder (ResNet-50) with the simplest fusion (concat), making it a clean, minimal-contrast test of 'does image information complement RNA features?' If accuracy improves substantially, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies investing subsequent experiments in richer encoders/fusion. If it does not improve, it signals that the modalities are redundant or poorly aligned under this setup, redirecting effort toward better RNA encoders or profile strategies. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-leverage design axis (modality combination) before committing budget to finer-grained choices like encoder type, aggregation, or fusion strategy.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, single profile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a clear +4.2% improvement over the RNA-only baseline (config_001, 0.485 acc). This confirms that adding the image modality with concat fusion is beneficial. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the concat fusion strategy is optimal or whether a weighted fusion could yield further gains. Question tested: config_017 is identical to config_016 except fusion is changed from concat to weighted, providing a clean single-variable A/B comparison. Why best next step: It is the lowest-risk, highest-information experiment—directly exploiting the strongest evidence while isolating the fusion mechanism. The result will inform the fusion choice for all subsequent multimodal experiments (multiprofile, alternative encoders), making it the most efficient use of the next budget slot before branching into larger architectural changes like multiprofile or alternative encoders.

Evidence: We have RNA-only (config_001, acc=0.485) and multimodal (config_016, acc=0.527) baselines, showing a +4.2% gain from adding the image modality. However, we lack the image-only baseline, so we cannot decompose whether the multimodal gain comes from strong image features or from true cross-modal synergy. Question: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly measures the standalone image contribution under the same encoder and profile settings as the multimodal runs. Why this is the best next experiment: With only 3 experiments completed, the most critical uncertainty is the relative contribution of each modality. This single experiment, combined with the existing RNA-only and multimodal results, gives a complete three-way decomposition (RNA, image, combined) that will guide all subsequent decisions—whether to invest in better image encoders (ViT), better RNA encoders (scvi/scGPT), or more sophisticated fusion. Without this baseline, exploring multiprofile or alternative encoders would be done in the dark regarding which modality is the bottleneck.

Evidence: Our best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, single-profile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, concat) at 0.527 acc, modestly above RNA-only (0.485) and far above image-only (0.208). The concat vs weighted difference is negligible (~0.3%), so fusion type is a minor factor. The major untested design axis is single-profile vs multiprofile, which could substantially change how both modalities contribute. This experiment (config_018) extends our best configuration to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, keeping all other variables identical to config_016. It directly tests whether multiprofile representation (with simple average pooling) improves over single-profile, resolving a key uncertainty before committing budget to more complex aggregation strategies (transformer) or alternative encoders. If multiprofile helps, it opens the aggregation-strategy question for all future experiments; if it does not, we can confidently focus on single-profile variants and encoder improvements, saving limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, showing a large ~9% jump over single-profile multimodal (config_016, 0.527). This confirms multi-profile aggregation is the most impactful design axis. However, we have only tested avgpool aggregation in the multi-profile setting; transformer aggregation is completely untested and could allow the model to learn profile-specific attention weights rather than uniform averaging. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for combining multiple profiles in the multimodal setting? This is a clean one-variable change from the current best (config_018 → config_020: avgpool → transformer, everything else identical). Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, testing the aggregation mechanism in the already-validated multi-profile multimodal regime directly targets the largest remaining uncertainty in the most promising architecture. A positive result would identify a new best configuration; a null/negative result would confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., image encoder quality via ViT-L). Either outcome significantly reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc.
