The image modality contributed ~4 pts over RNA-only in singleprofile (0.485→0.527) yet was very weak alone (0.208), suggesting the ResNet50 encoder may not be extracting sufficient cellular morphology features. Question tested: Does upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L unlock more complementary visual information in the multiprofile+avgpool+concat setup? Why this is the best next experiment: It isolates a single high-impact variable (image encoder quality) while holding all other parameters at their known-best values (multiprofile, avgpool, concat, pca_n2000), making the result cleanly interpretable. If ViT-L improves performance, it opens a productive direction; if not, we learn the image contribution is encoder-limited and should focus budget on RNA encoder alternatives (scvi/scgpt). This is more informative than testing fusion type (concat vs weighted showed negligible difference) or transformer aggregation (already shown inferior to avgpool).

Evidence: The current best is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 acc. RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.485 vs image_only 0.208), yet we have only ever tested pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder. This is the largest unexplored design dimension. Question: Does a learned RNA representation (scvi_n200) outperform PCA in the current best multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/concat/ViT setting? This experiment isolates exactly one variable (RNA encoder) relative to config_024, giving a clean comparison. Why best next: If scvi_n200 improves, it validates learned RNA encoders and motivates further testing of scgpt; if it does not, PCA suffices and we can focus budget on fusion/aggregation refinements. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty on the most impactful untested axis, making it the highest-information experiment under the limited budget.

The largest single improvement in the search came from switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (0.629 → 0.715 acc, config_024 → config_036), establishing that the RNA encoder is the most impactful design choice. However, we have no evidence on whether this gain is specific to scvi's VAE-based architecture or generalizable to other learned encoders. config_048 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) holds all other hyperparameters at their best-known values and swaps only the RNA encoder to scgpt, a generative-model-based encoder with different inductive biases. If scgpt approaches scvi's performance, it tells us 'any learned encoder ≫ PCA' and broadens the viable design space; if it lags substantially, it identifies scvi's specific representational properties as critical. Under a limited budget, resolving this encoder-architecture question is more informative than fine-tuning aggregation or fusion, which have shown only small effects so far.

The current best (config_036, scvi_n200 + ViT-L, avgpool, concat, 0.715 acc) shows that the RNA encoder is the dominant factor: switching from PCA to scvi_n200 gave a ~9-point gain, while avgpool vs. transformer aggregation previously showed a ~4-point gap (0.619 vs 0.579) but only under the much simpler PCA representation. config_038 isolates a single variable—changing aggregation from avgpool to transformer—while keeping the strong scvi_n200 + ViT-L backbone. This tests whether the learned, structured embeddings from scvi_n200 interact differently with attention-based aggregation than with simple pooling. If transformer matches or beats avgpool here, it reveals an important encoder-aggregation interaction and opens a new design axis; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool is robustly superior regardless of encoder quality. This is the most informative single-variable extension of the current best, balancing exploitation of the scvi_n200+ViT-L direction with exploration of a design choice whose prior evidence was collected under a weaker RNA encoder.

No experiments have been completed, so the highest-priority task is to establish a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest and most standard configuration: RNA is the primary modality in cellular profiling, PCA is the most widely used and interpretable dimensionality-reduction encoder, and singleprofile is the minimal profile setting. This experiment will give a reference validation accuracy/F1 for the RNA-only, single-profile case. Every subsequent experiment—image-only baselines, multiprofile variants, alternative encoders (scvi, scgpt), and multimodal fusion—can be meaningfully compared against this anchor. Without this baseline, performance differences from more complex configurations would be uninterpretable. Under a limited budget, spending the first experiment on the simplest, most informative baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment and sets the stage for efficient exploration of the remaining design dimensions.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical open question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding an image modality to the RNA baseline actually improves performance. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the most direct, controlled extension of config_001: it holds the RNA encoder and profile setting constant while introducing the image modality with the simplest standard fusion (concat). This single experiment will (a) establish whether multimodal integration is worthwhile at all, (b) provide a multimodal baseline against which to later compare fusion strategies, image encoders, and profile settings, and (c) reduce the largest source of uncertainty in the design space. If multimodal helps, we exploit that direction; if not, we efficiently rule out an entire branch of the search. No other single experiment reduces uncertainty about this fundamental design choice as cleanly.

With only two completed experiments, the evidence is very sparse. config_016 (multimodal, resnet50, concat) outperforms config_001 (RNA-only) by ~4.2% accuracy, but we cannot yet determine whether this gain comes from the image modality alone or from the synergistic combination of both modalities. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the critical ablation: it isolates the image contribution using the same encoder and profile setting as config_016. If image-only approaches or exceeds the multimodal result, the RNA channel adds little value and future budget should focus on image encoder/architecture choices. If image-only is substantially lower, the fusion is truly synergistic and we should invest in refining fusion strategy and multiprofile aggregation. This single experiment resolves the most fundamental uncertainty in the search space and will most efficiently guide all subsequent decisions under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the current best at 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, outperforming rna-only (0.485) and far exceeding image-only (0.208). The multiprofile axis is completely untested across all three model settings, representing the largest remaining source of uncertainty. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) on top of the best-known multimodal setup yield a meaningful gain over singleprofile? Why this is the best next experiment: config_018 is the minimal, clean extension of the current best (same encoders, same concat fusion) that isolates the multiprofile + avgpool variable. avgpool is chosen over transformer to keep the aggregation simple and reduce overfitting risk with limited data. A positive result would justify investing further in multiprofile configurations (transformer aggregation, other encoders); a null or negative result would efficiently rule out that axis and redirect budget toward image-encoder or RNA-encoder variations. Under a tight budget, resolving this high-impact, unexplored design axis provides the greatest expected information gain per experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.619 acc, a large jump over single-profile multimodal (config_016, 0.527) and RNA-only single-profile (config_001, 0.485). This confirms multi-profile aggregation is the dominant performance driver. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation strategy or whether a transformer-based aggregation (which can model inter-profile relationships) would further improve performance. config_020 is a clean single-variable change from config_018 (avgpool → transformer, all else identical), directly testing whether more expressive profile aggregation yields gains. This is the best next experiment because it exploits our strongest finding (multi-profile is critical) while resolving a key design-axis uncertainty with minimal confounding, and the result will inform whether to invest further in aggregation complexity or pivot to other dimensions (fusion strategy, encoder quality).

The strongest evidence so far points to config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc as the current best, with multiprofile contributing the largest single gain (+0.092 over singleprofile) and avgpool outperforming transformer (+0.04). However, the fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' across all multimodal runs. config_019 is the minimal controlled change from the best config—swapping concat for weighted fusion while holding every other factor constant. This directly tests whether the modality combination strategy can be further optimized, which is a high-leverage design choice given that the image modality alone is very weak (0.208) and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (+0.042 in singleprofile). If weighted fusion helps, it is a free improvement; if not, it confirms concat is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward image encoder or RNA encoder upgrades. Under a limited budget, this single-variable test from the best-known configuration is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: The dominant signal is clearly RNA (0.485 vs 0.208 for image-only), and the best configuration so far (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, acc=0.639) uses only a linear PCA encoder for RNA. The aggregation (avgpool > transformer) and fusion (weighted > concat) choices are now well-established. The largest unexplored dimension that could move performance is the RNA encoder quality, since RNA drives most of the signal. Question tested: Does replacing PCA with scgpt (a pretrained single-cell foundation model capturing non-linear transcriptomic structure) improve on the current best in the otherwise-identical multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/weighted setting? Why this is the best next experiment: It isolates exactly one variable (RNA encoder) from the best-performing configuration, so any performance change is attributable to the encoder choice. If scgpt helps, it opens a high-impact axis for further gains; if it does not, we learn PCA is sufficient and can redirect budget toward image encoder or other factors. This is more informative than testing a better image encoder (given image-only is only 0.208) or re-testing aggregation/fusion combinations already shown to be suboptimal.

The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest design so far. However, every multimodal experiment to date has used resnet50 as the image encoder, and the image-only baseline (config_010, resnet50) was very weak (acc=0.208), suggesting resnet50 may not extract sufficiently informative visual features for this task. config_025 tests the same proven architecture (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, weighted) but swaps in imagenet_vit_l, a substantially stronger image encoder. This is the highest-value next experiment because: (1) it isolates a single, completely unexplored design dimension (image encoder capacity) while holding all other proven-optimal choices fixed, (2) it has high potential upside if ViT-L captures richer morphological features, and (3) it has high information value even if it underperforms, as it would confirm that image encoder choice is not a bottleneck and redirect effort toward other variables. Under a limited budget, this single experiment resolves a major source of uncertainty about whether the current performance ceiling is driven by the image backbone.

Evidence: With concat fusion, avgpool aggregation outperformed transformer by ~4% (0.619 vs 0.579), and weighted fusion outperformed concat by ~2% (0.639 vs 0.619) under avgpool. However, the aggregation×fusion interaction is untested: we do not know whether the avgpool>transformer gap persists when fusion is weighted. Question: Does transformer aggregation remain inferior under weighted fusion, or does weighted fusion partially compensate for the weaker aggregation? Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most direct logical extension of the two strongest findings (avgpool superiority and weighted superiority), it cleanly isolates the aggregation variable in the context of the best-performing fusion strategy, and its result will determine whether transformer can be ruled out entirely for all remaining experiments—saving budget from exploring a potentially dead branch. If transformer+weighted is also clearly worse, we can confidently focus all subsequent experiments on avgpool variants and new encoders; if it is competitive, it reveals an important interaction that changes the search strategy.

Evidence: The current best (config_019: multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest architecture. Among RNA encoders, pca_n2000 (0.639) far outperforms scgpt (0.525), but scvi_n200 remains completely untested in the multimodal multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether a variational autoencoder (scvi), which learns a nonlinear latent representation of single-cell data, can match or exceed the linear PCA projection. scgpt's poor performance suggests learned encoders may struggle here, but scvi is architecturally distinct (VAE vs. generative transformer) and its behavior is genuinely unknown. What this tests: config_031 isolates the RNA encoder as the sole variable from the current best, directly measuring whether scvi_n200 can compete with pca_n2000 under the best-known aggregation/fusion regime. Why it is the best next experiment: It resolves the most important remaining design uncertainty (RNA encoder choice) with a single clean comparison, and the outcome will either confirm PCA as the optimal encoder (closing that search axis) or reveal a new promising direction—maximizing information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile strategy, or fusion method performs best. The most critical unknown is the performance floor—how well the simplest possible model does. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal, interpretable baseline in the search space. It isolates the RNA signal with the most basic linear encoder (PCA to 2000 dims) and a single profile, removing all confounding complexity from learned encoders, multi-profile aggregation, or cross-modal fusion. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: Establishing this anchor is essential before any comparative conclusion can be drawn. It is also the cheapest configuration to train (no learned image encoder, no transformer aggregation, no fusion), preserving compute for subsequent experiments. Once this floor is known, the next experiments can efficiently test whether (a) image modality adds value, (b) richer RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) improve over PCA, and (c) multimodal fusion outperforms either single modality—each a high-uncertainty, high-impact design question that this baseline makes interpretable.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), we have essentially no information about whether the image modality contributes useful signal. The most critical structural question is whether multimodal fusion improves over the RNA-only baseline. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is a minimal, controlled extension of config_001: it keeps the same RNA encoder and profile setting, and adds only the image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). This directly answers 'does adding image information help?' If accuracy jumps substantially, we know to invest subsequent budget in multimodal variants (better encoders, multiprofile, weighted fusion). If it stays near 0.485, we know the image modality (at least with ResNet-50) is not the bottleneck and should pivot to improving the RNA side (multiprofile, scvi/scgpt encoders). This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-leverage design axis under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a meaningful +4.2% improvement over the RNA-only baseline (config_001, 0.485/0.464), confirming that adding the image modality is beneficial. However, we have zero data on whether multiprofile (capturing multiple spatial profiles per cell) provides additional signal over singleprofile. This is the largest unexplored design axis. config_018 is the minimal logical extension of config_016: it keeps the same model setting (multimodal), RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat), changing only the profile setting to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the effect of multiprofile while minimizing confounding variables (no new encoder, no new fusion method, no complex aggregation). Under a tight budget, resolving whether multiprofile adds value is the highest-information experiment: if it helps, it unlocks a large family of improved configs; if it does not, we can rule out that axis and focus on fusion method or encoder choice next.

Evidence: The largest performance gain so far came from switching to multi-profile with avgpool aggregation (config_018: 0.619 acc vs config_016: 0.527 acc, +9.2 pp), confirming that multi-profile aggregation is a critical design axis. However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool) and one fusion strategy (concat). Uncertainty: It is unclear whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) that can model inter-profile relationships will outperform simple averaging, or whether the current avgpool is already near-optimal for this task. This experiment (config_020) tests transformer aggregation while holding all other variables constant (PCA, ResNet50, concat, multi-profile), providing a clean ablation of the aggregation choice. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly extends the current best configuration along the most impactful design axis (multi-profile aggregation), and the result will inform whether to invest further in transformer-based architectures or pivot to other dimensions (e.g., weighted fusion, ViT-L image encoder).

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, showing that multiprofile+avgpool is a strong recipe. However, all multimodal results so far used concat fusion; the weighted-fusion alternative is completely untested. Question: config_019 is identical to config_018 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, giving a clean one-variable A/B test of whether learned/adaptive modality weighting outperforms simple concatenation. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it directly exploits the strongest configuration found so far, (2) it isolates a single high-impact design choice (how modalities are combined) with zero confounds, (3) the answer generalizes—knowing whether weighted fusion helps or hurts informs every future multimodal configuration, and (4) under a tight budget, a controlled comparison against the current best is more informative than jumping to a second untested variable (e.g., a new image encoder or RNA encoder) where the result would be harder to attribute.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves acc=0.639, and we have strong evidence that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the optimal architecture for the resnet50 image encoder. However, the image encoder choice (resnet50 vs. imagenet_vit_l) is a major untested design dimension — we have only ever used resnet50. Question: config_025 tests whether upgrading the image encoder to a larger, ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L (while holding the otherwise-best multiprofile/avgpool/weighted/pca_n2000 settings constant) yields a meaningful accuracy gain over resnet50. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable exploitation of the strongest evidence (config_019) along the most impactful untested axis. A positive result opens a new performance ceiling; a null result tells us resnet50 is sufficient and shifts focus to the RNA encoder or other factors. This is more informative than testing transformer+weighted (config_021), where the 4-point gap between avgpool and transformer under concat makes a reversal under weighted unlikely.

The current best config (config_019: PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.639 acc. Key evidence shows multiprofile and weighted fusion are strong, avgpool beats transformer, and image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) makes negligible difference. The major untested axis is the RNA encoder: all experiments so far use PCA (a simple linear projection). config_031 (scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable change from config_019, isolating whether a learned nonlinear RNA representation (scVI latent) can outperform PCA. This is the highest-value uncertainty to resolve: if scvi_n200 improves performance, it opens a productive exploration direction for RNA encoders; if not, it confirms PCA is sufficient and we can focus budget on other axes. Under a limited budget, this experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about an important design choice while maintaining all other settings at their empirically validated best values.

The strongest single-factor improvement in the history is the RNA encoder upgrade from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (config_019→config_031: 0.639→0.678 acc), suggesting that learned RNA representations are the most impactful design axis. The current best (config_031: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) has not yet been compared against scgpt, another learned/generative RNA encoder. config_043 is a clean single-variable swap (scvi_n200→scgpt) holding all other settings at their validated best (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted). This directly tests whether the RNA encoder axis can be pushed further or whether scvi_n200 already captures most of the benefit of learned encodings. Given that the RNA encoder produced the largest observed gain (~4 acc points), resolving whether scgpt offers additional improvement is the highest-information experiment: if scgpt wins, it opens a new optimization direction; if it ties or loses, it confirms scvi_n200 as the ceiling on this axis and redirects budget toward image encoder or aggregation refinements.

Evidence: config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is the current best at 0.678 acc, clearly outperforming pca_n2000 (0.639) and scgpt (0.525) under identical settings. The avgpool+weighted aggregation/fusion combo is well-supported by multiple experiments. The remaining uncertainty in this top pipeline is the image encoder choice: with pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l (0.635) was marginally below resnet50 (0.639), but the interaction with scvi_n200 is untested. Question: Does imagenet_vit_l complement scvi_n200 better than resnet50, potentially pushing past 0.678? Why this is best: config_037 is a clean single-variable change (image encoder only) from the current best, directly testing the most important remaining design decision in the top-performing pipeline. It either yields a new best or confirms resnet50 sufficiency, reducing uncertainty efficiently under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200 + ViT + avgpool + weighted, 0.7062 acc) was reached through a consistent pattern: multiprofile >> singleprofile, avgpool > transformer (config_018 vs 020), weighted > concat (config_019 vs 018), scvi_n200 >> PCA >> scgpt, and ViT > ResNet with scvi_n200. The key remaining uncertainty for this top-performing combination is whether the avgpool-over-transformer finding generalizes to the scvi_n200 + ViT setting. Config_039 (scvi_n200 + ViT + transformer + weighted) directly tests this by changing only the aggregation from the current best. If avgpool still wins, it confirms the aggregation choice is robust across encoders and we can confidently lock in the architecture. If transformer unexpectedly performs comparably or better, it would indicate that the richer scvi+ViT features benefit from attention-based aggregation, opening a new optimization direction. This is the highest-information single experiment: it exploits the strongest direction while reducing uncertainty about a core architectural choice, making it the best use of the next budget slot.

With no prior experiments, the highest-priority need is to establish a reliable performance baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest and cheapest configuration in the search space: it uses the most basic RNA encoder (PCA), a single profile (no aggregation needed), and no image modality. This gives a fast, low-variance reference point. All subsequent experiments—testing multiprofile aggregation, learned encoders (scVI, scGPT), image modality, and multimodal fusion—can be interpreted relative to this floor. Starting here maximizes information per experiment: if it performs well, we know the task is tractable with minimal machinery; if it underperforms, we immediately learn which axis (encoder quality, multi-profile aggregation, or image modality) to explore next. Under a limited budget, spending the first slot on the cheapest, most interpretable baseline is the most efficient use of resources.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), giving us essentially no information about whether the image modality contributes useful signal. The most critical uncertainty to resolve before committing budget to multimodal or encoder variations is whether image features alone are informative for this task. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-variable comparison against our existing RNA-only baseline: it isolates the image modality's contribution using a standard, well-understood encoder. If image-only accuracy is comparable to RNA-only (~48%), it suggests neither modality is sufficient alone and multimodal fusion is essential. If image-only is substantially higher, it redirects our search toward image encoders and multimodal fusion strategies. If substantially lower, it confirms RNA as the primary signal and justifies focusing on RNA encoder upgrades (scvi, scgpt) and multiprofile aggregation. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design axis (modality) before we spend budget on more complex multimodal or encoder configurations.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA-2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) is much weaker at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) improves over singleprofile for the RNA modality. This experiment (config_002) is a clean, single-variable comparison against config_001—only the profile setting changes from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation—directly isolating the effect of multi-profile aggregation. If multiprofile helps, it validates investing in transformer aggregation (config_003) and better encoders with multiprofile; if it does not, we avoid wasting budget on all multiprofile variants. Under a tight budget, this controlled A/B test on our strongest modality maximally reduces uncertainty about a core architectural choice before committing to more complex multimodal or encoder variants.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a strong +10.5pp gain over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming multiprofile is highly beneficial. However, we have not yet tested transformer aggregation, leaving a critical architectural question unresolved. Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest configuration so far, while image-only resnet50 (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak in isolation. The central open question for a multimodal profiling study is whether the weak image signal carries complementary morphological information that, when fused with the strong RNA signal, improves over RNA alone. This experiment (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests that question by taking the best-validated RNA pipeline and adding the image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). If it significantly beats 0.591, it confirms multimodal value and justifies further fusion/image-encoder exploration; if it does not, it tells us to focus remaining budget on RNA encoder alternatives (scvi, scgpt) rather than image fusion. This is the highest-information single experiment because its outcome bifurcates the entire remaining search space.

Evidence: The best-performing config so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1. RNA carries most of the signal (RNA-only multiprofile avgpool = 0.591 vs image-only = 0.208), and avgpool aggregation clearly beats transformer (0.591 vs 0.519). However, PCA n2000 is the only RNA encoder tested across all experiments. Question: config_030 swaps only the RNA encoder to SCVI n200 (a learned 200-dim latent) while holding every other hyperparameter identical to config_018. This isolates whether a nonlinear, dimensionality-reduced learned representation can match or beat a 2000-dim linear PCA projection. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is the highest-leverage untested design axis because RNA dominates the signal. If SCVI n200 outperforms PCA n2000, it opens a productive direction across all fusion/image-encoder variants; if it underperforms, we confirm PCA's robustness and can redirect budget toward image encoder or fusion strategy. This single experiment reduces the most critical uncertainty with minimal confounds (one-variable change from the current best).

The current best is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc=0.632). All multimodal results so far used concat fusion, leaving the fusion strategy entirely unexplored. config_031 is an isolated one-variable change (concat → weighted) from the current best, directly testing whether the way RNA and image features are combined matters. This is a fundamental design decision: if weighted fusion outperforms concat, it can be applied across all multimodal configurations to improve performance; if it is equivalent or worse, we can rule out that axis and focus budget on image encoder or aggregation choices. Under a limited budget, this clean A/B comparison maximizes information gain about a high-impact, currently untested design dimension.

The current best (config_031: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.678) shows that weighted fusion and multiprofile aggregation are strong contributors. However, the image encoder (ResNet50) performed very poorly in isolation (config_010: acc=0.208), raising the question of whether the image modality's contribution in the multimodal setting is bottlenecked by encoder capacity. Config_037 is a clean, single-variable extension of config_031 that swaps ResNet50 for the much stronger Imagenet ViT-L while keeping all other settings identical (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted). This directly tests whether upgrading the image encoder unlocks additional signal that ResNet50 cannot capture. If performance improves meaningfully, the image encoder becomes a key lever for further gains; if not, we can confidently rule out image-encoder quality as a bottleneck and redirect budget toward RNA encoder (scgpt) or fusion/aggregation refinements. Under a limited budget, this experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about one of the two modalities' contribution while staying anchored to the current best configuration.

Evidence: The current best (config_037, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, 0.706 acc) establishes a strong multimodal configuration, and scvi_n200 has shown a modest edge over pca_n2000. The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.706). In the RNA-only setting, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), but that comparison was made without a strong image encoder. With no completed experiments, all design decisions are uncertain. The most informative first experiment is a minimal, well-understood baseline that establishes a performance floor for all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) uses the simplest profile setting and the most standard, interpretable RNA encoder (PCA), isolating the contribution of RNA data alone without confounding from image modality, learned encoders, or multi-profile aggregation. With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality adds predictive signal at all — the core premise of multimodal cellular profiling. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the cleanest controlled extension of the baseline: it keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting identical to config_001, so any accuracy difference is attributable to the addition of image features via a standard resnet50 encoder and simple concat fusion. This single experiment simultaneously tests (a) whether image modality carries complementary information, (b) whether concat fusion is a viable starting point, and (c) whether resnet50 is a reasonable image encoder. If config_016 substantially exceeds 48.5%, we exploit the multimodal direction in subsequent runs; if it is comparable or worse, we learn that the image modality (at least with resnet50) is not contributing, redirecting effort toward RNA encoder or profile-setting improvements. Under a tight budget, resolving the modality question first prevents wasting experiments on hyperparameter tuning of a potentially unhelpful modality.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a clear ~4% improvement over the rna_only baseline (config_001, 0.485 acc). This confirms that adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion is beneficial. However, all experiments so far use singleprofile; the multiprofile axis is entirely untested and represents the largest remaining source of uncertainty about whether additional per-cell profile information can further boost performance. Question tested: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile (with avgpool aggregation) improve on the validated multimodal+concat setup, while keeping RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat) identical to config_016? This isolates the profile-setting effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the minimal, cleanest extension of our best-performing configuration along the most impactful untested design axis. A positive result would justify investing further in multiprofile variants (transformer aggregation, other encoders); a null or negative result would let us redirect budget toward RNA/image encoder choices and fusion strategy, avoiding wasted experiments on a less productive axis. Under a tight budget, resolving this binary question about multiprofile value is more informative than, e.g., testing weighted vs. concat fusion on singleprofile, where the expected delta is smaller.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile aggregation is the dominant design lever (+0.092 over singleprofile multimodal). However, we have no evidence on whether transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool for combining multiple profiles. Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at acc=0.619/F1=0.610, and we've confirmed that multiprofile+avgpool is strongly preferred over singleprofile and transformer aggregation. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform concat fusion when combined with the proven multiprofile+avgpool pipeline? This is a single-variable A/B test against our best result, isolating the fusion mechanism. Why best next experiment: It is the lowest-risk, highest-information extension of the strongest evidence—either it confirms concat is sufficient (freeing us to explore image/RNA encoder upgrades) or it reveals that fusion weighting is a meaningful lever (opening a clear exploitation path). Under a tight budget, resolving this one binary design question before committing to larger architectural changes (ViT-L, scGPT, scVI) is the most efficient use of the next run.

Evidence: The current best is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639). Key findings: (1) multimodal >> RNA-only, (2) multiprofile >> singleprofile (~9% gain), (3) avgpool > transformer for aggregation, (4) weighted > concat for fusion. The one major design axis untested within the winning configuration is the image encoder: we have only used ResNet50, while ImageNet ViT-L is available and substantially more expressive. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L further improve the already-strong multimodal pipeline, or is the image contribution already saturated? Given that the image modality contributes meaningfully (multimodal vs. RNA-only gap), resolving whether a stronger visual backbone helps is the highest-information next step under a limited budget, and it avoids confounding multiple changes.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as pca_n2000 across all multimodal experiments. This directly tests whether a learned, biologically-informed RNA representation (scVI) can outperform a linear PCA projection in the multimodal setting. A positive result would open a productive new search direction (scvi/scgpt encoders); a null result would confirm PCA sufficiency and let us focus remaining budget on other axes. Evidence: The current best (config_031, scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc 0.678) clearly outperforms the prior best (config_019, pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc 0.639), confirming that the learned scvi encoder is a major driver. With pca_n2000, resnet50 and imagenet_vit_l were nearly equivalent (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison was made with a linear PCA representation. Question: Does the richer, learned scvi_n200 representation interact synergistically with the larger ViT image encoder, or does resnet50 remain sufficient? This is a single-variable swap from the current best (only image encoder changes), making it a clean, high-information experiment. Why best next: It directly exploits the strongest validated direction (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted) while resolving the one remaining uncertainty in the best configuration's design, giving the highest expected information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

The current best (config_037: scvi_n200 + vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706) has established that multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/weighted is the optimal architecture, and that scvi_n200 substantially outperforms pca_n2000. However, the scgpt RNA encoder is completely untested in any multimodal setting, representing the largest remaining source of uncertainty in the design space. config_049 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is a clean, single-variable comparison against config_037—only the RNA encoder changes. If scgpt surpasses scvi_n200, we identify a new best configuration; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 as the superior encoder and can confidently stop exploring that dimension. Under a limited budget, this experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most impactful untested design choice while staying anchored to the proven-optimal settings in all other dimensions.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200 + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706) has established that scvi_n200 and ViT-L are the strongest encoders, and avgpool > transformer was observed only under the weaker pca encoder (config_018 vs 020: 0.619 vs 0.579). The key uncertainty is whether transformer aggregation could outperform avgpool when paired with scvi's richer, learned nonlinear representations—scvi encodes cell-level latent structure that may benefit from attention-based cross-profile interaction in a way pca's linear projections do not. Config_039 is a single-variable change from the best config (avgpool→transformer), making the comparison clean and directly informative. If transformer matches or beats avgpool here, it opens a new optimization axis; if it confirms avgpool superiority, it consolidates the design and lets us focus remaining budget on other dimensions. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the one untested design choice in the best-performing setting.

With zero completed experiments, there is no performance reference point, making every subsequent result uninterpretable. The most critical first question is: what is the baseline performance of the simplest viable model? config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal configuration—no image modality, no multi-profile aggregation, no fusion—so it isolates the core RNA classification pipeline with a standard, well-understood encoder. With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries meaningful signal for this task. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly measures image-only performance using the simplest possible setup (no aggregation, standard pretrained encoder), isolating the modality effect. Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA-2000) achieves 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50, singleprofile) achieves only 20.8% acc, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have no evidence yet on whether the multiprofile setting (with aggregation) improves upon the single-profile baseline. Why this is the best next experiment: The profile setting is a fundamental architectural decision that gates whether aggregation is needed at all and interacts with every downstream choice (encoder, fusion, image modality). Testing it first with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and the already-validated PCA encoder gives a clean, interpretable signal. If multiprofile+avgpool improves on 48.5%, we gain a strong exploitation direction (try transformer aggregation, better encoders, multimodal fusion). Evidence: config_002 (RNA multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a substantial +10.6pt improvement over single-profile (config_001, 0.485), confirming that multi-profile aggregation is the most impactful design lever found so far. However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether transformer aggregation captures inter-profile dependencies better than simple averaging, which would matter for all downstream multimodal experiments that use multi-profile. This experiment (config_003) isolates a single variable—aggregation method—against the best-performing baseline, giving a clean, interpretable comparison. It is the best use of the next budget slot because the aggregation choice propagates into every multi-profile multimodal configuration (configs 020, 021, 026, 027, etc.), so resolving it now prevents committing multiple future experiments to a suboptimal aggregation strategy.

Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile+avgpool+pca_n2000 (config_002) achieves the best score so far (acc=0.591, F1=0.573), while image-only with resnet50 (config_010) is very weak (acc=0.208). This creates a critical uncertainty: does adding the image modality via fusion actually improve over the strong RNA-only baseline, or does the weak image signal introduce noise? Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It resolves the single most impactful architectural question—whether the multimodal setting is worth pursuing at all—before investing budget in 36+ multimodal variants. Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the best at 0.619 acc, but the multimodal gain over RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_002, 0.591) is only ~3%, and image-only is very weak (0.208). Evidence: The current best config (config_019, acc=0.639) uses PCA as the RNA encoder within a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted-fusion setup. RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.591 RNA-only vs 0.208 image-only), and PCA is a simple linear baseline. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) can capture non-linear structure that PCA misses, potentially improving the multimodal representation. This experiment (config_031) isolates the RNA encoder as the sole variable—keeping multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50, and weighted fusion at their validated best settings—directly testing whether scvi_n200 outperforms PCA in the multimodal context. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it addresses the most impactful untested design axis (RNA representation quality) within the already-validated architecture, and the result will determine whether to invest further in learned encoders (scgpt) or pivot to other variables (e.g., image encoder upgrade to ViT-L).

The current best configuration (config_031, acc=0.678) uses scvi_n200 + resnet50 + multiprofile + avgpool + weighted. The image encoder choice is a major unexplored dimension with this best RNA encoder: we only have evidence that resnet50 works, and the image-only baseline (config_010) was weak (0.208), leaving uncertainty about how much the image branch contributes and whether a stronger backbone (ViT-L) could add complementary features. Config_037 makes a clean single-variable swap (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) while preserving all settings validated as beneficial (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion). This directly tests whether upgrading the image encoder can push performance beyond 0.678, and if not, confirms ResNet50 is sufficient and redirects budget toward other dimensions (e.g., scgpt or transformer aggregation). The current best (config_037: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, 0.706 acc) was reached by sequentially improving RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy, all while holding aggregation at avgpool. If transformer matches or exceeds avgpool, it opens a new optimization axis; if it underperforms (as expected from RNA-only evidence), it confirms avgpool as the optimal aggregation for multimodal fusion and closes that design dimension, freeing future budget for the remaining untested variable (scgpt RNA encoder). Under a tight budget, this is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step.

Evidence: The current best (config_039: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. Across the completed experiments, the architecture (multimodal + multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is consistently the strongest, and the RNA encoder is the one major variable still unexplored at this optimal setting (pca_n2000 → 0.639, scvi_n200 → 0.725). Question: config_051 is identical to config_039 except it swaps scvi_n200 for scgpt, giving a clean, controlled test of whether a generative single-cell foundation model (scgpt) yields a richer RNA representation than the variational autoencoder (scvi) in the best-performing architecture. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends the strongest evidence with the single remaining untested RNA encoder in the optimal configuration, maximizes the chance of finding a new best, and—if scgpt underperforms—confirms scvi_n200 as the ceiling for RNA encoding, reducing uncertainty about further RNA-side improvements. No other available configuration tests as high-value an unexplored axis under the already-validated architecture.

Evidence: RNA-only with pca_n2000/multiprofile/avgpool (config_002) achieves 0.591 acc, the best result so far, while image-only with resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208.
