Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc / 0.620 F1. Adding image (resnet50) to the validated RNA pipeline (config_002, 0.591) yielded a meaningful ~5-point gain, confirming the image modality contributes. However, the image encoder dimension is entirely unexplored beyond resnet50. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a substantially larger, higher-capacity pretrained ViT) further improve multimodal performance, or is resnet50 already near the ceiling for the image contribution? Why this is the best next experiment: config_025 changes only the image encoder while holding every other parameter at its empirically validated best setting (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion, pca_n2000). This isolates the image-encoder effect cleanly. If it improves, it identifies a clear exploitation path; if it does not, it confirms resnet50 is sufficient and redirects attention to the RNA encoder dimension. This is a high-information, low-risk extension of the current best configuration under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.591 RNA-only vs 0.208 image-only), and the current best configuration (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder. We have zero data on alternative RNA encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt), making this the largest unexplored design axis. Question: Does a learned biological embedding (scvi_n200) outperform a linear PCA projection in the multimodal setting where RNA carries most of the signal? This experiment tests scvi_n200 in the exact best-known multimodal scaffold (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding all other factors at their empirically best values. Rationale: Since RNA drives most of the predictive signal, the encoder choice is a first-order design decision. A positive result would open a high-impact improvement direction; a null or negative result would efficiently rule out that axis. This is more informative than testing transformer aggregation (already strongly disfavored by the 7-point RNA-only gap) or re-testing image encoders (near-tie between resnet50 and ViT-L).

The strongest evidence so far is that switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 in the multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/weighted setting (config_031 vs config_019) yielded a substantial +3.9 pp accuracy gain (0.678 vs 0.639), making the RNA encoder the most impactful design axis. However, we have only tested one learned encoder (scvi_n200) and cannot yet tell whether this gain is specific to scvi or a general property of learned RNA encoders. config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is a clean A/B comparison against config_031 on the single variable of RNA encoder. It will clarify whether scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, or whether scvi_n200 is uniquely suited to this task. Under a limited budget, resolving the most influential design decision (RNA encoder choice) before further exploring the image-encoder or aggregation dimensions is the highest-information next step: if scgpt is competitive, it opens an additional viable path; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and can commit remaining budget to refining the image-encoder and fusion choices around it.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.678 vs 0.639 for pca_n2000, 0.525 for scgpt), and weighted fusion with avgpool aggregation is the strongest multimodal recipe (config_031: 0.678). The image encoder choice (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) showed a negligible gap with pca_n2000 (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison was made with a weaker RNA encoder. With scvi_n200's richer latent representation, the image branch's contribution may shift, and a larger pretrained ViT could provide complementary spatial features that a CNN misses. This experiment tests whether swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l in the current best configuration yields further gains, directly exploiting the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + weighted + avgpool) while resolving the remaining uncertainty about the optimal image encoder in this regime. It is the lowest-risk, highest-information next step: if it improves, we identify the full best config; if not, we confirm resnet50 suffices and can pivot to other axes (e.g., transformer aggregation or concat fusion) with confidence.

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is establishing a performance baseline against which all other design choices can be evaluated. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration: a single modality, a single profile (no aggregation needed), and PCA—a standard, well-understood linear encoder. This experiment will (1) reveal the baseline accuracy/F1 achievable from RNA data alone with a straightforward pipeline, (2) serve as a reference floor so that subsequent experiments can quantify the incremental contribution of each design axis (image modality, learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, fusion strategy), and (3) confirm that the pipeline runs correctly before investing budget in more complex configurations. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with the cleanest possible baseline is the highest-information-value first step, as it reduces uncertainty about the entire design space simultaneously.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), leaving almost no evidence about which design axes matter most. The single highest-impact structural question is whether the image modality carries independent predictive signal. Testing config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly answers this while keeping profile_setting (singleprofile) matched to config_001 for a clean modality comparison. If image_only substantially outperforms rna_only, we know to prioritize image-centric and multimodal configs; if it performs similarly, the key lever becomes multimodal fusion; if both are poor, encoder choice becomes the critical variable. This experiment partitions the ~51-config search space most efficiently, reducing uncertainty about the dominant modality before committing budget to encoder or aggregation variants.

Evidence: With only two completed experiments, RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image-only (resnet50, singleprofile) achieves just 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality but leaving the multiprofile question entirely untested. Question: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly tests whether aggregating multiple cell profiles per sample improves over a single profile, using the simplest aggregation (average pooling) to isolate the profile-count effect from aggregation complexity. Why this is the best next experiment: The multiprofile decision is a structural axis that governs ~24 of the 51 remaining configurations. If multiprofile provides no gain over singleprofile, a large portion of the search space can be deprioritized; if it does help, it validates investing in more sophisticated aggregations (transformer) and encoders (scvi, scgpt) under the multiprofile setting. This experiment is a clean, minimal extension of config_001 (same modality, same encoder) and thus maximally informative per unit budget under the current sparse evidence.

Evidence: multiprofile with avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) substantially outperforms singleprofile (config_001, acc=0.485), confirming that multi-profile representation is a major design lever for RNA. However, we have no evidence yet about whether the aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer) matters, which is a critical architectural choice that will affect all future multimodal configurations. Question tested: Does a transformer-based aggregation of multiple profiles yield meaningfully better performance than simple average pooling, holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (multiprofile) constant? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of our current best result, so any performance difference is directly attributable to the aggregation method. Resolving this question before scaling to multimodal or alternative encoders ensures we build subsequent experiments on the correct aggregation backbone, maximizing information gained per experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with multi-profile + avgpool + PCA n2000 (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest configuration so far, and image-only ResNet50 single-profile (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak. The central unresolved question is whether combining the strong RNA signal with image features in a multimodal setting can surpass the best RNA-only result. Question tested: Does concatenating ResNet50 image features with the proven-best RNA multi-profile/avgpool setup (config_002) yield a meaningful accuracy gain over 0.591, or does the weak image signal fail to contribute? Why this is the best next experiment: It is the direct multimodal extension of our strongest unimodal result, directly addresses the study's core hypothesis (multimodal > unimodal), and the outcome will sharply reduce uncertainty for the entire remaining multimodal branch—either confirming a promising fusion direction to exploit or indicating that image features are uninformative here, allowing us to focus budget on RNA encoder and aggregation choices.

Evidence: The current best (config_018, acc=0.619) uses resnet50 as the image encoder, but image-only resnet50 (config_010) achieved only 0.208 accuracy, suggesting very weak image signal. The multimodal boost over RNA-only (0.619 vs 0.591) is modest, likely because resnet50 provides limited complementary information. Question: Does a stronger, ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L encoder yield a substantially richer image representation that, when fused with the multiprofile avgpool RNA signal, produces a larger multimodal gain? This is a clean single-variable change (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) from the current best, keeping all other settings (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat) at their validated-optimal values. Why best next: The image encoder is the largest unexplored source of variance in the multimodal pipeline. If ViT-L substantially improves the image contribution, it unlocks a high-performing multimodal regime and guides all subsequent fusion/aggregation choices. If it does not, we learn that image modality has limited value regardless of encoder, letting us redirect budget toward RNA encoder alternatives (scvi, scgpt) or fusion refinements. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design axis.

Evidence: The top-performing configs (018, 024) both use pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, but no learned RNA representation (scVI, scGPT) has been tested yet. Multiprofile + avgpool + multimodal + concat is strongly supported (0.619–0.629 acc), and the image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) shows only a small, ambiguous difference. Uncertainty: Whether a biologically-informed learned RNA encoder (scVI) meaningfully outperforms PCA in the multimodal setting is the largest untested design lever. This experiment (config_030: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) isolates the RNA encoder change within the best-supported multimodal architecture. If scVI improves over PCA, it opens a high-impact direction; if not, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can redirect budget to fusion strategy or other variables. This is the highest-information experiment because the RNA encoder governs the representation of the dominant modality, and no evidence exists yet to guide that choice.

Evidence: (1) SCVI outperforms PCA in multimodal (config_030: 0.632 vs config_018: 0.619), and (2) VIT-L outperforms ResNet50 in multimodal (config_024: 0.629 vs config_018: 0.619). However, the combination SCVI+VIT-L has not been tested. Question: Are the individual encoder improvements additive, or does one encoder's gain subsume the other's? This experiment (config_036: SCVI + VIT-L + avgpool + concat, multiprofile) directly tests whether combining the best RNA encoder with the best image encoder yields a new best, while keeping all other variables (multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at their proven-optimal settings. It is the highest-value exploitation step: it has the strongest prior for high performance, and a negative result would reveal diminishing returns or redundancy between the two encoders—valuable information under a tight budget.

Evidence: The strongest result so far is config_036 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 acc / 0.687 F1, a substantial jump over all prior configs. This establishes that scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool is a clearly superior combination. The only untested design dimension within this best-performing setting is the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted). Question: Does weighted fusion improve upon simple concatenation when both modalities are already well-encoded? This is a minimal, targeted change to the current best, isolating the fusion mechanism as the sole variable. Rationale: Under a limited budget, exploiting the strongest evidence with a single-variable perturbation is the highest-information-per-experiment choice. If weighted fusion helps, we immediately identify a path above 0.715; if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect exploration to the next most uncertain dimension (e.g., scgpt encoder or transformer aggregation) without having wasted a run on a less-informative comparison.

The current best configuration (config_036: scvi_n200 + vit_l + avgpool + concat, 0.715 acc) establishes a strong baseline, but the RNA encoder axis remains critically under-explored: we have only tested pca_n2000 and scvi_n200, with zero evidence on scgpt. Config_048 (scgpt + vit_l + avgpool + concat, multiprofile) is a direct, single-variable comparison against config_036, isolating the effect of the RNA encoder in the most favorable multimodal setting. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the superior encoder and lets us focus remaining budget on aggregation/fusion refinements. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-uncertainty design axis is more informative than testing a second-order change (e.g., transformer aggregation, which prior RNA-only evidence suggests is inferior to avgpool).

With no completed experiments, the primary uncertainty is the baseline performance of the simplest RNA-only setup, which anchors all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal configuration: it uses PCA (a standard, fast, well-understood encoder) with a single profile, introducing no learned encoders, no aggregation, and no fusion. This establishes (1) the floor performance for the RNA modality, (2) a reference for the singleprofile setting, and (3) a known value for PCA_n2000, which is the RNA encoder shared by configs 016–027 in the multimodal space. By starting here, every later experiment—whether adding a better RNA encoder, switching to multiprofile, or introducing an image modality—can be interpreted as a controlled increment over a clear, simple baseline. Under a limited budget, this single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the fundamental signal available in the data before committing to more complex (and costlier) configurations.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), which gives a weak RNA-only baseline and tells us nothing about whether the image modality carries useful signal. This is a multimodal cellular profiling study, so the single most consequential design question is whether the image branch contributes any predictive value at all. Question tested: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides a clean unimodal image baseline using a standard, well-established backbone, directly comparable in structure to config_001. Why it is the best next experiment: (1) If image accuracy is substantially higher than 0.485, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies investing subsequent experiments in fusion strategies; if it is similarly low, it suggests the image modality may not be informative and we should focus budget on RNA encoder and profile improvements. (2) It partitions the remaining 50 untested configs into two strategic branches (image-useful vs. image-not-useful), dramatically reducing search-space uncertainty with a single run. (3) resnet50 is a reasonable, fast-to-train first probe before committing to the heavier ViT-L variants. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the overall architecture under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image-only, singleprofile, resnet50) achieves only 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality with a large gap. The key uncertainty now is whether the profile setting (single vs. multi) and aggregation strategy can improve RNA performance, which is the foundational design choice for all subsequent multimodal experiments. This experiment (config_002: RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly tests whether aggregating multiple cell profiles via average pooling improves over the single-profile baseline, while holding the encoder constant. It is the minimal, cleanest extension of config_001, isolating the multiprofile+aggregation variable. If it helps, it validates the multiprofile direction and informs all multimodal configs; if it does not, it prunes a large portion of the search space (all multiprofile variants) under a limited budget. Choosing avgpool over transformer first is conservative: it tests whether any aggregation benefit exists before committing to a more complex aggregator.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a substantial +10.6% gain over config_001 (single-profile, 0.485), confirming that multi-profile aggregation is a high-impact design choice. However, we only have one data point on aggregation method (avgpool). Uncertainty: It is unclear whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) further improves over simple averaging, which would change the aggregation choice for all downstream multimodal experiments. This experiment (config_003) isolates exactly one variable—aggregation method (transformer vs avgpool)—while holding RNA encoder (PCA n2000), profile setting (multi), and modality (RNA-only) constant, making it a clean A/B comparison with config_002. If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it signals that learned aggregation is worth pursuing across encoders and modalities; if it is comparable, avgpool is sufficient and budget is better spent exploring encoder choice or multimodal fusion. Under a limited budget, resolving this binary design question with a controlled comparison is more informative than jumping to a less certain multimodal or new-encoder configuration.

Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile+avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the clear best so far, while image-only is very weak (config_010, acc=0.208). We also know avgpool > transformer for aggregation. The critical open question is whether the image modality provides any complementary signal when combined with the strong RNA features, which is the central premise of this multimodal study. Config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the most direct logical extension of our best result: it keeps the proven RNA setup (multiprofile + avgpool + pca_n2000) and adds the image branch with the simplest standard fusion (concat). If it beats 0.591, multimodal fusion is validated and we can explore weighted fusion and better image encoders; if it does not, we learn that image adds no value and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi/scgpt). This single experiment resolves the highest-uncertainty design decision under the limited budget.

Evidence: Our best result (config_018, acc=0.619) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder in a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, concat setup. All completed experiments have used only PCA as the RNA encoder, leaving the learned-encoder dimension (scvi_n200, scgpt) completely unexplored. Question: config_030 is a clean single-variable change from config_018, swapping pca_n2000 → scvi_n200 while holding multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, and concat fixed. This directly tests whether a nonlinear, biologically-informed learned encoder outperforms linear PCA in the multimodal fusion context. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is a fundamental architectural choice with potentially large upside—if scvi captures richer cell-type structure than PCA, the gain would transfer to all downstream multimodal configurations. Conversely, if it does not improve over PCA, we can confidently rule out learned encoders and concentrate remaining budget on image-encoder and fusion-strategy variations. Compared to testing weighted fusion (config_019), which is a more incremental change with likely smaller effect size, the encoder choice carries higher information value per experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieves acc=0.632/F1=0.607, and all multimodal results so far use concat fusion. The fusion strategy is a critical, completely untested design axis in the multimodal setting where two modalities of potentially different informativeness (RNA >> image) are combined. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation when combining a strong RNA signal with a weaker image signal? config_031 changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) relative to config_030, providing a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the current best configuration while resolving the single largest untested design decision in the multimodal pipeline. If weighted fusion helps, it indicates the modalities contribute unequally and a learned or fixed weighting is beneficial; if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., image encoder choice or scgpt). This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.678). The largest single improvement came from switching concat→weighted fusion (+4.6%), and SCVI gave a modest boost over PCA. The one major untested axis in the current best is the image encoder: we have only used resnet50, which alone scored a very weak 0.208. Config_037 changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l (a substantially larger, pretrained ViT), keeping the otherwise-best settings (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted). This directly tests whether a stronger image encoder can extract more informative morphological features that complement the RNA signal under weighted fusion. If it improves, it justifies further investment in the image branch; if it does not, it confirms the image modality's marginal contribution is encoder-limited and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-side or fusion refinements. This is a clean single-variable extension of the current best, making it the highest-information next experiment under a tight budget.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.706) establishes that multimodal with multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion, and a strong image encoder is the dominant design. The remaining untested variable in this top region is the RNA encoder: we've seen pca_n2000 → scvi_n200 yield a modest gain (~1.3%), but scgpt has never been tested. Config_049 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) directly swaps only the RNA encoder in the best-known setup, giving a clean comparison against config_037. This is the highest-value experiment because it (1) exploits the strongest known configuration, (2) tests whether the RNA encoder is still a performance bottleneck or whether scvi_n200 is near-saturated, and (3) if scgpt outperforms, it opens a new optimization axis; if not, it confirms scvi_n200 is sufficient and redirects budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., transformer aggregation with vit_l). Under a limited budget, this single experiment resolves the most consequential remaining uncertainty about the top-performing region.

The current best config (config_037: scvi_n200, vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.706 acc. The strongest evidence from RNA-only experiments shows avgpool (0.591) substantially outperforms transformer (0.519) aggregation, but this has not been confirmed in the multimodal regime with the top-performing encoders. Config_039 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other variables at their best-known values (scvi_n200, vit_l, multiprofile, weighted). This single-variable test will clarify whether the avgpool advantage persists with a stronger image encoder and weighted fusion, or whether transformer aggregation becomes competitive in the multimodal setting. If transformer underperforms (as expected), it confirms avgpool as the correct choice and directs remaining budget toward other unexplored axes. If transformer is competitive or better, it opens a new optimization direction. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves a key architectural uncertainty at the top of the performance landscape with a clean, interpretable comparison.

With zero completed experiments, there is no evidence to guide exploitation; the priority is to establish a clear, interpretable performance baseline that anchors all future comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: it uses a deterministic, parameter-free RNA encoder (PCA), a single profile (no aggregation complexity), and no image pipeline. This minimizes confounding factors and running time while giving us the 'floor' performance of the RNA modality. Knowing this baseline is essential before interpreting any multimodal or learned-encoder result: without it, we cannot determine whether a multimodal configuration's accuracy reflects genuine cross-modal synergy or simply the contribution of one modality. It also calibrates how much headroom exists for the other design axes (profile setting, encoder choice, image modality, fusion strategy), making every subsequent experiment more informative under the limited budget.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001, rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000) with a low baseline accuracy of 0.485 and F1 of 0.464, leaving substantial uncertainty about which modality and design choices drive performance. Question: Does the image modality alone carry meaningful predictive signal for cellular profiling? config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is structurally parallel to config_001 (singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion), making it a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the modality effect. Why best next step: Before committing budget to multimodal fusion or more complex encoders, establishing the image-only ceiling is the highest-information experiment. If image_only substantially outperforms or underperforms RNA-only, it immediately informs whether multimodal fusion is worthwhile, which image encoder to prioritize, and whether the RNA or image branch needs more attention. This reduces the most fundamental uncertainty with a single experiment, making every subsequent multimodal result interpretable.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image-only with ResNet50 (config_010) is very weak at 20.8%, confirming RNA is the dominant modality. However, we have only tested singleprofile for RNA, leaving the single-vs-multiprofile axis completely unexplored. This is a fundamental design choice that gates half the search space (all multiprofile and multimodal configurations). Config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the cleanest possible test: it changes only the profile setting and adds the simplest aggregation (avgpool) relative to config_001, isolating the effect of multiple profiles. If multiprofile+avgpool improves over 48.5%, it validates the multiprofile axis and motivates testing transformer aggregation (config_003) and multimodal extensions. If it does not improve, we can deprioritize all multiprofile configurations and focus budget on RNA encoder variation (scvi, scgpt) or image encoder upgrades. Under a tight budget, resolving this binary design question on the strongest modality with the simplest change maximizes information gain per experiment.

Evidence: config_002 (multiprofile + avgpool, pca_n2000) achieved 0.591 acc, a +0.106 jump over singleprofile (config_001, 0.485), confirming that multi-profile representation is the dominant design lever. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), so the RNA pathway is where gains will come from. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for combining multiple profiles—this is a critical axis because it will also govern all multimodal fusion experiments. What this tests: config_003 isolates exactly one variable (aggregation: transformer vs. avgpool) while holding everything else at the best-known RNA settings (multiprofile, pca_n2000). Why it is the best next use of budget: it is a minimal, controlled comparison against the current best (config_002), so any performance difference is cleanly attributable to the aggregation method. The result directly informs whether transformer aggregation is worth the added complexity in every subsequent multimodal configuration, making it high-information-value under a limited experiment budget.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208). Multiprofile + avgpool clearly outperforms singleprofile and transformer aggregation. Question: Does adding image features via concatenation to the best RNA-only setup improve performance, or does the weak image signal (resnet50 alone = 0.208) degrade the strong RNA signal? Why this experiment: config_018 is the most controlled multimodal test—it holds the RNA side identical to config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only resnet50 image features with simple concat fusion. This directly isolates the marginal contribution of image features. If it beats 0.591, fusion is promising and we can explore stronger image encoders and weighted fusion; if it underperforms, we learn that resnet50 features are too weak to contribute, redirecting effort toward ViT-L or alternative fusion. This is the highest-information next step under budget constraints because it answers the fundamental 'does multimodal help?' question with minimal confounding variables.

Evidence: Multi-profile with avgpool aggregation is clearly superior (config_002: 0.591 vs config_003: 0.519), and adding ResNet50 image features via concat fusion yielded our best result (config_018: 0.619 vs RNA-only config_002: 0.591). However, image-only ResNet50 was very weak (config_010: 0.208), raising the question of whether the modest 3-point multimodal gain is limited by the image encoder quality. Question: Does a stronger, ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L encoder unlock substantially more signal from the image modality in the multimodal setting? Why this is the best next experiment: It directly extends our best configuration (multimodal, multi-profile, avgpool, concat) along the most impactful untested axis—image encoder capacity. A large gain would confirm the image modality has real complementary signal and justify further image-encoder investment; a small gain would indicate the image contribution is inherently limited, redirecting effort toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi/scgpt). This single experiment resolves a critical design uncertainty that would shape all subsequent choices.

Evidence: The best-performing config so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) with acc=0.629. All completed multimodal experiments used concat fusion; weighted fusion has not yet been tested. The fusion method is a critical design decision that directly governs how RNA and image representations are combined, and its effect is currently unknown. Question: Does weighted fusion (which allows the model to learn modality-specific importance) improve over simple concatenation in the best-performing architecture? Why this is the best next experiment: config_025 is a single-variable change from the current best (only fusion: concat→weighted), making it a clean, high-information exploitation step. A positive result would immediately identify a new best config and confirm fusion as a tunable lever; a null result would confirm concat is sufficient and redirect remaining budget toward other unexplored dimensions (e.g., RNA encoder choice). Under a limited budget, testing the most promising unexplored knob on the known-best backbone is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

Evidence: The current best (config_025, acc=0.635) uses PCA_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all completed experiments share this encoder. We have zero evidence about whether a learned encoder (SCVI) could improve on PCA in the multimodal pipeline. The other design axes (profile=multiprofile, aggregation=avgpool, image=ViT-L, fusion=weighted) are well-supported by the data. Question: config_037 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to SCVI_n200 while holding every other parameter at its best-known value, directly testing whether a deep generative RNA representation outperforms linear PCA in the multimodal fusion context. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is the single largest unexplored design dimension, and its impact could be comparable to or exceed the profile-setting effect (~10%). Testing it in the strongest known configuration (rather than in a weaker RNA-only setting) gives the most decision-relevant information: if SCVI matches or beats PCA here, it opens a high-value branch; if it underperforms, we efficiently rule out that direction and consolidate on PCA. This maximizes information gain per limited experiment.

The strongest evidence so far is that switching the RNA encoder from PCA to SCVI in the best multimodal setup (ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) yielded the largest single improvement (0.635→0.706 acc, config_025→config_037). However, the SCGI encoder is completely untested across all experiments. Config_049 (scgpt + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted) is the direct counterpart to config_037, isolating the RNA encoder choice while holding all other design decisions at their best-performing values. This experiment will clarify whether SCGI offers a comparable or superior representation to SCVI in the multimodal setting. If SCGI matches or exceeds SCVI, it opens a new optimization direction; if it underperforms, it confirms SCVI as the preferred encoder and allows us to focus remaining budget on aggregation/fusion refinements around SCVI. Under a limited budget, testing the single largest unexplored variable in the top-performing configuration is the highest-information next step.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) achieves 0.7062 accuracy. The only prior evidence on fusion method comes from pca_n2000, where weighted (0.6352) narrowly beat concat (0.6287) by ~0.007. However, scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different (nonlinear, learned) representation than linear PCA, so the optimal fusion strategy may shift. Config_036 is a minimal single-variable ablation of the best config (changing only weighted→concat), directly testing whether the small fusion-method gap observed with pca_n2000 persists or reverses with scvi_n200. If concat performs comparably, fusion method is not a critical design axis and remaining budget can target higher-impact choices (e.g., aggregation method with scvi_n200). If weighted clearly wins, it confirms the current design and reduces uncertainty about the remaining search space. Under a tight budget, this clean ablation of the top configuration is the most efficient way to either confirm or challenge a key design decision before committing further experiments.

With no prior experiments, there is complete uncertainty about the performance landscape. The most informative first step is to establish a simple, well-understood baseline: RNA-only with the simplest encoder (PCA, 2000 components) and singleprofile (no aggregation or fusion decisions needed). This experiment tests the fundamental question of how much signal a basic RNA representation carries for the classification task. It serves as a reference floor against which all subsequent experiments—multiprofile aggregation, learned RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), image-only, and multimodal fusion—can be meaningfully compared. Choosing the minimal configuration first avoids conflating multiple design variables and ensures that any future gains are attributable to specific architectural choices rather than an already-complex baseline.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides meaningful signal in this multimodal cellular profiling task. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) is the cleanest A/B comparison to config_001: it holds the RNA encoder and profile setting constant while introducing the image modality with a standard encoder and the simplest fusion strategy. If accuracy improves substantially, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies further exploration of encoders, aggregation, and fusion. If it does not, it redirects the budget toward improving the RNA-only pipeline (better encoders, multiprofile). This single experiment resolves the most consequential design question in the study and is the highest-information use of the next limited budget slot.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat, singleprofile) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a clear +4.2% improvement over rna_only baseline (config_001: 0.485/0.464), establishing that the multimodal concat pipeline is the current best direction. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) meaningfully affects performance, and this is a critical design choice that will propagate to all future multimodal experiments. What this tests: config_017 is identical to config_016 except fusion=weighted, giving a clean single-variable A/B comparison of fusion strategies with the same encoders and profile setting. Why it is the best next step: with only two experiments completed, we should first lock down the best fusion strategy within the already-promising multimodal + pca_n2000 + resnet50 region before branching to other axes (multiprofile, alternative encoders). The result will be unambiguous—either weighted improves on concat (a direct gain) or concat is confirmed as the better choice—reducing uncertainty about a decision that affects every subsequent multimodal configuration. This is a low-risk, high-information exploitation step that maximizes the value of the next experiment under a tight budget.

Evidence: Adding the image modality (resnet50) to the RNA-only baseline improved accuracy by ~4.2% (0.485→0.527), confirming multimodal fusion is beneficial. The concat vs weighted fusion difference is negligible (~0.3%), so fusion method is not the key lever. The largest untested architectural dimension is profile representation: all three completed experiments use singleprofile, yet multiprofile with aggregation could capture richer cellular state information. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) in the multimodal setting improve over the singleprofile baseline, while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat) constant at the values from our best result (config_016)? Why this is the best next experiment: It isolates the effect of multiprofile+aggregation as the only changed variable relative to config_016, making the comparison clean and informative. Avgpool is a conservative, low-overfitting-risk aggregation that tests whether the multiprofile signal is present at all before committing to a more complex transformer aggregation. If multiprofile helps, we then know to invest in better aggregation; if it doesn't, we save budget by avoiding transformer experiments. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

The strongest signal so far is that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (config_018, acc=0.6186) dramatically outperforms singleprofile (config_016, acc=0.5266), a +9.2% jump. The fusion method (concat vs weighted) showed negligible difference in singleprofile (~0.3%), so that axis is low priority. The key remaining uncertainty within the multiprofile setting is whether the aggregation method matters: does simple average pooling suffice, or can a transformer learn profile-level interactions that further improve performance? config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other variables constant (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat), making it a clean single-variable test that directly extends the best-performing configuration. If transformer aggregation helps, it opens a high-impact architectural direction; if not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward the image encoder (ViT-L) or RNA encoder axes. This is the highest-information next step under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc. Key learnings: (1) multimodal >> rna_only, (2) multiprofile >> singleprofile (largest single gain), (3) avgpool > transformer for aggregation, (4) concat ≈ weighted for fusion. The two major untested dimensions in the best config are the image encoder (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) and the RNA encoder (pca vs learned). Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to a much larger ViT-L improve performance in the already-optimized multiprofile+avgpool+concat setup? Why this is the best next experiment: The image modality has been the single largest source of improvement (multimodal vs rna_only), and ViT-L represents a substantial capacity jump over ResNet50. Testing it in the known-best configuration isolates the image encoder variable cleanly. If it helps, we've identified a new promising axis; if not, we rule out image encoder quality as a bottleneck and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder choices (scvi/scgpt) with greater confidence.

Evidence: The current best (config_024, acc=0.629) uses PCA for RNA encoding, and all multimodal experiments to date have used pca_n2000. The RNA encoder is the largest unexplored design dimension—PCA is a linear projection while scvi_n200 is a learned nonlinear representation that may capture biological structure better. Aggregation (avgpool > transformer) and fusion (concat ≈ weighted) are relatively well-characterized. Question: Does replacing PCA with a learned scvi encoder improve performance in the established best multimodal setup (multiprofile, avgpool, concat)? This experiment (config_030) is a clean one-variable comparison against config_018 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat, acc=0.619), isolating the RNA encoder effect. Why this is the best next step: It addresses the highest-uncertainty design choice with a direct A/B comparison, uses the well-validated ResNet50 backbone to avoid confounding with the ViT-L/F1 discrepancy seen in config_024, and if scvi helps, it opens a clear path to config_036 (scvi + ViT-L) as a follow-up; if it does not help, we save a more expensive ViT-L experiment and can pivot to other dimensions.

Evidence: The top three configurations (config_030: scvi_n200+resnet50=0.632, config_024: pca_n2000+vit_l=0.629, config_018: pca_n2000+resnet50=0.619) all share multiprofile + avgpool + concat, confirming these as the best design choices. Two small but consistent improvements are observed: scvi_n200 over pca_n2000 (+0.013) and imagenet_vit_l over resnet50 (+0.010). Question: config_036 tests whether these two encoder improvements are additive by combining scvi_n200 with imagenet_vit_l under the already-validated avgpool+concat setting. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the most direct exploitation of the strongest evidence, has the highest expected performance among untested configs, and if the gains are additive it identifies a clear winner; if they are not, it reveals a negative interaction that would redirect remaining budget toward exploring scgpt or other untested axes.

The current best (config_036: SCVI + ViT-L + multiprofile + avgpool + concat, acc 0.715) establishes that a learned RNA encoder (SCVI) combined with a strong image encoder (ViT-L) is the dominant design choice. However, SCGPT—a generative single-cell model that may capture different biological structure than SCVI—has not been tested in any experiment. Config_048 isolates this single variable (SCGPT vs SCVI) while holding all other settings at their proven-best values (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), making it directly comparable to config_036. This is the highest-information next step: if SCGPT outperforms SCVI, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms SCVI as the optimal RNA encoder and lets us redirect effort toward aggregation or fusion refinements. Under a limited budget, resolving this untested encoder dimension is more valuable than testing a second-order variable (e.g., transformer vs avgpool) where existing evidence already favors avgpool.

The strongest evidence points to scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + avgpool as the dominant configuration (config_036: 0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1). The only untested design dimension within this top-performing setting is the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted). The sole prior fusion comparison (config_016 vs 017) showed a negligible difference (~0.3% acc) in a much weaker singleprofile/pca_n2000/resnet50 context, so the evidence is sparse and the question is unresolved for strong multimodal settings where both modality representations are rich. Config_037 isolates this single variable (weighted fusion) while holding all other components at their best-evidenced values, making it a clean, low-risk exploitation step that either yields a free improvement or confirms concat sufficiency—maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.
